---
title: "4. Metaphysical Rivals"
---

With the positive argument in place, the chapter turns to rival accounts, each taken up in its most demanding form rather than its most convenient one. The question put to every rival is the same: does it actually eliminate T, S, and Φ — Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality, borne by Time, Space, and Substance — or does it only redescribe them?

At the limit, a rival can make one of three moves. It can *deny* the structural conditions, holding that they do not obtain. It can *ground them prior*, granting that they obtain but locating them downstream of something more fundamental. Or it can grant the conditions while charging them with *insufficiency*: T, S, and Φ obtain, but do not exhaust what Reality contains. The chapter follows each position to where it actually leads.

What is at stake is whether the derivation survives contact with the live literature — so no deflationary program is dismissed as unserious, and no classical-theist position is treated as unavailable. The standard is the strongest version currently on offer; where a rival has a stronger form, known or yet to come, the argument is answerable to it, not exempt from it.

Four directions organize the engagement: modal and semantic foundations ([§4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1)), time and change ([§4.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2)), physics and mind ([§4.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3)), and modal variants ([§4.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4)). The same question is put to each, and [§4.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-5) draws together what the pattern across them reveals.

The chapter inherits the formal framework secured in Chapter 2, but it does not treat every rival as answering to one uniform reply. Some engagements test the fixed global domain of real possibility and the modal semantics that follow from it ([§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)). Some test whether a rival realizes only a thin abstract analogue of directed order, difference, or bearing, or realizes the fuller types required by genuine change. Others accept the structure and test whether it is rich enough. The verdict in each section therefore tracks the rival's actual burden: incoherence, relocation, compatibility, explanatory cost, or an open seam.

## 4.1 Modal and Semantic Foundations {#sec-4-1}

This first cluster gathers attempts to ground, deflate, or bypass the argument's modal and structural claims: accounts that would explain modal talk away, that would relocate Time, Space, and Substance to a simulated or solipsistic substrate, or that would derive them from something more fundamental still, sufficient reason, Humean succession, or information. These positions differ, but they share one aim: to account for change and its structural conditions without appeal to the structure the argument derives. One entry shares no such aim: Pizzi's impossibility of nothingness ([§4.1.11](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-11)), the literature's nearest convergence — the same closure of modal space against ∅, reached by kindred machinery and stopping short of naming the necessary content. Three further entries close the cluster on the modal side proper. Dispositionalism about modality ([§4.1.12](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-12)) grounds possibility in the potentialities of actual objects rather than in a plurality of worlds, and is the account nearest to this one. Modal epistemology ([§4.1.13](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-13)) grants the vocabulary and ordinary modal knowledge alike, and challenges the reliability of the modal faculty at the distances this argument works at. Impossible worlds and relative modality ([§4.1.14](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-14)) ask whether the quantifier in □(T∧S∧Φ) ranges over everything, or over a domain that could be widened by admitting impossible worlds or narrowed by a contextual modal base.

The question is whether any of them can describe a reality in which Time, Space, and Substance are absent. The reply is that none can. A simulation still needs a host that really changes; a solipsistic mind still runs on succession and distinction; a deflationary theory still needs the structure it redescribes. The challenge bears most directly on §[§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)–2.6 and the Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6): change-possibility and the joint obtaining of T, S, and Φ are one fact stated from two sides.

A preliminary note before the named engagements. The objection that everything we take to be reality might be a simulation (that what we take to be physical succession, extension, and persistence could be virtual artifacts of a deeper computational substrate) does not escape structure. It relocates it. Any host system capable of hosting simulated succession must itself instantiate genuine succession; any host system capable of hosting simulated extension must itself instantiate relational extension: distinct positions standing in a traversable interval (the thin, structural S of [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7)), not necessarily a metric manifold of any particular geometry; any host system capable of hosting simulated persistence must itself persist. What the relocation secures is the structural role at each level (succession, traversable distinctness, persistence), not the contingent metric character (a particular spacetime or geometry), which is physical content established downstream ([§7.3](nature-alone.html#sec-7-3)).

The same diagnosis applies to hard solipsism: a solipsistic mind whose experience exhibits succession, distinction, and exchange is itself a configuration within T, S, and Φ. The question of whether anything else exists does not affect the necessity of T, S, and Φ. Both retreats relocate structure; they do not remove it.

A second preliminary note concerns alethic and doxastic modality. The engagements throughout this chapter operate in alethic modality, what holds across possible worlds independently of what any mind conceives or believes. Oppy [-@oppy1995; -@oppy2006; -@oppy2013] argues that conceivability-to-possibility inferences are unreliable because conceivability tracks cognitive limitations rather than modal facts, and expresses agnosticism about whether broadly logical and metaphysical modality are genuinely distinct. Both points are well-taken against arguments that derive alethic modal claims from doxastic premises. The argument of this book does not make that move. Its modal claims are grounded in actuality: change, reading, and conceiving are actually occurring, and the actuality-to-possibility inference, every actual fact is possible ([§1.2](groundwork.html#sec-1-2), the Actuality definition), is logically valid. Alethic modality is prior to doxastic modality because doxastic states presuppose it: a belief that P is a belief that P is true, truth conditions are alethic, and the very existence of a cognizer capable of doxastic states is itself an alethic fact. Oppy's agnosticism about the broadly logical/metaphysical distinction is not dissolved merely by the Condition-Individuation Criterion ([§2.6.11](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-11)). As [§2.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-10) now states, distinguishing the temporal, spatial, and physical subject matters does not by itself derive three separate consequence relations. The book proposes three formally differentiated disciplines or readings, but whether broadly logical and metaphysical modality are distinct remains a substantive semantic question rather than something the criterion settles by itself.

### 4.1.1 Rigid Designation {#sec-4-1-1}

The Kripkean challenge is a wedge any argument for necessary existence has to clear. The move separates necessary co-extension (two terms picking out the same set of things in every possible world) from necessary identity (two terms picking out the very same thing as a matter of what it is), and presses that the argument has established only the former. Wherever change is possible, T, S, and Φ are correctly described as its preconditions; but this is a truth about how we specify what change requires, not a truth about what must exist. The replies that follow grant Kripke's narrower point (necessary co-extension does not by itself establish identity, and many necessary-existence arguments fail by conflating the two) and contest a different one. In this case the two descriptions pick out one fact, and [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) discharges the burden of showing it, especially the Modal Identity at [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) and the Triconditional Identity at [§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10).

Necessarily, if something is water, it is H₂O. But water itself might not have existed: on another planet, or in a world with slightly different chemistry, there could have been no water at all. The necessity belongs to the identity of water with H₂O; it does not secure that water exists in every possible world. @kripke1980 [Lecture I] draws the distinction: some necessities are de dicto, holding of the description, while others are de re, holding of the thing. @putnam1975 presses the same point with Twin Earth: the same words can pick out different substances in different worlds. Necessity lives in reference, not in existence.

The distinction has force because it exposes a pattern common to arguments that appear to prove necessary existence. An ontological argument that moves from conceivability to necessary existence needs more than rigid designation: it needs a justified possibility premise and a valid modal bridge. Kripke's analysis does not itself collapse such arguments; rigid designation can instead help state their de re conclusion. The live question is whether the argument has earned the relevant possibility and existence claims. A Leibnizian cosmological argument moves from 'something exists' to 'a necessary being explains it,' but the necessity attaches to the explanation, not to the being explained. Kripke's wedge has closed more arguments than it has opened; the question is whether it closes this one.

The challenge bears directly on [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6). If the necessity is hollow (a consequence of how 'change' is defined rather than a modal fact), the argument collapses into conditional necessity and the classical theist regains room for a changeless necessary being outside structure. The claim of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is narrower: that change-possibility and T ∧ S ∧ Φ are not two correlated facts that march together across worlds but one structural fact disclosed from two directions. Three forms of the move take up the objection.

*First.* The sparse-world move does not require a fully empty world, only one in which T, S, and Φ are present by description without being metaphysically robust. Call it w′, stipulated here as a test-case for the conditional in the manner of Kripke's Lecture I naming conventions, though the dichotomy that follows holds equally if w′ is surveyed as an independently real Lewisian world. In w′, the descriptions apply, but what they pick out is thin: no causally structured succession, no relational extension, no causal persistence, only the verbal placeholders. The argument's necessity then reduces to a truth about descriptions, not about what worlds contain.

The move faces a dichotomy it cannot survive. Either (i) w′ contains some metaphysical content beyond the descriptions, or (ii) it contains none. If (ii), w′ is ∅, foreclosed by [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7): a description without a world to describe is not a description at all but a string of words with no being. If (i), the remaining content either suffices for change or it does not. If it suffices, T, S, and Φ obtain in their operative sense after all and w′ is not sparse in the relevant way. If it does not, there is no change in w′, and the world is not a counterexample to the conditional but a witness to its antecedent failing. There is no third reading on which w′ contains metaphysical content while failing to instantiate the operative sense of the conditions, because the operative sense *is* what structural content *consists in*.

*Second.* Exempting the preconditions from S5 grants the ∅ result but restricts S5's reach. The refinement concedes that T, S, and Φ obtain in every change-permitting world but denies that S5 licenses the further step to their obtaining in every world *simpliciter*. S5 governs inferences within the space of possibilities; it does not settle the status of that space itself. So the modal behavior of the preconditions can be governed by S5 while S5 still fails to bridge the conditional.

The refinement sharpens the problem rather than loosening it. There may be worlds without actual change that are nevertheless structured and distinct from ∅; a frozen or silent world is the obvious test case. Section 2.7 rules out absolute structural absence, not every world in which change fails to occur. The Kripkean therefore is not forced into a simple change-or-∅ dichotomy. To close the exemption move, the argument needs the separate claim that every possible world retains the capacities or role-structure required for change, and the role-to-type bridge must not be assumed in stating that claim. The local retorsion does not supply this cross-world result; it is supplied independently by the role-level convergence of §[§3.2](convergence.html#sec-3-2)–3.3, which earns structure in every possible world at role-resolution, with the role-to-type bridge earned at [§3.5.3](convergence.html#sec-3-5-3) rather than assumed.

*Third.* The rejection of the Modal Identity is the form of the objection that goes deepest: it grants the prior replies but denies the underlying identity of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6). Necessary co-extension is not identity (Kripke himself distinguishes necessary identity, water = H₂O, from mere necessary biconditionals) and so the possibility of change and the instantiation of T, S, and Φ may be necessarily co-extensive without being one fact. Fine's [-@fine1994] distinction between essence and necessity cuts the same way: Socrates and {Socrates} are necessarily co-present without the singleton being part of Socrates's essence. The wedge would hold, and the structural conditions would be necessarily co-present with change-possibility without being what change-possibility essentially consists in.

Fine's point reinforces rather than undermines the argument. The distinction between necessary biconditional and necessary identity is genuine, and Kripke is right to insist on it; but it cuts against the objector here. A necessary biconditional between two distinct facts is established by the world: the world just happens to be such that whenever one obtains, the other does. A necessary identity between two descriptions of one fact is established by examining the descriptions themselves: they are revealed — empirically in Kripke's case, by analysis here — to pick out the same thing. Kripke's water/H₂O case is the second kind. The Modal Identity of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is of this second kind, not the first.

This is shown at [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) by analyzing what change consists in: a succession (Time) of states (Substance) across a structured interval (Space). The analysis does not establish a biconditional between change-possibility and T ∧ S ∧ Φ; it shows that the right-hand side *is* what the left-hand side *is*, spelled out. By Fine's lights, the argument's claim is an essence claim: T, S, and Φ *are* what change essentially *is*, not merely what change necessarily entails. Kripke's wedge works only where the description and the substance are logically independent, where 'water' and 'H₂O' could, in principle, have picked out different things. The structural conditions are not like that.

One point is still owed to the objector who wants more than assertion for why the analytic reading beats the discovered-identity reading. The water/H₂O case supports a genuine two-description gap because the Twin Earth scenario that exhibits it is set up using ordinary space, time, and chemistry, and only then asks which of two candidate substances a surface concept picks out; the scenario does not itself presuppose water or H₂O. No parallel scenario is available here. To construct a world in which 'causally structured succession' turns out, on investigation, to pick out something other than Time, the construction needs a succession across which the investigation unfolds, a distinction between the surface concept and the candidate referent under examination, and a persisting investigator to carry the inquiry from setup to verdict. The thought experiment that would exhibit the gap cannot be run without the very structure it is trying to show is merely co-extensive with change rather than identical to it. This is not the cheap point that any act of arguing takes time; it is the narrower one that *this particular* thought experiment's own machinery is drawn from the domain the gap is supposed to open up in, which the water/H₂O case's machinery is not.

The objection will press that this shows only an epistemic limit — that *we* cannot represent the counterexample — not a metaphysical fact. But imaginability was never the measure. One can imagine what is merely false: that one is not reading this sentence, that one is elsewhere entirely. Imagination reaches those because they are genuinely possible though not actual — contingent facts it is free to lift. What it cannot lift is the standing it lifts them *from*: the succession across which the imagining unfolds, the standpoint it is entertained at, the persistence of the one entertaining it. To deny change is already to transition from not-denying to denying ([§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1)); to imagine Nature away is to instantiate the Conditions in the imagining ([§2.8.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-2)). w′ does not ask us to imagine a contingent fact otherwise; it asks us to imagine beneath this floor, and beneath it there is not a scenario hard to reach but no scenario — ∅ ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)). The inability is therefore not epistemic. The counterexample would have to be *specified* through the very roles it denies, and a specification that consumes its own content is not a possibility we cannot access but a description that never closes. This is Cartesian in the exact sense the book uses: not that the identity is vivid to us, but that its denial cannot be performed.

Their referring status is fixed accordingly. T, S, and Φ are not definite descriptions that might have designated something else, but the irreducible existence-axes individuated at [§2.6.11](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-11) — real structural joints holding across every world ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)). And 'Reality' is reference-fixed at [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5) as their joint complex, its definiendum rather than a predicate merely co-extensive with it. That fixed reference is what makes the identity an essence claim rather than a truth about how 'change' is labeled. They *are* not what we call the preconditions of change but what any possibility of change *consists in*.

A kindred deflationary move drops rigid designation entirely in favor of modal conventionalism [@sidelle1989; @cameron2010; @sider2011]: necessary truths are analytic consequences of our classificatory conventions rather than discoveries about reality. The same reply applies: classificatory conventions presuppose classifiers that persist across a domain and operate through time: Substance, Space, and Time under different names. Modal structure cannot be a convenience of our conceptual apparatus unless that apparatus is itself instantiated in the structural conditions the argument describes.

Adjacent modal deflations are engaged in their own sections: two-dimensionalism ([§4.1.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-2)), the Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR) demand ([§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3)), modal collapse ([§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9)), and the changeless-being objection ([§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1)).

One last consideration, stated narrowly. The retorsion that follows (a retorsion being an argument that turns an objection back on its maker, showing that the very act of stating the objection presupposes what it denies) establishes the conditions' actuality wherever the Kripkean objection is articulated, not their necessity across worlds where no such articulation occurs. The modal ascent is the work of §§3–7 and does not rest here. What the retorsion shows is narrower: the Kripkean vocabulary is parasitic on the structure it purports to loosen.

*What closes.* Three forms of the Kripkean wedge, and none opens the gap. Each candidate world has either content enough to individuate it (in which case T, S, and Φ obtain in their operative sense) or it is ∅; the S5-exemption move collapses into that same dichotomy. Fine's essence/necessity distinction, the deepest form, cuts the other way. The Modal Identity at [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) is one fact under two descriptions, not a necessary biconditional between two: Kripke's own distinction, turned against the objector.

The narrower Kripkean point (that necessary co-extension does not entail identity) is not what the argument contests. On Kripke's own taxonomy, □(T∧S∧Φ) is not a necessary a posteriori truth on the water=H₂O model either. The one place the derivation touches actuality is the datum that change occurs ([§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)), and even that enters not as ordinary empirical discovery but as Cartesian certainty, epistemically inescapable, surviving the strongest skeptical scenario ([§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1)). The structural identity is constitutive rather than discovered: [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) recovers it by analysis, and its necessity is fixed a priori by the S5 lift of that datum (P2), not read off the world as the water=H₂O identity is. □(T∧S∧Φ) is therefore an a priori, constitutive necessity reached from an inescapable datum. The two-dimensional bookkeeping this raises is handled at [§4.1.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-2).

Kripke's own theory of reference is causal-historical: a name picks out its referent through a chain of transmissions from a baptismal event, preserved across time, through persistent speakers, in writing and speech stable enough to carry reference forward. Rigid designation is not a free-floating stipulation; it is analyzed as an actual causal chain. The paradigm case ('water = H₂O') reached philosophy through exactly such a chain: chemistry to laboratory to textbook to *Naming and Necessity* to here, rigidly designating the same content at every point on the way. The Kripkean apparatus presupposes what [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) describes: a manifold individuated by structural content, a referent preserved across positions, an asymmetric chain from origin to use. The machinery driving the Kripkean wedge is itself an instance of the Modal Identity the wedge was meant to loosen.

The paradigm case remains formulated within ordinary chemical and spatiotemporal theory: H₂O describes molecular structure and its physical realizations. That shows that the water/H₂O example does not itself provide a structure-free countermodel. It does not show, merely from the molecular formula, that every possible realization must exhibit motion or the book's full loaded types. Every essence-specification, fully unpacked, runs back to T, S, and Φ. The wedge exposes necessary identities that hold in virtue of what their relata structurally consist in, and the relata, here as elsewhere, consist in the conditions.

### 4.1.2 Two-Dimensional Semantics {#sec-4-1-2}

Two-dimensional semantics promises a wedge between what a concept picks out when a world is considered as actual and what it picks out across possible worlds. If that wedge holds at the constitutive level, the Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) (□(◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ) read as one fact under two descriptions, connecting change-permission with co-instantiation of the three structural roles) will not survive. The challenge presses at three points: the two-intensions machinery itself, the water/H₂O analogy that most cleanly exhibits it, and the indexical anchor on which primary intensions depend. Chalmers is right on a narrower point, conceded here without qualification: the primary/secondary distinction is a genuine feature of natural-kind terms, and arguments that ignore it routinely overstate what necessary co-extension delivers. The claim contested below is narrower and specifically targeted: that the structural role definitions are natural-kind terms, and that the two-intension machinery has purchase where the appearance/nature separation it exploits does not exist.

Chalmers [-@chalmers1996; -@chalmers2010] makes the cleanest contemporary case that meaning and reference come apart. Every concept, on the two-dimensional semantic framework, admits two intensions. The primary intension picks out what the concept would refer to in any world considered as actual: what 'water' would pick out if the world turned out one way rather than another. The secondary intension picks out what the concept refers to across all possible worlds, given what it in fact refers to here. For natural kind terms the two come apart cleanly: 'water' picks out the clear drinkable stuff in any world considered as actual (primary), but once we discover the actual stuff is H₂O, 'water' rigidly designates H₂O across all possible worlds (secondary). The framework tracks a gap between description and reference that rigid designation alone cannot capture.

@jackson1998 develops the apparatus in parallel, pressing that conceptual analysis tracks primary intensions and that every metaphysical necessity has an *a priori* scrutable counterpart at the primary level (one derivable from a compact base by ideal *a priori* reasoning alone, without further empirical input). @chalmersJackson2001 extend the framework into a general theory of reductive explanation: wherever a target fact is not *a priori* entailed by a non-target base, a two-dimensional gap opens. @chalmers2012 generalizes the move still further in *Constructing the World*: all truths are *a priori* scrutable from a compact base, and wherever primary intensions fail to track secondary ones, a genuine modal gap has been uncovered. The most aggressive deployment for modal epistemology is @chalmers2002: ideal *a priori* conceivability, properly regimented by 2D, entails primary possibility, and primary possibility is the kind of possibility that matters for disputes over necessary existence. The framework is not a regional tool for natural-kind terms; it is a general theory of where modal weight sits and where it does not.

Applied to the present account, the framework presses a precise threat. The argument of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) holds that 'causally structured succession' and Time are not merely co-extensional descriptions but the same structural fact under two modes of presentation: that the role definitions are constitutive rather than descriptive. The two-dimensionalist replies that even for terms the argument labels constitutive, primary and secondary intension can diverge: what 'causally structured succession' picks out when a given world is considered as actual may differ from what it picks out across possible worlds. The Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) would then fail, and with it the step from □◇C to □(T∧S∧Φ): from the necessary possibility of change to the necessary co-instantiation of the three structural conditions. A wedge between description and reference at the constitutive level would leave the structural roles necessarily co-extensive with change without being identical to it: the exact space the classical theist needs to reassert an uninstantiated ground.

Three forms of the move take up the objection; the narrower point about natural-kind terms stands untouched.

*First.* The two-intensions move holds that every concept admits both intensions and that the argument illicitly collapses them at the point of constitutive terms. The pressure is sharpest in its epistemic-possibility form. The primary intension captures what the world could turn out to be for all we know *a priori*, and the Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) is precisely the kind of *a priori* necessity claim @chalmers2002 has shown can fail even where the secondary intension holds necessarily. For all the argument has established analytically, the objector presses, 'causally structured succession' could turn out (in some world considered as actual) to pick out something other than Time as [§1.4.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-4-1) defines it. Scrutability [@chalmers2012] generalizes the pressure well beyond natural-kind terms: wherever a concept is *a priori* scrutable from a base that does not itself entail the target, a primary/secondary gap is in principle available, and the constitutive identities this argument rests on fall within that scope.

The reply runs on the analytic/*a posteriori* distinction the 2D framework itself respects, but it must keep two resolutions apart. At role-resolution, a constitutive definition fixes what counts as directed order, relational differentiation, or real bearing. At type-resolution, further arguments identify temporal succession, spatial extension, and causal persistence as the relevant realizers in genuine change. The Modal Identity does not treat the names alone as settling those richer types.

The Kripkean cases 2D was built to accommodate are *a posteriori* identities: 'water is H₂O' was discovered, not defined, and the primary/secondary gap tracks exactly what the discovery added. The structural claim is different at role-resolution: 'causally structured succession' specifies the role T plays in a genuine change-realizer rather than reporting a discovery that two independently identified things coincide. Where that role specification is analytic, primary and secondary intensions have no independent residue to track. A critic may still contest the type-level realization, but that is a dispute over the realizer arguments, not a primary/secondary gap generated by the role definition itself.

The 2D matrix is a function from possible worlds to extensions, and functions require a domain. In the present account, real possibility ranges over a fixed global domain W ([§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)). Two-dimensional semantics may offer a different representation of modal evaluation, but it must say whether its primary-intension scenarios range over that same global possibility-domain, a relative accessibility relation, or an epistemic space. Only the first is the book's alethic operator ◇. The semantic tool therefore does not by itself overturn the fixed-domain account; it either represents the same real possibilities at another level or shifts to a different relative modality. The structural roles become relevant where a scenario is offered as a genuine change-realizer, not merely because any semantic matrix is being described.

The disanalogy with the paradigm case can be stated directly. The water/H₂O primary intension is evaluable without presupposing water or H₂O: the evaluation is built from chemistry, sense-perception, and an ordinary spatiotemporal setup, none of which is the disputed term. No parallel construction is available here. Evaluating the primary intension of 'causally structured succession' requires exactly the apparatus in question: a scenario individuated from its alternatives (Space), a reasoner who carries the evaluation from premises to verdict (Time), and content held fixed long enough to be compared against the secondary intension it is meant to diverge from (Substance). The act of running the semantic tool is structured, but that act-side fact does not show that every scenario represented by the tool instantiates the loaded temporal, spatial, and causal types. The object-side question remains whether a scenario is admitted as a genuine change-world or only as an epistemic representation.

*Second.* The water/H₂O analogy sharpens the pressure. Scientists discovered water is H₂O *a posteriori*: the identity holds necessarily but was not analytically given. @chalmersJackson2001 generalize the pattern: every necessary *a posteriori* identity admits a corresponding primary-level contingency, and the identity's modal weight is confined to the secondary level. If 'causally structured succession' and Time stand in this relation, the objector presses, their identity is a discovery rather than a definition, and a discovered identity is necessary only in the restricted secondary sense that leaves the primary-level gap open, which is the gap the theist needs.

The analogy works in the natural-kind case precisely because 'water' and 'H₂O' pick out different levels of description: surface features on one side, microstructure on the other. The gap opens because a world could present the surface features while hosting different microstructure (Twin Earth's XYZ). The structural role definitions do not operate at two separable levels. 'Causally structured succession' names nothing except asymmetric directed succession among states: the full specification of what Time *is*. There is no surface/microstructure distinction to exploit, no layer of appearance hiding a different metaphysics underneath. The 2D gap requires exactly the appearance/nature separation the role definitions are designed to eliminate.

The water/H₂O example operates within an ordinary physical setting, but that does not dissolve the semantic distinction it illustrates. The relevant reply is narrower: role specifications and natural-kind identifications have different logical forms. Whether the book's type-level identifications behave more like definitions or discoveries must be defended by the realizer arguments rather than inferred from the physical setting in which semantic evaluation occurs.

*Third.* The indexical anchor presses the objection furthest. The primary intension is evaluated from the perspective of a world considered as actual, and 'considered as actual' is an indexical that depends on the evaluator's position rather than any mind-independent fact. The indexicality drives the 2D framework, the objector concludes, and if it survives so does the gap.

The indexical objection establishes an act-side point, not immediately an object-side result. Any concrete act of evaluating a primary intension unfolds through succession, distinction, and persistence. That does not by itself show that every primary-intension scenario instantiates the full temporal, spatial, and causal types. The object-side issue is semantic: whether the scenario is offered as a genuine world in W or merely as an epistemic representation. If it is a world in W, it answers to the Structural Requirement; if it is merely an epistemic representation, its variation does not by itself yield a metaphysical possibility.

Two lines support the claim rather than asserting it. First, Lewis individuates worlds as maximal fusions of spatiotemporally interrelated things (*On the Plurality of Worlds* [-@lewis1986], [§1.6](groundwork.html#sec-1-6)). That criterion requires the relevant worldmate relations where there are multiple inhabitants, but it does not by itself prove asymmetric temporal ordering in every sparse or changeless world. Lewisian individuation therefore supplies a concrete-world constraint without independently establishing the book's full T-type. Second, the Chalmers/Jackson scrutability framework requires an idealized *a priori* reasoner conducting the evaluation exercise from within a world considered as actual (*Constructing the World* [-@chalmers2012], Ch. 2). That idealization strips cognitive limitations (bounded memory, finite inferential steps) while preserving the structural conditions of reasoning: directed inference from premises to conclusions (T), distinction among propositions being evaluated (S), and persistence of the cognitive state across the derivation (Φ). Any actual token of idealized reasoning is performed through an ordered cognitive practice. That establishes an act-side condition on evaluators; it does not place a temporal coordinate inside every scenario they evaluate or settle whether an abstract ideal inference is itself temporally extended.

Fine's [-@fine1994] distinction between essence and necessity sharpens the point. The indexical 'actual' is not merely necessarily co-present with a Time coordinate; it is essentially anchored in one. Any attempt to reconstruct an 'actuality' perspective from non-temporal resources either covertly reimports the succession from which 'now' acquires content, or fails to individuate one world from another at all. Chalmers' own framework, applied to the structural role definitions, reinstates Time in the act of trying to prise meaning loose from metaphysics.

That the indexical reading of 'actual' is itself contested only tightens the anchor rather than loosening it. Van Inwagen's 'Indexicality and Actuality' [-@vanInwagen1980] argues the indexical theory is not true as Lewis states it: the words Lewis uses are ambiguous across several readings, on none of which the analysis is both genuinely indexical and correct; relatedly he presses that the indexical reading presupposes we inhabit just one possible world [-@vanInwagen1980, 416]. Adams's 'Theories of Actuality' [-@adams1974] goes further and rejects indexicality outright: actuality is a primitive, absolute property that exactly one world possesses. The structural point is indifferent to which side prevails. If 'actual' is indexical, its token use is centered on a speaker or evaluator, but indexicality need not supply a single temporal frame spanning isolated worlds. If actuality is primitive and absolute, its application need not depend on a standpoint inside the actual world. On either account, actual evaluations are structured performances; neither account alone proves that every evaluated world instantiates T, S, and Φ. The bearing is on the theory of actuality, not on the inventory of worlds: nothing here counts the plurality down to one. It shows only that whichever account of 'actual' survives presupposes the structure the argument names.

A kindred deflation drops the 2D apparatus entirely for conceptual-role semantics: @block1998 and @harman1987 argue meaning is exhausted by inferential role within a conceptual system, and the constitutive identity of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) becomes one inferential-role equivalence among many rather than a modal truth. The reply is the same in thinner vocabulary. Inferential roles require reasoners whose inferences succeed each other (T), operate on distinct premises (S), and carry content across the derivation (Φ). Conceptual-role semantics has not replaced the structural roles; it has renamed them.

The adjacent modal objections are answered elsewhere. The Kripkean challenge (that necessary co-extension is not necessary identity) is handled at [§4.1.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-1), which fixes the modal-epistemic status of the necessity claim and defers to this section the two-dimensional bookkeeping that status raises. The PSR-based modal objection is handled at [§4.1.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-3). The modal-collapse objection (that necessary instantiation flattens modal distinctions) is handled at [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9).

*The bookkeeping, made explicit.* The modal-epistemic status of □(T∧S∧Φ) is fixed at [§4.1.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-1) as *a priori* and constitutive, and that section defers to this one the two-dimensional accounting that status invites. Here it is.

Run the derivation through the 2D matrix and the existential datum that change occurs ([§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)) is the clearest contingent input. The role definitions may be analytic at thin resolution, but the role-to-type bridges and the claim that they exhaust genuine change-realizers are substantive metaphysical premises, not analytic consequences of the vocabulary alone. Even that datum does not enter as ordinary empirical discovery; it is Cartesian-certain, surviving the strongest skeptical scenario ([§2.2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-1)), so the lone contingent-primary element is not *a posteriori* in the water=H₂O way.

And the constitutive identity the datum feeds into (that the possibility of change just is the co-instantiation of the three roles, ◇C ⟷ T∧S∧Φ) has no primary/secondary gap to track. As the replies above establish, 'causally structured succession' is not scrutable from an independent base but *is* the base under another description, so its primary and secondary intensions collapse. That collapse is derived, not stipulated. A primary intension diverges from its secondary only where the concept holds some individuating feature independently of its secondary referent, a handle the primary keeps fixed while the referent varies, as 'watery stuff' keeps the surface profile while the microstructure shifts to XYZ.

The Modal Identity removes the handle. What [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) establishes is that between 'causally structured succession' and Time there is no individuating surplus in either direction: every specification of the one is already a specification of the other, with nothing left over. A primary intension therefore has no feature to track independently of the secondary, and no profile of its own with which to diverge. To conceive the referents coming apart, an ideal reasoner would need some feature on which they could differ; the no-surplus result is the absence of any such feature, and where there is nothing to differ on there is nothing left to conceive as different. That no-surplus result is itself fixed structurally at [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6), established by the role definitions of §[§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3)–1.4 together with the converse at [§2.4.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-10), and it holds independently of any premise about what is conceivable. Leaning on it here therefore closes the primary-intension gap without circularity. Metaphysical no-surplus is in this way epistemic no-residue, and the gap closes at the level the objection needs it open.

With the fixed-domain modal lift and the constitutive arguments at the full Condition resolution, □(T∧S∧Φ) is argued *a priori*, not read off the world as an empirical identity. The point is not that S5 alone turns an existential datum into the structural conclusion; the Structural Requirement supplies the necessary conditional, and the type-level realizer arguments supply its content. The resulting necessity is structural and constitutive in the book's intended sense. The 2D framework, asked to locate where modal weight sits, returns the verdict to the constitutive level it was built to prise open.

*What converges.* Across all three pressure points the 2D framework either requires the structure or redescribes it in more layered vocabulary. The two-intensions move needs modal space as its evaluation domain (which the roles constitute rather than presuppose) and finds no gap where the target is analytic rather than *a posteriori*. The water/H₂O analogy needs an appearance/microstructure seam the role definitions do not admit: 'causally structured succession' names nothing except what Time *is*. And the indexical anchor needs a Time coordinate from which 'actual' has determinate content at all: any attempt to reconstruct actuality from non-temporal resources either reimports the succession or fails to individuate worlds.

What stands, untouched by any of this, is Chalmers' narrower point about natural-kind terms; what falls away is the attempt to import it to the constitutive level. The role definitions of §[§1.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-3)–1.4 are not natural-kind terms waiting to be pulled apart at a seam between surface and nature; they are role specifications whose content is exhausted by what they require. The 2D framework, turned on constitutive role definitions, does not discover a gap but reinstates the architecture it was designed to distinguish semantic layers from.

### 4.1.3 Principle of Sufficient Reason {#sec-4-1-3}

The rationalist demand for sufficient reason is an exacting standard any necessary-existence argument has to meet on its own terms. Applied to T, S, and Φ, the demand takes three forms (a contrast demand, an origin demand, and Pruss's modal refinement). The replies below grant the Leibnizian point freely. A rationalist argument that terminates in a brute fact has betrayed its own standard, and a conclusion terminating in brute necessity would betray the standard this argument was raised under. The argument does not so terminate. It terminates where the demand itself runs out of contrast.

@leibniz1714 gives the demand its canonical form: nothing exists without a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise. @pruss2006 has given it the most rigorous contemporary defense: if every contingent fact has an explanation, the chain must terminate in something whose existence is not contingent. The demand is not parochial; it is the demand that reality be intelligible all the way down.

Applied to this argument, it presses that T∧S∧Φ obtaining necessarily is itself a fact about reality, and facts about reality are subject to the PSR. If the necessity is brute, the argument has violated its own commitment. If it is grounded, whatever grounds it stands outside or beneath structure as the true necessary ground. Three forms of the objection are taken up below.

*First.* The contrast demand presses that without a reason why the structure obtains rather than not, the argument has merely relocated bruteness from physics to metaphysics, and a brute necessity is not more intelligible than a brute contingency, only more deeply hidden.

The demand presupposes a contrast the argument has already foreclosed. 'Why structure rather than not?' supposes that ∅ is a coherent alternative whose non-obtaining requires explanation. As [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) establishes, ∅ is not: nothing individuates it, nothing distinguishes its obtaining from its non-obtaining, nothing for any description to attach to. The PSR demands a reason for obtaining rather than not obtaining; where the 'not obtaining' side is incoherent, the demand does not find a gap but fails to articulate one. The question presupposes a contrast its own terms cannot sustain.

*Second.* The origin demand grants the ∅ result but presses for a beginning: even if ∅ is incoherent as a state, the structure must have begun, and there must be some account of why T, S, and Φ obtain now rather than a prior arrangement.

The demand, on this analysis, is not unanswered but unaskable in the form it was issued in. A beginning is an event: a transition from non-existence to existence. Such a transition requires T, S, and Φ to take place: a temporal succession in which the prior state does not contain the structure and the subsequent state does, within a Space that can host both, carried by Substance. To propose a beginning for the structure is to propose a transition before transitions are possible, which is to describe nothing at all. The word 'prior' has no application outside the succession it names. The demand uses T, S, and Φ in its own formulation and then asks why they obtain, using the very conditions of the asking.

*Third.* Pruss's modal refinement drops the demand for explanation of necessary facts and confines the PSR to contingent facts. The modal PSR does not require ∅ to be coherent as an alternative. It simply notes that every contingent fact admits of explanation, and asks whether the structure's instantiation in this world is such a contingent fact.

The refinement survives, but it survives by conceding the conclusion. A PSR confined to contingent facts leaves the necessity of T, S, and Φ unchallenged: that is what 'confined to contingent facts' means. The structure is not in its scope. What the modal PSR captures are the causal sequences and events within the structure: why this reaction rather than that, why this memory rather than another. The present account (necessary structural conditions plus contingent investigation of everything within them) leaves every such question open to investigation. A theist who adopts the modal PSR is no longer arguing against the structure's necessity but engaging contingent facts within the structure, the domain the present account is designed to accommodate.

One further engagement is owed at this site. Pruss's central deployment of the modal PSR is not the abstract form addressed above (why T∧S∧Φ rather than ∅) but the *Big Conjunctive Contingent Fact* argument (*The Principle of Sufficient Reason* [-@pruss2006]; *Necessary Existence* with Rasmussen [-@prussRasmussen2018]): the conjunction of all contingent facts (the BCCF) is itself contingent and by modal PSR requires an explanation outside it.

On the book's framework the BCCF is the conjunction of all contingent configurations of Nature: this cosmos, these initial conditions, this particular sequence of events. Each contingent fact within Nature has a contingent cause or explanation within Nature's causal structure; the modal PSR is satisfied at that level. This is compatible with genuine chance and does not quietly presuppose determinism. Where a transition is governed by an objective probability distribution rather than a deterministic law, the distribution itself, fixed by the prior state and Nature's causal structure, is what the modal PSR is owed. It is a reason why the outcome falls within a determinate range of possibilities, weighted in a determinate way, not a further hidden fact that secretly settles which member of the range is realized. To demand the latter is to demand that chance covertly be non-chance, which begs the question against genuine indeterminism rather than pressing a live PSR violation. This is exactly the room [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) draws on when it invokes quantum indeterminacy against modal collapse: an open token outcome is not a PSR debt left unpaid but the kind of contingent fact the modal PSR was always going to leave open once explanation is distinguished from determination.

The reply does not, however, rest on the Hume–Edwards principle that explaining each contingent conjunct thereby explains their conjunction, the very inference Pruss's BCCF argument is built to reject. Its load-bearing move is instead the foreclosure of the external demand itself. The demand for an explanation *outside* the BCCF commonly motivates a necessary explainer, but the three candidates considered here—∅, Nature itself, and a necessary being whose free act selects the BCCF—do not exhaust every theory of explanation by logic alone. They organize the principal options engaged by this book. ∅ is foreclosed. Nature does not explain the BCCF *necessarily*; if it did, the BCCF would be necessary, and contingent facts would collapse into necessities (the modal-collapse risk [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) addresses). The third candidate is the theist's actual proposal — a necessary agent whose libertarian choice explains a contingent outcome without necessitating it, escaping the modal-collapse horn. It is engaged, not ignored: that a ground external to Nature is available at all is what [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) and the Supernatural Preclusion of Chapter 6 foreclose, while whether the necessary ground is *personal and agent-causal* is taken up on its own terms at [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1), [§5.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1), and Chapter 6. What this site settles is narrower — the modal PSR does not by itself convert the demand for an external explainer into a demand for a *necessary personal* one; that inference is what those sections test, not one the PSR delivers here. Nature explains the structural preconditions under which contingent configurations obtain; the contingent selection among configurations is internal to Nature.

The selection-among-possibilities question (why this configuration rather than another) is addressed at [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4) and [§5.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1): contingency is a property of configurations within Nature, not of Nature itself, and the demand that selection receive an external necessary explanation posits a grounding framework outside Nature. Section 2.7 forecloses ∅, but it does not by itself refute every proposed external ground; those proposals require the dedicated engagements in Chapters 5–6. This is the disambiguation the reply turns on: the BCCF is not *granted* an internal sufficient reason for the conjunction-as-a-whole (that would be the Hume–Edwards move Pruss is right to reject) but *exempted* from the external demand, because that demand has no coherent target. Each contingent conjunct keeps its contingent explanation within Nature's causal structure; the conjunction as a totality is neither handed a further internal explanation nor left awaiting an external one, since each candidate external explainer is foreclosed as set out above.

The BCCF argument does not by itself establish a necessary personal explainer; further premises are needed to identify the explainer as personal and external to Nature. Conversely, the present section has not shown that no coherent totality-level explanatory demand can be raised. Its narrower reply is that local explanations within Nature and the necessity of Nature do not automatically generate the personal-explainer conclusion.

The dissolution carries further than the deflection of three demands. It shows that the demand was never available as a motivation for the argument to an external necessary ground in the first place. If ∅ is not a coherent alternative to the structure of Reality ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)), then the contingency of the structure cannot serve as a starting point for the argument to a necessary divine cause, because the structure has been shown to be not contingent but necessary. Its necessity renders the demand incoherent rather than redirecting it toward a divine answer. The PSR argument for theism is not answered by the Necessity of Nature; it is dissolved at its foundation.

A fourth move deserves naming. The Thomist may press that structural necessity is not the right kind of necessity: that classical theism demands the necessity of essence possessed by a being whose essence is its existence [@feser2017; @koons1997; @rasmussen2019]. The observation is correct and the counter-construction is live, but it is not a fourth variant of the PSR; it is taken up on its own terms in [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1) (a being outside the structure) and §5 (a being beneath it).

A fifth move presses a structural parallel rather than a PSR variant. If structure is self-grounding, why is the classical God not equally so? The *causa sui* construction holds that the divine nature is its own sufficient reason, requiring no external explanation, and the suggestion is that the present reading must concede the same status to whatever it proposes as the necessary ground.

The setup is incomplete on its face. Nature does not need an outside ground in the way that objects within Nature need their grounding conditions, because Nature is not an object that occupies anything outside itself. Nature *is* what occupying-anything consists in. The question 'what makes Nature possible?' assumes something outside Nature within which its possibility could be grounded, but that outside does not exist. To be possible is to be permitted by Nature. Nature does not permit itself from some external vantage point; it is what permission consists in.

The parallel fails because the two cases are structurally different in a precise way. Nature is not self-grounding in the sense that it is an entity which happens to satisfy the conditions for grounding from the inside. It is self-grounding in the stronger sense that it just is the conditions under which grounding operates: the logical space within which any explanatory demand, any sufficient reason, any grounding relation first becomes possible. There is no grounding framework outside Nature within which the question of Nature's own ground could be posed, because the framework is Nature.

The distinction is sharp: God, on the *causa sui* construction, is proposed as a thing that grounds itself. Nature is not a thing. It is what things are in. A self-grounding thing still requires the conditions in which self-grounding is possible, and those conditions are Nature.

A constructive complement to the three deflections is available once the cyclic-recurrence result of [§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6) is in view. The BCCF paragraph above handles the modal PSR at the contingent-fact level via Nature's internal causal structure; the cyclic-recurrence result closes two further pressures the contingent-fact reply leaves standing. The Kalām-style press for a first state at which the causal regress would otherwise terminate without a reason is foreclosed twice over. The structural closure of Temporality — □T together with ∅-preclusion and the domain-local reading of negation (§[§2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-3)–2.4, [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)) — leaves no coherent "before" or "outside" from which a first state could depart. The second closure is Singularity Preclusion (the Corollary of T6 at [§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6)); a least moment of the manifold, if there is one, is a boundary with nothing on its far side, not an absolute beginning. This is not ad-hoc denial but the same structural argument applied at cosmological scale. The Leibnizian press for an external explainer of the cycle-as-totality is foreclosed because the cycle's recurrence under invariant law is the modal necessity of □(T∧S∧Φ) playing out across past-unbounded time, not a further contingent fact requiring external grounding. The PSR is met on rationalist terms at both levels at which it can coherently be pressed against the present account: every event has a sufficient reason within the cycle, and the cycle's recurrence is the structural necessity playing out rather than a contingency requiring an outside reason.

*What closes.* Three forms of the demand, and none finds a gap: the contrast demand presupposes ∅ as a coherent alternative [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) forecloses; the origin demand uses T, S, and Φ in the very act of asking why they obtain; and Pruss's modal refinement, confined to contingent facts, leaves structural necessity outside its scope. Two further results follow once the deflections are in place. The dissolution removes the contingency-of-Reality starting point that would otherwise carry the PSR to an external necessary ground, and the *causa sui* parallel fails on the thing-versus-conditions distinction: structure is not a thing that grounds itself but what grounding consists in.

One last consideration, stated narrowly. The PSR is a live rationalist commitment this argument endorses, not a threat to be neutralized. The narrower Leibnizian point (that contingent facts admit of explanation) is not what the argument denies. What the argument denies is that the structural necessities are contingent facts in need of explanation against an available alternative. Humean contingency is taken up at [§4.1.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-4): whether bare succession can be granted while the productive bond that makes it a succession is denied.

### 4.1.4 Humean Contingency {#sec-4-1-4}

Hume's challenge is a generous and disciplined attempt to thin Time. He grants that states follow states. He just does not see anything holding them together: one state, then the next, and the "then" does no work. No necessary connection, no causal arrow. Just sequence.

The replies here grant his narrowest claim (constant conjunction does not by itself entail necessity) and contest the broader one by testing whether each form can state succession without handing over directional succession through Substance. The structural-level engagement (defending the producing-relation against eliminativist pressure) is carried by [§2.6.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-8); this section takes up the modal-contingency arm.

@hume1748 [§VII] argues that our impression of causal necessity is a psychological habit projected onto the world, not a feature discovered within it. His contemporary inheritors (@lewis1986 [pp. ix–xvi], @loewer1996, @beebee2006) sharpen the point into the Best System Account: laws of nature are the axioms of the simplest, strongest systematization of the pattern of events, not constraints that govern it. Succession without enforcement — order that simply obtains.

Time, as [§1.4.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-4-1) defines it, is different. Not bare sequence: directional, asymmetric, productive, with the earlier state grounding the later, an arrow running through. Hume grants the sequence and denies the arrow. The three forms we are about to take up each miss the same thing: directional succession through Substance cannot be granted while the arrow is denied. The concession and the denial are the same sentence.

*First.* The bare-succession form holds that states can follow one another without any carrying medium. States follow states, the ordering is all Time needs, and nothing about Substance makes the next state follow the previous. Indexed order, not enforcement.

That concession is already enough, but note where it is enough. Try thinning succession further. Read "indexed order" as a block universe (B-theory; Mellor [-@mellor1998], *Real Time II*): time-slices arranged by index, all moments equally real, ordered by a tenseless before/after, no privileged now. On this reading, "persistence" just means qualitative similarity across slices; nothing is carried through. Can the thinner reading hold?

Consider what the thinning requires. An ordering of slices by index is one of two things. Either it is a function from integers to qualitative profiles applied to the manifold, in which case the manifold itself has to have enough structure to be indexable at all, an intrinsic distinction of positions that the arithmetic is tracking, not supplying. Or the ordering is free-floating abstract, a function unattached to any manifold, in which case it is not a time-series anymore, just a set of profiles paired with numerals, two disjoint structures sitting next to each other.

The first reading borrows the structural fact it is trying to replace. The second yields an abstract set of profiles paired with indices rather than a concrete temporal manifold. It does not collapse into ∅: the set still has members and formal structure. Its limitation is instead that the abstract pairing does not by itself realize temporal succession or causal persistence. Grant succession at any strength sufficient to state the position, and the Mutual Containment Result ([§2.6.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-5)) takes over: succession requires something that persists (Substance) across a structured interval (Space). Whether it is called "produced" or "enforced" is not the hinge; that something is sequenced at all is.

The bare-succession form is the wager that replacement is never more than mere sequence. Put exactly: replacement is not bare succession. It requires something that can be replaced, something that replaces it, and structure in which the replacement counts as replacement rather than mere juxtaposition. Strip the being, the interval, and the relation, and the Humean has not described thinner succession. They have removed the conditions under which succession is describable at all.

*Second.* The asymmetric-before form grants more ground than the first and tries to hold a thinner line. Sequence is real. Co-instantiation is real. But before-and-after is treated as a brute relational fact between states: the ordering is there, causation is not. Tim Maudlin (*The Metaphysics Within Physics* [-@maudlin2007]) goes further, making time's arrow a fundamental primitive of the manifold: asymmetry that needs no further grounding.

Consider what this does. An asymmetric relation between states is either a label applied from outside (a convention we impose, with nothing in Nature answering to it) or a structural fact about Nature itself. If it is a label, it is a label for one of two things. Either it removes the ordering along with the arrow (leaving co-present states with nothing to index, the ∅ distribution [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) forecloses) or it keeps the ordering and imposes only the direction: the direction-conventionalist's line, on which the series is real but no fact of Nature settles which way it runs. The second reading does not thin Time; it relocates the arrow to a mind-independent gradient, the thermodynamic move [§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3) takes up. Neither branch yields an asymmetry that is real, in Nature, and not already Exchange under another name. If it is structural (whether read as a consequence of deeper machinery or as a Maudlin-style primitive) then "asymmetric relation" and "Exchange" are doing exactly the same work. Two names, one structure.

Maudlin's primitivism (the view that time's directionality is a fundamental feature of the world, not reducible to anything more basic) refuses reduction in any direction. Time's passage is not to be analyzed via entropy gradients, nor reduced to tenseless B-theory relations, nor deflated to psychological flow; it is a fundamental directional structure of the world that fundamental physics already presupposes whenever its laws are stated as differential equations evolving an initial state forward (*The Metaphysics Within Physics* [-@maudlin2007], ch. 4). Take the position on its own terms. The directionality is real, primitive, ontologically irreducible. It still attaches to states standing in directional relation across a manifold that bears the primitive. The primitive is the directionality of something: three structural conditions the primitivism cannot dissolve. Maudlin's primitive is what T, S, and Φ jointly amount to once a defender insists on irreducibility. The role structure does not refute the primitivism. It states what the primitivism is the structure of.

*Third.* The Best System Account (BSA) is a sophisticated deflationary form of the challenge, and it is genuinely beautiful as a systematization. On BSA, laws of nature are the axioms of the simplest, strongest way to describe the total pattern, not constraints that govern it. Regularities get described, not enforced. The picture is the Humean mosaic: a distribution of local matters of fact, no necessary connections between them [@lewis1986; @loewer1996].

The standard non-Humean replies in the contemporary literature treat laws as relations among universals [@armstrong1983, *What Is a Law of Nature?*] or as primitive necessitating relations between properties [@dretske1977; @tooley1977]. The reply here is structurally different. It is not that something enforces the regularity above and beyond the distribution; it is that any vocabulary capable of stating the regularity already runs on the structural conditions the Humean meant to deflate.

Lewis's doctrine of Humean supervenience says everything supervenes on the distribution of local qualities together with the spatiotemporal relations among their instances. Those relations belong to the supervenience base rather than being derived from the qualities alone. The mosaic is therefore distributed across an already structured manifold, not used to construct that manifold [@lewis1986, pp. ix–xvi]. This is the load-bearing concession, and it runs under the whole account.

Consider what a regularity actually is. For events of type A to be reliably followed by events of type B, the Humean has already granted a distribution across a spatiotemporal manifold and a pattern stated over that distribution. That concession is enough. If the regularity is brute, the Humean offers systematization rather than a governing explanation; that is a deliberate feature of the view, not an internal contradiction. If the regularity is grounded in an invariant feature of the manifold, the account moves toward a non-Humean structure. The present argument can therefore claim that BSA presupposes spatiotemporal structure, but it cannot infer a productive causal arrow from regularity alone. A mosaic without a manifold is not a mosaic: it is a set with no ordering.

The BSA does not escape structure. It describes structure in Humean vocabulary, having already conceded the primitive spatiotemporal manifold that is the structure in question. The Humean wants regularity without necessity. Strip Nature and regularity has nothing to regulate.

A kindred deflationary move drops causal vocabulary entirely in favor of symmetric functional relations between variables: @russell1913 ["On the Notion of Cause"] argues causation has no place in mature physics; @norton2003 carries the case forward. The reply is the same, shaped differently: functional relations between variables presuppose the variables' distinctness (Space) and persistence (Substance), and any functional relation with a privileged direction of dependency presupposes Time's asymmetry. Thermodynamic variants (that temporal asymmetry emerges from entropy gradients rather than obtaining structurally) come up in [§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3).

One narrower point, stated exactly. The self-refutation charge (that a denial of the structural conditions presupposes them in the act of denying) establishes the conditions' actuality wherever the denial is performed, not their necessity across worlds where no such performance occurs. The move from actuality to necessity is the work of §§3–7 and does not rest here. The result is narrower: the deflationary vocabularies are parasitic on the structure they are meant to replace, wherever they are stated.

One rejoinder remains. A Humean might grant the parasitism and insist it is just how description works: any vocabulary capable of saying anything borrows structure from what it says it about, and that is no refutation of deflationism, just a feature of having a language at all. Look at the words the deflation reaches for. Holds. Runs. Deeper. Reach. Underneath. Ground. Foundation. Each one names the structure the deflation was meant to do without.

The reply runs at a deeper level than vocabulary. Hume published the *Enquiry* in 1748, and the argument has reached every reader since through a directed causal chain: ink pressed into paper, the marks holding their positions from Edinburgh to here, each transmission running forward and not back, copied and carried across 278 years with the content intact. The content of Hume's position denies the productive bond; the vehicle by which that content has reached readers is the very causal structure the content denies.

The same reply reaches a closer case. Hume's account of necessity runs from observation through habit to projected expectation: repeated conjunctions, formed habit, projected necessity. There is a class of cases where that order is reversed: cases where the regularity is *established*, in a single act, by an agent who specifies it. The Anscombean and interventionist traditions [@anscombe1971, "Causality and Determination"; @woodward2003, *Making Things Happen*] have pressed a kindred line against the spectator's epistemology for half a century: an agent who establishes a regularity by an intervention has first-person access to causal efficacy that no abstraction-from-conjunctions can supply. A programmer who specifies a function settles in advance what the function will return on inputs it has never been called on: no series of conjunctions, no time for habit to form, just a stipulation that holds because the system bears it. The constant conjunction is *constituted* by the stipulation, not abstracted from a history of it. The deflationary epistemology has no machinery for the reversed order, and the cases where the order runs that way are not exotic: they are the cases where regularities are most cleanly established. What the stipulation requires to take effect is the same triple the descriptive case required to be statable: a structural setting, a domain across which the stipulation ranges, and something the regularity holds across. The structure is met from the agent's side as it was met from the describer's side.

*What converges.* Time is the Condition [§1.4.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-4-1) defines, bearing the succession role [§1.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-1) extracts, and each deflationary form fails to remove it: bare succession cannot be indexed without borrowing the manifold it meant to replace (or thinning into an abstract pairing that realizes no succession at all); asymmetric before-and-after is either a label applied from outside, which removes the ordering or relocates the arrow ([§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3)), or a structural fact about Nature, which is Exchange under another name; and the Best System Account admits the spatiotemporal manifold into its own supervenience base rather than deriving it, describing the structure in Humean vocabulary rather than replacing it.

Three forms, each conceding the structure they mean to deflate, and one rejoinder undone twice over: by the medium of its own transmission and by the cases its spectator's epistemology cannot reach. The deflationary move reinstates the structure it meant to remove. The narrower Humean point (that constant conjunction does not entail necessity) is not what the argument contests; it is a constraint the argument accepts and obeys, refusing to read necessity off bare regularity and routing the necessity claim instead through structural analysis and the Cartesian datum that change occurs. That discipline is Hume's bequest, inherited rather than overturned. The causal-transmission point is narrow and literal: the argument has reached us only through the structure its content tries to deflate. The next section takes up the information-theoretic challenge ([§4.1.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-5)): whether reality reduces to bits from which T, S, and Φ emerge rather than hold as structural conditions.

### 4.1.5 Information-Theoretic Foundationalism {#sec-4-1-5}

Wheeler's *it from bit* proposes that reality is informational all the way down: binary distinctions are fundamental, and spacetime and matter emerge from the relational structure of information processing. The picture has real purchase in physics (Shannon's [-@shannon1948] formalism, Landauer's [-@landauer1961] thermodynamic cost of erasure, information-theoretic reformulations of quantum mechanics) and none of it is in dispute. What is contested is the ontological inversion: the claim that information is more fundamental than the structural roles, that T, S, and Φ are emergent features of an information-processing substrate rather than conditions of what information consists in. T, S, and Φ are the three structural conditions whose necessity [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5) declares, borne by Time, Space, and Substance. Three forms of the inversion follow. The replies test whether each can sustain the inversion without handing over what it meant to deflate.

*First.* The bit-first move holds that reality at the most fundamental level consists of bits (yes/no distinctions) with spacetime and matter emerging from their relational structure [@wheeler1990].

A bit requires difference to be a bit. Bateson's [-@bateson1972] phrase names the contrast at the core: information concerns a difference that can matter within some system. But Shannon's [-@shannon1948] formalism is deliberately abstract. Its sender, receiver, channel, and signal are formal roles in a communication model; the formalism by itself does not establish that every bit must have a physical bearer, spatial manifold, or temporal transmission. The stronger claim belongs only to physically realized information processing: where a difference is registered, propagated, or acted upon in a concrete system, there must be a persisting realization, distinguishable states, and an ordered process. That is a claim about realization, not a consequence of information theory alone. Information-theoretic foundationalism must therefore show how an abstract informational base is physically realized without already relying on the structural roles it proposes to derive.

*Second.* The Mathematical Universe Hypothesis [@tegmark2014] goes further: reality does not resemble mathematics but is a mathematical structure, and all mathematically consistent structures equally exist.

For a mathematical structure to be a structure at all, its elements must stand in determinate relations. That directly supports a role of differentiation. It does not follow from determinate relatedness alone that the relations are asymmetric, temporally ordered, continuous, or borne by a concrete substance. Those further roles enter only when the mathematical structure is claimed to be concretely realized or dynamically operative. Tegmark's own account requires the mathematical structure to be the kind of thing whose elements stand in determinate relations; this concedes the difference-role at the level of what a mathematical structure consists in. The plenitude reading compounds the concession: every mathematically consistent structure supports that role under abstraction. The Platonist has not escaped differentiation, and the temporal and bearer roles fall due wherever the structure is claimed to be concretely real.

What the section's account requires Tegmark to give up is not the mathematical-identity thesis as such but its unrestricted plenitude complement. The Mathematical Universe Hypothesis at Level IV holds that all mathematically consistent structures equally exist (*Our Mathematical Universe* [-@tegmark2014]). If T∧S∧Φ are necessary conditions for a mathematical structure to be concretely real rather than merely abstractly consistent, then the Level IV plenitude is structurally bounded: only T∧S∧Φ-consistent structures are candidates for physical instantiation. The section's claim is not that MUH is false but that it requires the structural conditions as a constraint on plenitude. Tegmark's account can absorb T, S, and Φ as specifying what it takes for a consistent structure to be physically instantiated; the cost is giving up the claim that mathematical consistency alone is sufficient for physical existence.

*Third.* The computational-universe move presses the cleanest form. @lloyd2006 holds that the universe is a quantum computer: physical processes are computations, particles are data, interactions are logic gates. @deutsch1997 and @wolfram2002 develop parallel variants. The common commitment is that computation precedes the structural roles ontologically.

A physically realized computation instantiates each of the three roles at the level of the computing. For a bit to be processed in a concrete machine, there must be an ordered transition between states through a medium capable of realizing it; this supplies the relevant temporal role. An abstract computation, considered only as a mathematical mapping, does not by itself establish physical succession. For information to be held, maintained, and updated, something must persist as the being that bears the informational state, that *is* Substance.
