The dispositionalist is right that a plurality of concrete worlds is an extravagant truthmaker for a modest claim; right that modal truths should answer to what is actually the case rather than to what is elsewhere the case; right that the possible-worlds apparatus is a formal convenience whose metaphysical reading was never obligatory. On the negative program the present account and the dispositionalist are allies, and [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1) is where that alliance does its work. The disagreement is entirely about the positive one.

*First.* The reduction form runs directly at the Convertibility. Its claim is that ◇p holds if and only if some actual object has a potentiality for p, so possibility is not a structural feature of reality but a summary of what things can do. The Way–Possibility Convertibility ([§3.2.5](convergence.html#sec-3-2-5)) is then a redescription of the powers facts rather than a rival to them, and the structural triad is read off potentialities rather than presupposed by them.

The reply is that a potentiality already exhibits the triad, and exhibits it in the form the decomposition specifies. A potentiality is a directedness: it runs from a bearer, through a medium of manifestation, to an outcome that is not yet the case. That is an ordering with an asymmetry (the T-role), a distinctness between latency and manifestation without which nothing has been directed at anything (the S-role), and something that has the potentiality rather than the potentiality free-floating (the Φ-role). [§2.8.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-1) already makes the point on the laws side: a disposition without a persisting bearer, without relational extension through which it manifests, and without an interval between latency and activation is not a disposition. The dispositionalist has not produced an alternative to the way-structure. A potentiality is a way, individuated as one, and taking it as primitive does not remove what individuates it.

The reply is deliberately not the stronger one available. It does not say that necessitation *is* directional production, or that the manifestation relation supplies the content of T. That would give the structural conditions a second, analogical sense, which [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4) forecloses. The claim is the deflationary one: the potentiality is described in the structural vocabulary because it instantiates the structure, not because the structure is a species of causal production.

*Second.* The primitiveness form concedes the exhibition and contests the direction of explanation. Grant that potentialities display direction, difference, and bearing; the dispositionalist may hold that potentiality is metaphysically primitive and the triad is a true description of primitives rather than a condition on them. Description does not establish priority.

The reply asks which side survives the removal of the other. A potentiality stripped of its directedness is not an undirected potentiality but no potentiality; strip the distinctness of latency from manifestation and there is nothing the potentiality is *for*; strip the bearer and there is nothing whose potentiality it is. The triad is therefore not a description that happens to fit but the individuation-condition of the primitive, and an individuation-condition is not posterior to what it individuates. The structural claim also takes a weaker form than the dispositionalist's own. The Convertibility runs as a convertibility, with neither *possibility* nor *way* reducing to the other, whereas dispositionalism is a reduction in one direction and therefore owes an account of its reduction base. What sits in that base is a property of an actual object, and a property of an actual object is specified from within the modal field in exactly the sense the Modal Exclusivity trilemma at [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10) identifies.

*Third.* The coverage form is where the position is under most pressure from inside its own literature, and where the disagreement with the present account becomes visible rather than verbal. @wang2015 presses that dispositionalism cannot reach possibilities for which nothing actual seats the relevant potentiality: alien properties, radically different physical regimes, possibilities concerning how things stood before there was anything with powers of the requisite kind. @vetter2015 answers with iterated and joint potentialities, extending the base by chaining what actual things can bring about.

The reply is that the internal dispute is settled, whichever way it goes, by asking whether there is something actual to seat the potentiality, and that question concedes the structural point rather than answering it. Both parties agree that possibility must be seated in actual reality. They differ only over whether the seat is a property of an object or the conditions any object-involving state already instantiates. At ordinary scope the difference is hard to see, because objects are available to bear the powers. At global scope the difference is decisive.

::: {.premise}
**The Bearer Problem** · *Premises*

1. Dispositionalism about modality: for any p, ◇p holds in virtue of the potentiality of some actual object (Reduction).

1. A potentiality is borne. There is no potentiality that is not the potentiality *of* something (Bearing).

1. Consider the possibility that there be objects at all.

1. By (1) and (2), that possibility holds in virtue of the potentiality of an object.

1. So the possibility that there be bearers presupposes a bearer, and the account has supplied its own manifestation-condition as its ground.

1. The dispositionalist must therefore either accept the circle at (5) or exempt the limit case from (1), which concedes that not all possibility is dispositionally grounded.

:::

Neither horn is available at low cost, and the structural reading takes the second one without paying. What seats the possibility that there be objects is not a further object but the conditions any object-involving state instantiates: succession, distinction, and exchange are not properties an item has but the structure any item-involving state is. The dispositionalist's seat runs out at precisely the scope the argument of Chapter 2 operates at, and it runs out for a reason internal to the position rather than imported against it: powers are borne, and the global case has nothing to bear them.

A rejoinder is available and should be recorded. The dispositionalist may deny that *there being objects at all* is a genuine possibility requiring a ground, holding instead that it is necessary, so that no potentiality need seat it. That reply is not obviously wrong, but it is a concession in the relevant sense: it grants that something is necessary without being dispositionally grounded, and once one such necessity is admitted the reduction is no longer general. It also moves the dispositionalist onto the terrain of [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4) and [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10), where the question is no longer what powers ground but what a necessity that grounds nothing further can be. @williamson2013 reaches a structurally similar place from the opposite direction, and the answer [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6) gives applies here.

*What closes.* Dispositionalism is not refuted as an account of laws, and [§2.8.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-1) already grants it what it is owed there. As an account of modality it does not bypass the structural requirement but instantiates it, since a potentiality is individuated as a directed, differentiated, borne thing and is therefore a way rather than an alternative to ways. The order of explanation runs from the individuation-condition to the primitive, not the reverse. And the reduction does not reach the global case, because the possibility of there being bearers cannot itself be seated in a bearer. What the position establishes, and what the present account keeps, is that modality answers to actual structure rather than to a plurality of worlds. Where it locates that structure in the powers of things, the account locates it in what any thing with powers already presupposes.

### 4.1.13 Modal Epistemology and the Remoteness Objection {#sec-4-1-13}

Quine denies that the modal vocabulary is intelligible. Van Inwagen grants it and denies something else: that the faculty by which we reach modal verdicts is reliable at the distances philosophy asks it to work at. @vanInwagen1998 is the canonical statement. Ordinary modal knowledge is secure, on this view, because it operates by small variation on the actual: the table could have stood two feet to the left, the meeting could have run long. Remote modal claims (that there could be a being than which none greater can be conceived, that there could be a physical duplicate of a person lacking consciousness, that transparent iron is possible) are cases where the faculty has been carried far past anything that calibrates it, and the confident verdicts philosophers return are not knowledge.

This is not the skepticism of [§4.1.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-6), and the two must not be run together. The Quinean refuses the vocabulary. Van Inwagen keeps the vocabulary, keeps ordinary modal knowledge, and refuses the extension. A reply that vindicates the intelligibility of *necessarily* leaves his objection entirely untouched, which is why it needs its own address. Its compositional half is discharged at [§4.3.11](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-11); the half taken up here is the one that section explicitly defers.

The objection lands with more force here than almost anywhere, because □(T∧S∧Φ) is about as remote as a modal claim gets. It quantifies over every world, including worlds bearing no resemblance to anything experienced, and it returns a verdict of necessity rather than mere pervasiveness. By van Inwagen's own criterion of similarity to ordinary life, no claim in the book is further from the calibrated range.

The concession runs in full, and it is larger than the concessions elsewhere in [§4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1). Van Inwagen is right that a great deal of analytic metaphysics has run on brute intuitions about distant scenarios; right that no one has produced a credible account of a faculty that would deliver such verdicts reliably; right that the modal ontological argument and the zombie argument both turn on exactly this move; right that the burden falls on whoever wants a remote modal conclusion. [§3.3.4](convergence.html#sec-3-3-4) already agrees, and the agreement there is not tactical. The book's own treatment of conceivability is closer to van Inwagen's than to his opponents'.

*First.* The remoteness form runs directly. Ordinary modal knowledge proceeds by imaginative variation from the actual, the reach of that method is short, and □(T∧S∧Φ) lies far outside it. So whatever warrant the conclusion has, it cannot be the warrant ordinary modal claims have.

The reply is that the conclusion is not an output of that method, and the point is methodological rather than defensive. The argument nowhere asks the reader to imagine a world and report what is found there. It asks the reader to *specify* one and observe what the specification requires. Those are different operations, and only the second is publicly checkable. [§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5) is the clearest case: it does not invite the objector to picture a world lacking the structural conditions, it invites the objector to describe one, and the argument turns on what the description turns out to contain. An invitation to describe can be accepted or declined in a way an invitation to imagine cannot, and its results can be inspected by someone who does not share the imaginer's phenomenology. Van Inwagen's skepticism is calibrated against a faculty; the derivation does not run on that faculty.

The inversion is worth stating plainly, because it is the book's general shape. Where the standard method treats *I can conceive of it* as evidence for possibility, the method here treats *the attempt to specify it consumes what it denies* as evidence for impossibility. The first is a report about the person; the second is a result about the attempt.

*Second.* The parity form presses that the reply has not escaped anything. The premises of the derivation are themselves modal claims (that a way must have direction, difference, and bearer; that no world can lack the conditions), and modal claims are what the skepticism targets. Relocating the warrant from imagination to specification changes the vocabulary of the defense without changing what is being defended.

The reply distinguishes two ways a modal verdict can be reached. One surveys possibilities and reports what is found among them, and that method requires epistemic access to the possibilities surveyed, which at remote distances is exactly what van Inwagen denies is available. The other attempts to construct a specification and finds that the construction cannot be completed, and that method requires no access to anything remote. The attempt is made here, with materials available here, and its failure is observed here. That *no way* and *impossible* are two names for one verdict is the surface expression of the point: a no-way result is reached by trying and failing, not by looking and not finding. The premises the parity objection targets are of the second kind. They are not reports about distant worlds but results about what a description must contain in order to be a description of anything at all, and their test is performable at zero distance.

*Third.* The reliability form is the strongest, and it comes from both directions. @rocaRoyes2011 presses that conceivability-based methods do not deliver *de re* modal knowledge of the kind essentialist conclusions require. From the other side @hawke2011 argues that van Inwagen's own similarity-to-ordinary-life criterion is unstable, either permitting too much or forbidding the ordinary knowledge it means to protect. Pressed at the present argument, the form asks why an inability to complete a specification should indicate impossibility rather than a limit on the specifier. Every argument from failure-to-construct risks being an argument from ignorance.

The worry is granted in general and answered in the particular. Inability to specify is defeasible evidence, never proof, and an argument that rested on bare inability would be worthless. What distinguishes the cases the book relies on is that the failure is *diagnosed* rather than merely encountered. When the objector attempts to specify a world lacking the structural conditions, the attempt does not simply stall; it proceeds by individuating that world from others, locating it as a state that obtains, and contrasting it with the worlds it differs from, which is to deploy distinction, succession, and bearing in the act of denying them. That is a demonstrated self-defeat with a stated mechanism, not an absence of imagination. The distinction between *I cannot think how* and *the attempt consumes what it denies* is the whole of the reply, and only the second carries weight.

::: {.premise}
**The Specification Test** · *Standard*

1. For a remote candidate p, the question is not whether ◇p is imaginable but whether p can be specified.

1. A specification is adequate only if it does not deploy what p denies.

1. Where every attempted specification deploys what p denies, and the deployment can be exhibited, the failure is diagnosed rather than merely encountered.

1. A diagnosed failure is evidence of impossibility. An undiagnosed failure is evidence only about the specifier.

1. Negative results are claimed here only where (3) holds, and are to be marked as conjectural where it does not.

:::

The standard cuts against the book as well as for it, which is the reason to adopt it. It commits the argument to marking which of its negative results are diagnosed and which rest on nothing better than an unproductive search, and any result of the second kind is owed a downgrade rather than a defense.

That marking has been carried out rather than promised. Across the load-bearing negative results of Chapters 2 and 3 — the Negation Seal at [§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), the null-state reductio and the subtraction reply at [§3.2.6](convergence.html#sec-3-2-6), the fictionalist escape at [§3.3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3-3), the masking test at [§2.4.12](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-12), the conceivability trap at [§3.3.4](convergence.html#sec-3-3-4) — and across every verdict in the Chapter 4 ledger, the results the argument relies on are diagnosed in the sense clause 3 requires. One exception was found and corrected. A verdict on strict temporal unreality had been recorded as an incoherence result when the section supporting it claims only an act-side burden and leaves the object-side error theory open ([§4.2.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-5)); it now states the weaker result. The exception is reported here rather than silently repaired, because a standard whose first application finds nothing is not being applied. The pattern behind it is worth naming as well: the failure was not an undiagnosed argument but a summary that claimed more than the section beneath it, which is where this standard is likely to be broken again.

An ally is available and should be recorded, though the argument does not depend on it. @williamson2007 [ch. 5] argues that modal knowledge is not the deliverance of a special faculty at all but a byproduct of the ordinary capacity to evaluate counterfactuals, which is exercised constantly and is not obviously less reliable at metaphysical distances than at everyday ones. If that account is right, van Inwagen's skepticism loses its target, because there is no distinct modal faculty whose calibration range can be exceeded. The present reply is deliberately weaker and does not require Williamson's account to be correct. It requires only that specification is a different operation from imagination, and that its failures can be diagnosed.

*What closes.* Van Inwagen's challenge is not answered by showing that modal vocabulary is meaningful, which is why [§4.1.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-6) does not answer it, and it is not answered by producing a confident intuition at the relevant distance, which is what the challenge forbids. It is answered by declining the method the challenge is calibrated against. The conclusion is reached by attempted specification and diagnosed failure rather than by imaginative survey, and those failures are exhibited rather than reported. What remains of the objection is a standing demand, correctly placed: that the book distinguish the results whose failures it can diagnose from the results where it has not succeeded in finding a counterexample. The demand is accepted. Van Inwagen was right about the faculty, and right that most of what has been built on it should be given up; the argument here is built on something else.

### 4.1.14 Impossible Worlds and Relative Modality {#sec-4-1-14}

Two pressures are often filed together and should be separated, because they attack different parts of the same sentence. One enlarges the space of worlds to include impossible ones [@priest2005; @bertoJago2019; @nolan1997]. The other relativizes the quantifier to a contextually supplied background [@kratzer2012]. The first asks whether □(T∧S∧Φ) has been quantifying over too little. The second asks whether its □ means anything absolute at all.

*First.* The non-normal worlds form is the technically sharpest objection in this section, and it is aimed at the S5 derivation rather than at the structural conclusion. Non-normal worlds are the standard device for invalidating the rule of necessitation: at such a world, logical truths may fail, and modal formulas are evaluated by stipulation rather than by the accessibility clause. Admit them and the characteristic S5 axiom is no longer guaranteed, since ◇C may hold at the actual world while □◇C fails at a non-normal one. A semantics that includes them yields a non-normal modal logic in which the lift the argument uses is simply unavailable.

The reply has two stages, and the first is a redirection rather than a defense. The book does not need the lift. [§3.5.4](convergence.html#sec-3-5-4) and [§3.5.5](convergence.html#sec-3-5-5) reach the conclusion along a route that does not run through S5 at all, and a critic who blocks the lift by admitting non-normal worlds still arrives at the same place. The S5 derivation is one line among several, and the semantic objection reaches one line.

The second stage is the substantive one. An impossible world is admitted as a *representation* of an inconsistent content, not as a genuine alternative way for reality to be. @nolan1997 makes the point in defending the modest approach: impossible worlds earn their keep as representational devices for reasoning about inconsistent scenarios, and admitting them carries no commitment to their being possibilities. But a representational device is an item with content, and content is structured. The reply developed against linguistic ersatzism at [§4.4.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-2) applies here without modification: distinct representations must be distinct (the S-role), must be evaluated in an ordered succession of acts (the T-role), and must be borne by something that carries the content (the Φ-role). Enlarging the space of representations enlarges the space of representations. The □ in □(T∧S∧Φ) ranges over genuine alternatives, and no number of additional representations adds one.

A further point closes the limit case. An impossible world at which T, S, and Φ all fail is not merely an inconsistent scenario but the null state, and the argument of [§3.2.6](convergence.html#sec-3-2-6) is that the null state is unspecifiable rather than merely inconsistent. The distinction matters exactly here, because the impossible-worlds theorist is professionally in the business of hosting inconsistent contents. A round square is hostable: it has parts to describe, and the description can be given and then found contradictory. The null state has no parts to describe, and [§3.3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3-3) makes the corresponding point against the fictionalist. An impossible-worlds semantics can host any content that can be stated. What it cannot do is supply a content where none can be stated, and that is the case the necessity claim turns on.

*Second.* The hyperintensionality form is the actual motivation behind most of the literature, and the honest response is concession rather than reply. @bertoJago2019 argue that necessity is too coarse a sieve for many of the distinctions metaphysics needs: necessarily equivalent contents are not thereby the same content, and a framework whose finest grain is necessary equivalence will misdescribe the differences between them.

That is granted without reservation, and nothing in the argument resists it. The claim defended is that T, S, and Φ obtain at every genuine alternative. It is not the claim that they are constitutive in a hyperintensional sense, nor that the propositions expressing them are individuated by anything finer than necessity. Whether a further, more discriminating notion is required to state what the structural conditions *are*, as opposed to where they obtain, is the essence-prior question, and it is engaged at [§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10) rather than settled here. Hyperintensional distinctions cut below the necessity claim without cutting into it.

*Third.* The relative-modality form runs from linguistic semantics. On the standard account [@kratzer2012], a modal expression is interpreted relative to a contextually supplied modal base together with an ordering source, and the many flavours of necessity (epistemic, deontic, nomic, metaphysical) are one machine supplied with different backgrounds. If that is right, metaphysical necessity is not a privileged absolute but one setting among many, and □(T∧S∧Φ) reduces to a claim about what follows given a particular background. Another background, another verdict.

The reply is that context-relativity in this framework operates on the *restriction*, not on the *domain*. A modal base selects a subset of the worlds to quantify over; it does not introduce worlds that were not there. The structural claim is about what every member of the domain instantiates, and a subset of a set whose members all instantiate the conditions has no member that fails to. Varying the background varies which necessities are salient and which are worth asserting. It cannot vary what a world is.

::: {.premise}
**Restriction Adds Nothing** · *Premises*

1. A modal base restricts the worlds quantified over to some subset of the global domain (Kratzer semantics).

1. □(T∧S∧Φ) states that every member of the global domain instantiates the structural conditions.

1. Every subset of the global domain has only members of the global domain.

1. So no choice of modal base delivers a world lacking the conditions.

1. Context-relativity therefore varies which necessities are asserted, not what any world is.

:::

The conclusion generalizes past Kratzer's framework specifically. Any relativization that proceeds by restricting a domain inherits the argument, because restriction is a subset operation and a subset operation cannot manufacture a member. A relativization that instead *replaces* the domain, supplying worlds the global domain lacks, is no longer a restriction and owes an account of where the new worlds came from and in what sense they are alternatives. That account is the one [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1) and [§4.4.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-2) already press for, and the demand is unchanged by relabeling the framework as semantic rather than metaphysical.

One clarification of scope is owed. Nothing above denies that there are genuinely relative modalities, or that most ordinary uses of *must* and *can* are relative in exactly Kratzer's way. The [§4.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4) overview grants this already. The claim is narrower: that a relative modality is a restriction on the field rather than a rival to it, and that the field is what the structural conclusion describes.

*What closes.* Impossible worlds and relative modality both appear to widen or shift the quantifier and neither does. Non-normal worlds block one derivation of S5, which the argument can afford because [§3.5.4](convergence.html#sec-3-5-4) supplies a route that never used it, and they otherwise multiply representations rather than alternatives; the representations are themselves structured, so the multiplication runs the ersatzist's problem again. Hyperintensionality is conceded outright and leaves the necessity claim standing at its own grain. Kratzer-style relativization restricts a domain it does not populate, and a restriction cannot produce a world the domain lacked. What all three share is a move from the formal apparatus to the metaphysics, and in each case the apparatus turns out to be describing the field rather than adding to it.

## 4.2 Time, Change, and the Changeless {#sec-4-2}

This cluster asks whether change can be absent from a real world. Each candidate is tested in the same way: does it genuinely describe a reality without change, or does it restore the conditions that make change possible?

The challenge bears most directly on the proof's claim that any reality permits change and on the identification of change-possibility with T∧S∧Φ. The subsections test whether a supposedly changeless account can do more than redescribe Time, Space, and Substance under another vocabulary.

A preliminary note before the named engagements. Two general intuitions support the positions taken up below. The first is that change might be denied at the limit: that some level beneath, above, or beside the changing world is itself unchanging, and that the unchanging level is the truer one. The second is that the appearance of change might be misleading: what looks like succession may be juxtaposition, what looks like persistence may be pattern. The argument grants the intuitions as intuitions and contests what they license: the structural conditions are derived at §[§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4)–2.7 from the actuality, possibility, and impossibility profile of change. Clearing the candidates below turns on the permission side alone: each is introduced as a reality from which change is absent, and each, on inspection, instantiates the conditions it was introduced to lack. That a candidate permits change suffices to answer it, and that sufficiency is the load-bearing claim for the cluster. The Frozen-World Test at [§2.4.11](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-11) argues that fully typed structure makes change possible; it does not show that every world must contain an actual transition or that every changeless interval is ∅. A frozen or silent world may retain the capacities and role-structure required for change. The cluster therefore tests whether the candidates remove those capacities. The subsections press the weaker, sufficient point and leave the stronger result standing behind it.

### 4.2.1 The Changeless Ground {#sec-4-2-1}

The classical theist proposes the most important exception to the claim that change pervades reality: a changeless ground (atemporal, aspatial, immaterial) exempt from all of it. Not frozen in time but outside time altogether. The doctrine has two tightly linked expressions. The first is static-being: God as timeless in the sense of possessing being without temporal instantiation. The second is eternal-present: God as timelessly simultaneous with every temporal moment, possessing life *tota simul*, whole and all at once.

@aquinas1947 develops both: God is *actus purus*, pure act without potency, entirely without temporal or spatial extension; God is also eternal in the Boethian sense, possessing illimitable life in complete simultaneity. @boethius524 introduces the eternal-present doctrine to resolve the foreknowledge problem: God knows all temporal events not by foreseeing them but by perceiving them as simultaneously present. Plantinga [-@plantinga1974b; -@plantinga2000] defends a modern version: the Maximally Great Being is a necessary, immaterial mind whose changelessness grounds rather than instantiates the changing world. @stumpKretzmann1981 refine eternity through their doctrine of ET-simultaneity (eternity–time simultaneity), a non-temporal simultaneity relation between God and temporal events. @leftow1991 develops a quasi-temporal eternity (QTE) variant. @barbour1999 proposes a physical analogue: Platonia, a timeless configuration space from which the experience of time arises as an illusion. The intuition is ancient, the defenders are serious. If any such being is coherent, it grounds structure without being subject to it.

The counter-construction bears on the argument's most ambitious reach. The argument claims that wherever change is possible, Time, Space, and Substance obtain. The classical theist counter-proposes a being for which change is not possible (for which T, S, and Φ are strictly inapplicable) and which grounds structure rather than participating in it. If such a being can exist, then □(T∧S∧Φ) as a claim about all of reality fails. Structure obtains wherever there is change, but something else obtains changelessly, and that something else is the ground.

A clarification before the moves. The argument's intermediate conclusion is □◇C: Reality necessarily permits change, not that change must always be occurring. The static-being objection treats these as different claims. They are not. Permission is not a fact about whether change happens in a being. It is a fact about what Reality structurally allows. A static being that exists within Reality exists in a Reality that already permits change, and that permission is structure. The objector is proposing something stronger: a being that exists outside Reality-as-structured. The shared structural failure has a name in advance. *Changeless* is a parasitic negation of Change, a quantifier internal to the domain of transitions, not a state outside it ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), Parasitic Negation). A ground specified as changeless either reduces to that quantifier and grounds nothing, since a quantifier is not a substrate, or smuggles in determinate features that instantiate the very domain the construction was meant to escape. Five forms of the move test that dilemma.

*First.* The Maximally Great Being move proposes a being atemporal, aspatial, and immaterial that possesses being without instantiating any of the three roles, grounding the structure without being part of it. A changeless being cannot be identified with ∅ merely from atemporality, aspatiality, or immateriality. At most, its being determinate rather than nothing supplies a thin difference-role. The further step from qualitative or logical distinctness to Spatiality's loaded type — relational extension within a manifold — requires the independent bridge argued elsewhere ([§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7)); it cannot be assumed against the classical theist at the outset.

Now consider grounding: the static being is proposed as the ground of existence, something that produces or sustains structure. Any grounding relation, whether construed as causal production or as metaphysical/explanatory dependence, requires determinate relata, asymmetric direction between them, and real obtaining. An atemporal grounding theorist will deny that it must persist through a temporal interval; the simultaneous-causation move is taken up in detail at [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3). The local conclusion is therefore role-level: a wholly indeterminate ground cannot ground, while a determinate grounding relation instantiates difference, direction, and bearing. Whether those roles require the fully temporal and physical types is the separate role-to-type question. The proposal seeks a ground with none of the Conditions that grounding requires, and so leaves itself with no determinate way to specify that ground at all.

*Second.* The Aristotelian non-temporal priority move refines the claim: the static being is prior to the structure in the order of explanation, not in the order of time. Formal causes (what a thing essentially is) and final causes (what a thing is for) involve non-temporal ordering; a changeless being can stand in formal or final priority to the structure without standing in temporal priority. Non-temporal priority is still structural priority. Formal priority requires the ground to be structurally distinct from what it grounds, requiring the difference-role to hold ground and grounded apart. Final priority is not temporal succession, and the Aristotelian point should be granted in full. But it is still an asymmetric ordering relation: source and end, potency and actuality, orientation and fulfillment. The structural argument does not need to redescribe final causality as clock-time. It needs only the weaker claim that final priority is not structureless priority. To ground structure, the static being must stand to what it grounds in some determinate ordering relation (formal, final, logical, or temporal) and a determinate ordering relation already requires distinguishable relata, asymmetric priority, and a stable relation between them. The defining feature of the static being, its non-instantiation of the roles, is exactly what disqualifies it from standing in any grounding relation at all.

*Third.* The Boethian eternal present presses a different line: God exists not in time but in an eternal present, a timeless simultaneity from which the whole of temporal history is present at once, as a landscape is present to an observer on a hill. From eternity, all temporal moments are equally present, not as a series God remembers or anticipates but as a totality God possesses, *tota simul*. This is not static immobility but complete, simultaneous, perfect possession of illimitable life.

The eternal-present view should not be caricatured as requiring God to track a moving present from inside an A-series (McTaggart's term for the tensed past/present/future ordering, distinct from the tenseless B-series of earlier/later relations; [§4.2.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-5) develops the distinction). Its point is exactly the opposite: God knows each temporal event in its temporal location without occupying one moment rather than another. The pressure arises when the doctrine is asked to preserve more than tenseless total knowledge. Classical theism also wants divine responsiveness, providence, answer to prayer, and knowledge of creaturely events as events to which God stands in determinate relation. Those commitments require more than the passive possession of a static array. They require asymmetric dependence between prayer and answer, between creaturely event and divine knowledge, between what is asked and what is given.

If the Boethian account gives only B-series access to the whole temporal order, it has not yet supplied response in the operative sense; prayer and answer stand as correlated elements of the array rather than in a response relation. If it supplies genuine response, it has introduced ordered asymmetry, distinguishable relata, and a stable relation between them, the structural roles in the very place the doctrine was meant to exempt from them. The objection is not that God must know “currently” in the creaturely mode. It is that the theological predicates the doctrine wants to preserve require a structured relation that mere eternal co-presence does not by itself provide.

*Fourth.* Stump and Kretzmann's ET-simultaneity offers a technically refined version: a non-temporal simultaneity relation between God and temporal events. God is simultaneous with every temporal moment, not in the sense of being at the same time as each, but in the sense of standing in a “simultaneity in the mode of eternity” relation to each. This relation is neither temporal nor non-existent; it is a third kind, definable precisely.

ET-simultaneity replaces ordinary temporal simultaneity with a sui generis relation between eternity and temporal events. That relation supplies determinate relatedness, but relatedness alone does not entail spatial extension. The live objection is instead whether ET-simultaneity can support asymmetric response and agency without importing temporal succession; the doctrine should not be rejected simply by redescribing every relation as Space. @mctaggart1908 argues that genuine change requires the A-series; agency, which involves change, inherits the requirement, and ET-simultaneity forgoes that agency in the trade.

*Fifth.* Barbour's Platonia offers the most radical version, physical rather than theistic: a timeless configuration space with the experience of time an illusion arising from “time capsules”, configurations that happen to encode apparent memories. No being, just the static configuration space.

Platonia is a world whose description requires time in the describing. Configurations must be individuated (each is this configuration rather than that) requiring relational non-identity (Space). The configuration space must subsist as one structural whole that bears its configurations (Substance). Distinguishing one configuration from another requires cognitive succession from one to the next (Time). The act of describing Platonia occurs in time, but that establishes only an act-side fact about the describer. It does not by itself show that Platonia's represented content is temporal. The object-side question is whether the configuration space contains an intrinsic ordering or dynamical structure adequate to recover time; that must be argued from the model rather than inferred from the description event.

A kindred softening worth naming is Leftow's [-@leftow1991] QTE (quasi-temporal eternity) which allows God to stand in quasi-temporal relations to creatures while remaining intrinsically timeless. QTE is the weakest version of the doctrine, and it concedes most explicitly that relations to temporal creatures require some structural analog of Time. The position is honest about the cost: intrinsic atemporality is preserved only by distinguishing intrinsic from relational structural features, and the relational features do the work that the structural roles require. Open-theist softenings (Hasker, Sanders) concede still more (temporal duration, genuine response, real relation to creatures) and concede the structural commitments most explicitly.

*What converges.* The five forms exhaust the outside-proposal, and each fails the same way: reaching outside structure only to find structure already there. The Maximally Great Being has no foothold for specification (a wholly indeterminate ground cannot ground, and a determinate grounding relation instantiates difference, direction, and bearing); non-temporal priority is still structural priority, since formal and final precedence require the very conditions they were meant to escape; the Boethian eternal present either supplies only B-series co-presence, which is not yet response, or supplies genuine response and with it the ordered asymmetry it was meant to exempt; ET-simultaneity supplies determinate relatedness but forgoes asymmetric response and agency in the trade; and Platonia's configurations are individuated in a space that bears them, while the succession its description deploys poses a question the model has yet to answer.

The static being is proposed from within the structure it is supposed to precede: a present is a position in a sequence, and with the sequence removed, “present” names nothing.

Sibling theistic counter-constructions: the simultaneous-causation mechanism classical theism uses to connect the eternal God to the temporal world is answered in [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3), and the divine-simplicity construction of the eternal God's internal metaphysics in [§5.2.1](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-2-1).

### 4.2.2 Shoemaker's Time Without Change {#sec-4-2-2}

Sydney Shoemaker, writing at Cornell in 1969, constructs a universe built on local freezes: a region in which nothing moves, decays, or interacts for a stretch of time, then resumes exactly where it left off, displaced from the ongoing world by the length of the freeze. He multiplies the case into three rooms subject to periodic freezes on staggered intervals, a universe built to let observers in one region infer the freezes of another by clock comparison. Run the arithmetic long enough and the periodicities coincide: once every sixty years, all three regions freeze at once. During that year, by Shoemaker's construction, nothing changes anywhere in the universe. And yet, the argument runs, time still passes.

The inference is staged with such care that the paper became the canonical modern defense of time-without-change in the analytic literature, the standing objection to every Aristotelian who thinks time requires motion. The objection is serious. Pressed to the global limit, however, it collapses under its own construction.

Shoemaker ("Time Without Change," *The Journal of Philosophy* [-@shoemaker1969]) offers the most carefully constructed defense of time without change in the analytic literature. Local cessation of change is coherent: a region of a universe can freeze while the rest continues, and the frozen region can be re-integrated into the ongoing temporal order when it resumes. That is true, and the present account grants it without cost. What is contested is whether the scenario extends to a universe-wide cessation of change while time continues to pass: whether Shoemaker's construction, pressed to the global case, describes a coherent modal possibility or collapses into incoherence when the apparatus that supports the inference is removed.

The literature on time-without-change runs back to Aristotle's *Physics* [@aristotle1984, IV.10–14], where time is defined as the number of motion with respect to the before-and-after, and an unchanging universe therefore fails the conditions for time's obtaining. Newton's *Principia* [-@newton1687] develops the opposing substantivalist position: absolute time flows uniformly without regard to anything external, and its passage is independent of whatever change happens to take place within it. McTaggart ("The Unreality of Time," [-@mctaggart1908]) poses the foundational question of what change itself consists in, the A-series/B-series distinction that structures the modern debate. Prior ("Changes in Events and Changes in Things," [-@prior1968]) sharpens the change-theoretic tradition. Shoemaker's 1969 paper is the modern inheritor of Newtonian substantivalism (time as an independent substance whose passage does not depend on any change within it) and the argument's most rigorously worked-out form. Newton-Smith (*The Structure of Time* [-@newtonSmith1980]) defends the Shoemaker conclusion at length.

Against the substantivalist line: Le Poidevin (*Change, Cause, and Contradiction* [-@lePoidevin1991]) presses the verificationist worry about the global-freeze extension; Lombard (*Events: A Metaphysical Study* [-@lombard1986]) develops an events-based metaphysics on which change is constitutive of time; @forbes1993 challenges the inferential structure of Shoemaker's thought experiment; Mellor (*Real Time II* [-@mellor1998]) and Craig (*The Tensed Theory of Time* [-@craig2000]) defend change-theoretic views from B-theoretic and tensed angles respectively; Horwich (*Asymmetries in Time* [-@horwich1987]) works the change-primitive side of the debate; Sider (*Four-Dimensionalism* [-@sider2001]) develops the perdurantist alternative on which change is cashed out through temporal parts; Dainton (*Time and Space*, 2nd ed. [-@dainton2010]) gives the standard survey; Bardon (*A Brief History of the Philosophy of Time* [-@bardon2013]) places Shoemaker's contribution in its long historical arc. The present reply sits within the change-theoretic tradition, closest to the Mellor–Le Poidevin wing, and adds what neither specifies on its own: Shoemaker's inference runs on the very persistence the scenario was trying to eliminate, and that persistence is named explicitly by the structural-role apparatus of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6).

The challenge bears directly on [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6). The Modal Identity established there is bidirectional: necessarily, change-possibility obtains if and only if T ∧ S ∧ Φ obtains, and the two are one structural fact under two descriptions. Shoemaker's argument exhibits, if successful, time during an interval in which no change is occurring. That does not by itself break the book's Modal Identity, whose left side is the *possibility* of change rather than its continuous actuality. A globally frozen interval bracketed by change may still belong to a world in which change is possible. The relevant question is therefore whether the case preserves change-capacity and structural continuity, not whether a transition occurs during every interval. What follows is narrow by design. The reply locates the substantivalist move as a relocation rather than an elimination.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute is not with Shoemaker's local scenario: rooms that freeze while others continue are coherent, and the argument of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) does not contest them. Nor is the dispute with Shoemaker's inferential apparatus considered in isolation: given three regions freezing on staggered intervals, one can indeed calculate when they coincide, and the calculation is sound. What is contested is the step from the local scenario, where change continues in the unfrozen regions, to the global scenario, where the universe as a whole freezes. Three forms of the move take up the objection at three depths: the inferential-structure form, the level-invariance form, and the extension-to-the-limit form. The space they canvass is the space Shoemaker's argument can occupy. The reply argues that each confirms the Modal Identity rather than breaking it.

*First.* The inference is always from observed change, not to time-without-change. Shoemaker's observers reconstruct A's frozen interval by reference to B's and C's ongoing change: by counting B's cycles while A is frozen, by watching the clock. When all three regions freeze simultaneously, no such reconstruction is available from inside the freeze. The claim that time still passes during the global freeze is not a direct measurement but an extrapolation from the periodicities on either side of the gap, underwritten by the assumption that the pattern continues across it. That assumption is Substance (the persistence condition [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names) carrying the identity of the periodicity across the interval. Without Φ operating across the freeze, the post-freeze regions are not the pre-freeze regions resumed; they are new regions with coincidentally similar patterns, and the inference collapses into correlation. Shoemaker's reasoning works because the universe stays the same universe across the pause. A universe that does not stay the same across the pause cannot underwrite the reasoning. The scenario describes a gap inside a universe whose Substance remains intact across it. That persistence is precisely what the structural conditions name.

*Second.* Level-invariance ([§2.1.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-7)) applies to the containing universe, not just to each region. The regions are genuinely distinct (S). The freezes occur in a determinate order relative to one another (T). The containing frame persists across the freezes to underwrite each region's re-emergence with preserved identity (Φ). The simultaneous freeze is a local phenomenon within a structured universe, a phenomenon the universe's structural conditions make describable in the first place. Shoemaker has described a universe with change in which certain regions undergo periodic cessation, not a universe without change. The time-without-change the argument purports to exhibit is always the frozen region rather than the universe, and the scale of the freeze is not the scale of the claim.

*Third.* Pushed to the global limit, the scenario contains no internal clock or observer during the freeze. That creates an epistemic and verification problem, not an immediate metaphysical contradiction: a thought experiment may specify unobserved structure, and observers before and after may infer a duration from the wider history. The structural reply should therefore not depend on the absence of a thinker. Its narrower point is that the construction preserves cross-freeze identity, periodic dispositions, and the possibility of resumed change; it is a frozen interval within a change-permitting world, not a world lacking the conditions of change. The fully extended Shoemaker scenario is therefore not a universe with time but no change; it is a universe with change containing a region where nothing happens, which is exactly the case the first two replies already handle. The bidirectional identity survives because the scenario, followed through, never actually breaks it. The Aristotelian position is recovered by the structural apparatus: time is not the number of motion merely, but motion's structural conditions are internal to what time consists in. Strip them and what remains is not empty duration but ∅.

A kindred move drops the Shoemaker apparatus for classical Newtonian absolutism: time is an independent substance whose passage does not depend on any change within it. Newton's *Principia* [-@newton1687] articulates the position most clearly, and @newtonSmith1980 carries it forward. The reply is the same in older vocabulary, with one dependency made explicit. An absolute time independent of change must still be individuated (this moment of absolute time distinct from that moment), and, on the change-theoretic conception of Temporality defended at [§1.4.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-4-1) (Directionality as structural, not imposed) and abductively at [§7.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2), that individuation is the structural fact [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) identifies. Absolute-time substantivalism relocates the structural roles into the substance of time itself rather than eliminating them; the substance of time contains distinctness of moments (S), directed ordering (T), and persistence across the ordering (Φ) as the conditions of its being a time at all.[^4-2-2-absolute-time-substantivalism]

Another kindred: a deflationary verificationist move [@lePoidevin1991; earlier @ayer1936] that the global-freeze scenario is meaningless because no possible observation could confirm or disconfirm it. The structural reply accepts the verificationist point for the specific purpose for which it was introduced while declining the broader verificationism: the scenario is not meaningless; it is underspecified in a way that dissolves under analysis, which is a stronger claim than verificationism alone supports.

*What closes.* Three depths and none lets the global extension stand. The inference from local freeze to global freeze runs on Substance (the very persistence condition Φ specifies) carrying the identity of the periodicity across the interval; without that persistence the post-freeze regions are new regions with coincidentally similar patterns, and the inference collapses into correlation. Level-invariance: the scenario describes a structured universe containing regions of freeze, not an unstructured universe frozen entire. The fully extended scenario preserves cross-freeze identity, periodic dispositions, and the possibility of resumed change; it is a frozen interval within a change-permitting world, which is exactly the case the first two replies already handle.

The emergent-time objection, that time is derivative rather than fundamental, is [§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3). The momentariness objection, that persistence is illusory, is [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8). The changeless-ground objection, that a timeless being grounds the structure from outside, is [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1). The Shoemaker objection occupies a distinct position relative to these three: it grants that time is real and that persistence obtains, and contests only the bidirectional linkage of change and time. The reply is therefore correspondingly narrow: the target is the global extension of the local scenario, not the coherence of time or of persistence in general.

What Shoemaker's argument supports is stronger than merely local cessation: it gives a serious model of an interval, potentially global, during which no change occurs while temporal structure is retained. The structural account can grant this because its modal claim concerns permission for change, not uninterrupted occurrence. The claim of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is that the fundamental ontological structure cannot instantiate Time without instantiating change, not that every subregion must undergo change at every moment. Shoemaker has produced a counterexample to a claim the argument does not make.

One clarification for the Shoemakerian reader. The argument addressed here is the 1969 time-without-change paper, not Shoemaker's signature causal theory of properties (*Causality and Properties*, 1980; *Identity, Cause, and Mind*, 1984/2003), on which properties are individuated by their causal powers. That broader thesis is not a further counterexample to [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) but an instance of it: causal individuation presupposes the very structural roles the account names, since a causal power is exercised across an ordering (T), among distinct relata (S), and is borne by what persists long enough to exercise it (Φ). The omission of the causal theory from the reply above reflects the scope of the time-without-change objection, not a narrowing of the account.

What the paper actually gives its readers, followed through, is not the universe-without-change it seems to promise but something better: the sharpest available demonstration that inferring time-without-change requires a standpoint where change is occurring.

[^4-2-2-absolute-time-substantivalism]: The reply that absolute-time substantivalism relocates the structural roles rather than eliminating them is not neutral between conceptions of time, and the dependency is worth marking. A purist who takes time to be bare duration (mere ordering, with influence occurring within time rather than constituting it) can decline the identification of a moment's individuation with T ∧ S ∧ Φ. Two costs attend the exit, and the relational account pays neither. First, individuating the moments of an empty, changeless absolute time without relational extension requires primitive thisness: the haecceity Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles and the hole-argument literature press, which sophisticated substantivalism can absorb only by surrendering haecceitism; the relational individuation [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) supplies (S) needs no such posit. Second, by the lights of the change-theoretic conception defended here (a cost the purist will not grant is one) a duration stripped of all influence is ordering without succession, the [§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7) ordered-set structure rather than Time. The line can be held, but at the price of primitive identity and the divorce of time from succession: a trade the relocation reply exposes rather than the neutral refutation it can be mistaken for.

### 4.2.3 Emergent Time {#sec-4-2-3}

Suppose time is not fundamental. Suppose what we call time is a feature that emerges from a deeper, timeless level of reality: the way temperature emerges from molecular motion, or the way solidity emerges from atomic lattices. The fundamental description of the world, on this proposal, makes no reference to time; time is a useful approximation at our scale, a coarse-grained feature that drops out of the deeper physics in the appropriate limit. If this is right, then the structural account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is at best a description of the emergent layer, not of fundamental reality. The classical theist, sensing again an opening, can locate the changeless ground at the timeless fundamental level and the structural roles at the emergent surface.

The move is not idle. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation, the canonical equation of quantum gravity, contains no time variable; the wavefunction of the universe is timeless, and the appearance of time in our experience is to be recovered (somehow) from a fundamentally timeless formalism. @pageWootters1983 develop the most influential proposal: time emerges as a correlation between subsystems of a timeless universe, with one subsystem serving as a clock for the rest. Barbour's *The End of Time* [-@barbour1999] develops Platonia: a timeless configuration space from which temporal experience emerges as “time capsules,” configurations that happen to encode apparent memories. Rovelli's *The Order of Time* [-@rovelli2018] offers a relational account: time is the structure of correlations between physical systems, not a fundamental backdrop. Smolin's *Time Reborn* [-@smolin2013] takes the opposite line, defending time's fundamentality, but the position the present reply targets is the timeless-fundamental position, not Smolin's.

In the philosophy of time, kindred views include Albert's *Time and Chance* [-@albert2000], which derives temporal asymmetry from the past-hypothesis and statistical-mechanical considerations; Price's *Time's Arrow and Archimedes' Point* [-@price1996], which argues that the apparent directedness of time is a perspectival feature; Reichenbach's *The Direction of Time* [-@reichenbach1956], the classical mid-century treatment of time's arrow; Maudlin's *The Metaphysics Within Physics* [-@maudlin2007], which defends time's fundamentality against eliminativist readings. Anderson's *The Problem of Time* [-@andersonEdward2017] gives the technical state of play in canonical quantum gravity. The literature is vast and the technical questions are subtle. The present reply targets the structural claim: that time is derivative rather than fundamental, and therefore that the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) obtain at most at an emergent layer.

Three forms of the move develop the position at three depths: the strict-emergence form, the correlational-time form, and the relational-time form. The reply argues that each fails for the same structural reason at increasing levels of refinement.

*First.* The strict-emergence form claims that the fundamental level is timeless and that time is a phenomenon of the emergent layer only, in the way that temperature is a phenomenon of bulk thermodynamics and not of individual molecules. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation, on this reading, describes a fundamentally timeless universe, and the appearance of time at our scale is a coarse-grained illusion.

The analogy with temperature does not carry the weight the position needs. Temperature is emergent in the sense that it is a statistical property of an underlying dynamics that is itself temporal: the molecules move, collide, and exchange energy in time, and the bulk property of temperature is a statistical summary of that temporal dynamics. The molecular dynamics is not itself temperature, but it is itself temporal; the emergence is from a more fundamental temporal description to a less fundamental temporal description. For time itself to be emergent in the analogous sense would require a more fundamental description that is itself non-temporal but supports the emergence of time, and this is exactly what the strict-emergence form needs and exactly what the position cannot supply. The Wheeler–DeWitt equation does not describe a non-temporal dynamics from which time emerges; it describes a wavefunction satisfying a constraint, and the recovery of time from the wavefunction is the open problem the field has been working on for decades. To call the formalism “timeless” is to describe the constraint, not the dynamics; the dynamics, if there is to be one, is what the recovery program is meant to produce.

The deeper structural point: any proposed fundamental level that supports the emergence of time must contain the resources for time to emerge from it. Those resources are the structural roles [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names. Distinctness of fundamental states (S), an ordering across them sufficient to support the emergent direction (T), and a persistence spanning the ordering sufficient to underwrite the emergent identity of objects across the emergent time (Φ). The fundamental level can be called “timeless” only in the restricted sense that it does not contain time as we recognize time at our scale. It cannot be timeless in the sense of lacking the structural roles: if it lacked them, no time could emerge from it.

*Second.* The Page–Wootters correlational form is more refined: time emerges as the correlation between two subsystems of a timeless universe, with one subsystem (the clock) serving as a reference relative to which the other subsystem (the rest) appears to evolve. Mathematically, the global wavefunction is timeless; the conditional wavefunction (conditioning on the clock state) evolves in the clock variable. The conditional evolution is what we observe as time.

The correlation between subsystems requires distinctness of subsystems (S), an ordering of clock states sufficient to support the conditional evolution (T), and a persistence of the universal wavefunction across the conditional structure (Φ). The Page–Wootters construction is internally coherent and structurally informative: it shows that something that looks like time at one level can be derived from a timeless-looking formalism at another level. What it does not show is that the structural roles are absent at the fundamental level. The clock subsystem must be distinct from the rest (S obtains). The clock states must stand in an ordering that the conditional evolution tracks (T obtains in the clock structure). The universal wavefunction must persist across the conditional construction (Φ obtains globally). The construction is a relabeling of where T is located (in the clock variable rather than in a global parameter), not an elimination of T.

*Third.* The relational-time form, developed most influentially by Rovelli, claims that time is not a backdrop in which physical systems evolve but a structure of correlations between physical systems. There is no absolute time; there is only the relative evolution of one system with respect to another. Each system is a clock for the others, and the appearance of a universal time is the coarse-grained agreement of many such relative clocks.

Relational time is a thesis about the metaphysics of time, not its elimination. Rovelli's view is closer to Leibnizian relationism than to eliminativism: time consists in relations between physical systems rather than in an absolute backdrop, but the relations are real and structural and do the work that absolute time was supposed to do. The reply, accordingly, is not that relationism is incoherent (it is not) but that relationism is not a refutation of the structural conditions: it is a relocation of where the conditions are instantiated. The relations are between distinct systems (S), they support directed evolution (T), and they persist across the systems' interactions (Φ). Relational time *is* the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) in a relationist metaphysics.

A kindred move is the past-hypothesis style derivation (Albert, Price): the apparent directedness of time is derived from a low-entropy initial condition plus statistical mechanics, with no fundamental time-asymmetric law. The reply is the same. The derivation requires distinctness of microstates (S), an ordering across them sufficient to define entropy increase (T), and a dynamical evolution that preserves the relevant structural facts across the increase (Φ). The asymmetry of time is derived from the past-hypothesis, but the symmetric temporal structure is presupposed by the derivation, not eliminated by it.

Another kindred is the eternalist/B-theoretic position that the appearance of temporal becoming is a perspectival feature of conscious experience while the world itself is a four-dimensional manifold without genuine becoming. This is treated separately at [§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6) (the B-theoretic block). The B-theoretic eternalist accepts T (the four-dimensional manifold is temporally extended) and contests only the metaphysical reality of A-series becoming. The dispute is therefore not about whether T obtains but about its metaphysical character.

*What converges.* Three forms and none lets the elimination of T at the fundamental level stand. Strict emergence cannot supply a non-temporal fundamental dynamics; the Wheeler–DeWitt ‘timelessness’ is a constraint on the wavefunction, not a non-temporal dynamics from which time can emerge. The Page–Wootters construction relocates T from a global parameter to a clock subsystem; relocation is not elimination. Relational time is a metaphysics of time as relations between systems, not an elimination of the structural role time plays. Each move produces a redescription of where the structural conditions are located, not a description of a world in which they are absent. The shared failure is structural: *timeless* and *never* are parasitic negations of Time, quantifiers internal to the temporal domain rather than substrates outside it ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5), Parasitic Negation). A ¬∃t (the assertion that there is no t, no temporal coordinate, no instant) cannot ground an emergence of time, since a quantifier is not a level. The three forms collapse into relocations because there is nothing else coherent for them to be.

Sibling counter-constructions: the changeless-ground objection, on which a timeless being grounds the structure from outside, is [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1). The Shoemaker objection, on which time can obtain without change, is [§4.2.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-2). The momentariness objection, on which persistence is illusory, is [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8). The B-theoretic block objection, on which the temporal manifold lacks genuine becoming, is [§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6).

What the emergent-time literature genuinely establishes is worth preserving: the time of our experience is not the time of fundamental physics in any direct mapping. The clock-based time of relativity is not the conditional time of canonical quantum gravity; the entropic arrow is not the relativistic light-cone structure; the phenomenal flow of conscious experience is not the parameter of the Schrödinger equation. There are many time-like structures in physics, and the relations between them are subtle and partially open. The structural account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is consistent with this plurality. What the account requires is that any proposed fundamental level that supports the emergence or relocation or relabeling of time-like structure contains the resources (distinctness, ordering, persistence) for that emergence or relocation or relabeling to be possible. The structural roles are not the time of any particular physical theory; they are the conditions any theory must instantiate to have time-like structure at all.

The research program around the Wheeler–DeWitt equation has occupied physicists for over half a century; no consensus on the recovery of time has emerged. What has emerged is a more careful articulation of what the structural conditions of time actually are, and the present reply is a beneficiary of that articulation. The fundamental level may turn out to be very different from the time of our experience. It will not turn out to be without distinctness, ordering, and persistence, because if it were, no time could emerge from it, and the recovery program would have nothing to recover.

### 4.2.4 Platonism {#sec-4-2-4}

What of mathematics? Numbers seem to be the paradigm of changeless objects. The number 7 is not somewhere; it does not move; it does not decay; it does not depend on anything for its existence; it stands in eternal mathematical relations with the other numbers and with the structures it figures in. If anything is a counterexample to the present account, it is the realm of mathematical objects: abstract, atemporal, aspatial, immaterial, and indubitably real (or at least real enough that mathematical practice across cultures and millennia has converged on remarkably stable conclusions about them). The Platonist about mathematics has the most natural case for objects exempt from the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6).

The move is venerable. Plato's Forms, the original Platonist proposal, are paradigmatic of changeless reality: the Form of the Triangle, of Justice, of the Good, each eternal and unchanging, the temporal world of becoming a degraded copy of the timeless world of being. Frege's *Grundlagen der Arithmetik* [-@frege1884] revives mathematical Platonism in modern dress: numbers are objective abstract objects, and arithmetic is the science of their structure. Gödel [-@godel1944; -@godel1964] defends a robust Platonism on which mathematical objects are perceived through a faculty analogous to sense perception. Quine and Putnam's indispensability arguments [-@putnam1971; -@putnam1979] make mathematical realism respectable to naturalists who would otherwise have shied away from abstract objects. Shapiro's *Philosophy of Mathematics: Structure and Ontology* [-@shapiro1997] develops structuralism, on which mathematics is the science of structures rather than of particular objects. Maddy's *Defending the Axioms* [-@maddy2011] and *Naturalism in Mathematics* [-@maddy1997] defend a naturalized Platonism. Balaguer's *Platonism and Anti-Platonism in Mathematics* [-@balaguer1998] gives the comprehensive survey. The classical theist sometimes adopts a Platonism-plus theology: God's mind contains the abstract objects, and the realm of Forms is the divine intellect.

The target of the present reply is the structural claim: that mathematical objects are abstract entities exempt from the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6), and therefore that the Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) (the result that the necessary possibility of change entails the necessary co-instantiation of Time, Space, and Substance) holds at most for the concrete world while a wider reality contains entities that violate it. The reply is not that Platonism is incoherent. One available response is nominalist or modal-structuralist: mathematical objects can be treated as descriptions of what structured reality, actual and possible, affords. But that is a substantive philosophy of mathematics, not something established merely by the structural argument. A robust Platonist may instead retain abstract objects while denying that the book's concrete change-realizing types apply to them.

Four forms of the move develop the position at four depths: the classical-Platonist form, the structuralist form, the naturalized form, and the plenitudinous form. Each fails for the same structural reason at increasing levels of refinement.

A note on the shape of the reply before the four forms. The reply does *not* claim that mathematical objects are abstract entities possessing their own time-like, space-like, and substance-like structure in some rarefied mode. That move would only relocate the Platonist's exempt object and quietly stretch Time, Space, and Substance into a second, analogical sense, trading the determinacy of the concrete bearers for a metaphor. The reply runs the other way. There is no number 7 standing apart from things, awaiting structural analysis; there are pluralities that can be counted, structures that can be instantiated, and *7* is the description of a feature they have. Mathematical objects are descriptions of what structured reality affords, not residents of a separate realm that must be shown to satisfy the conditions after all. Because the conditions govern the *possible* and not merely the actual ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)), the descriptions reach as far as the possible reaches (to collections larger than anything the actual world contains, and to the infinite) without positing a single abstract object.

*First.* Classical Platonism (the Plato–Frege–Gödel line) holds that mathematical objects are particular abstract entities, each numerically distinct from the others, standing in eternal relations of mathematical structure. The number 7 is a particular object, distinct from the number 6 and from the number 8; the natural numbers stand in the successor relation; the relation is eternal and changeless.

Platonic Forms presuppose form. The word *form* (English *form*, Latin *forma*, Greek εἶδος) carries both the verbal sense (to take shape, to come into being) and the nominal sense (the eternal pattern, the abstract universal). εἶδος descends from ἰδεῖν, *to see*: it named originally what something looks like as it takes shape, the seen aspect of something undergoing process. Plato's move is to read the seen-aspect as an eternal pattern that prescribes the shape the process takes. We observe trees taking shape, mammals developing, planets accreting; the Platonist infers Forms of Tree, Mammal, and Planet prescribing what those processes converge on. The inference trades on the equivocation between the verbal sense (formation) and the nominal sense (the eternal Form): what follows from the observation is that formation-processes occur, and that the conditions of reality are such as to permit them, not that there is an eternal pattern prior to them prescribing what they must produce.

Three pressures on the classical-Platonist line are worth naming before the section turns to the math-Platonist refinements. *The natural-kind pressure.* Trees vary across species, climates, and life-stages; mammals span the spectrum from blue whale to shrew; the Form of Tree or Form of Mammal that would be at the same explanatory level as the Form of the Triangle becomes harder to specify the closer the inspection goes. Plato himself hesitates on this point in the *Parmenides* (130c–d), where Socrates flinches over whether there are Forms of hair, mud, and dirt. The modern reactivation runs through Wittgenstein's family-resemblance critique [@wittgenstein1953, §§65–71], Dupré's species pluralism [@dupre1993], and Boyd's homeostatic-property-cluster account of natural kinds [@boyd1991], each pressing the point that the kinds the world contains are not the kinds the Platonist's Form-talk requires.

*The process pressure.* A tree is not a static form: it is seed, sapling, mature, senescent, snag, and across seasons evergreen or deciduous. The Form of Tree would have to be either the form of a static cross-section (which is not what a tree is) or the form of the developmental sequence (which makes the Form temporal, conceding the present account). Aristotle presses this against his teacher in *Metaphysics* A.9, 991a8–b9 (where the Forms are shown useless for change and coming-to-be) and develops the immanent, hylomorphic alternative in *De Anima* II.1, 412a19–28; the process-philosophical tradition from Heraclitus through Whitehead [-@whitehead1929] and Bergson [-@bergson1907] develops the point systematically.

*The reflexive-substrate pressure.* The Platonist standing on Earth is held by what they describe (a planet) and owes an account of the Form of Earth that supports them. Retreat to property-universals (Armstrong, Tooley) abandons Forms of individuals; retreat to the *Timaeus* elemental geometries (53c–55c) confuses earth-the-element with Earth-the-planet; retreat to Plotinian emanation (*Enneads* V.9, VI.9) substitutes a Neoplatonist theology for the Platonist analysis; retreat to Lewisian modal realism [@lewis1986] changes the ontology under discussion. Each retreat concedes that the Form of the individual thing supporting the Platonist was not available.

The pressures share a structural diagnosis. The Platonist treats Forms as prescriptive: the Form of Tree explains why trees take the shape they do; the Form of Triangle explains why triangles have the angle-sum they have; the Form of Justice explains what just acts have in common. The structural account inverts the direction. That trees take the shape they do follows from the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) being such as to permit trees: the necessary co-instantiation of Time, Space, and Substance yields a Reality in which tree-formation is among the possible processes. The descriptive content the Platonist reads as the Form of Tree is the description of what those conditions afford for that kind of configuration. The 180° angle-sum of a Euclidean triangle is not prescribed by a Form of Triangle; it is a structural consequence of the metric specification of the relevant space ([§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7) develops the metric-as-contingent-specification point) and spherical and hyperbolic geometries produce different angle-sums under different metric specifications, all licensed within the structural conditions. What the Platonist calls a Form runs downstream of actuality plus structural conditions, never upstream.
