This is the polarity inversion: what looks like a prior pattern prescribing actuality is a description of what actuality, under the structural conditions, produces.

To be a Form, at all, is to be a determinate *this* rather than *that*: the Form of Justice, not Beauty; the Form of the Triangle, not the Circle. But that determinacy is borrowed, not native. The Form of the Triangle is determinate because triangles (actual or possible) are determinate; its distinctness from the Form of the Circle is the distinctness of the configurations it describes. The determinacy the Platonist reads as a property of the Form is the determinacy of the structured (possible) reality the Form is a description of. The Form is not a further object that must itself be located in the order of distinctness, placement, and persistence; it is the description that order makes available.

Take the number 7. What is 7 apart from seven of something? The classical Platonist's answer is: a particular abstract object, distinct from 6 and 8, sitting in the eternal successor relation. The present answer is that *7* is the count-structure of any seven-membered plurality there could be, the way any such collection is when it is enumerated. Its distinctness from 6 and 8 is the distinctness of those collections (one fewer thing, one more); the successor ordering is the ordering of the collections under the operation of adding a unit; the stability of "7 is the successor of 6" across every time, person, and culture is the stability of what *any* possible seven-membered collection would be. These can be represented as facts about actual or possible pluralities. Actual concrete pluralities have concrete members, but merely possible, infinite, or abstract pluralities cannot simply be assumed to occupy Space, stand in temporal order, or be made of Substance. The modal-structuralist analysis must explain those cases rather than treating concreteness as automatic. The number needs no private time, space, and substance of its own, because it was never an object over and above the things; it is the description of their count. And because the count is a count of *possible* collections, it reaches numbers larger than all the things that happen to exist, and the transfinite, without any object's being conjured to bear it. Classical Platonism does not exhibit a counterexample to the account developed here; once the number is seen as the description of structured possibility rather than as an object exempt from it, the apparent counterexample dissolves.

Two homely cases make the reading concrete. First, measure. No one is tempted to house "1.5 meters" in a realm of abstracta; it is how long a thing is, a magnitude borne by the rod that has it. Number belongs to the same family: *7* is a *how many* in the way a length is a *how long*, a feature of a plurality rather than an object standing beside it. The Platonist's temptation is to treat the one magnitude we happen to reach by counting as though it were unlike every other magnitude, a thing rather than a measure. Second, matching. A shepherd who cannot count can still keep his flock exactly: he drops a pebble into a sack as each sheep leaves the fold and removes one as each returns, and a pebble left over at dusk is a sheep unaccounted for. He has tracked the number without ever naming it, and the sheep and the pebbles share nothing beyond standing in one-to-one correspondence with none left over. That correspondence is what *7* records, and it is why collections with nothing else in common can be identical in number: sameness of number is sameness under pairing, not joint participation in a shared object. This is the content of Hume's principle [@frege1884, §63]: the number of *F*s equals the number of *G*s just when the *F*s and *G*s correspond one-to-one; on the present reading the principle fixes a fact about pluralities rather than introducing a name for an abstract particular.

*Second.* Structuralism (Shapiro, Resnik, Hellman) refines the classical position by holding that mathematical objects are not particular entities but positions in structures. The number 7 is not a particular abstract object but the seventh position in any ω-sequence (any infinite sequence ordered like the natural numbers, with a first element and a successor for every element); what mathematics studies is the structure of ω-sequences, not particular sequences. This is meant to handle the multiple-reductions problem (3 can be reduced to {{{{}}}} or to {{},{{}},{{},{{}}}}) by holding that any reduction that preserves the structure preserves what 7 is.

Structuralism makes the structural-conditions reply more direct, not less. The structures mathematics studies are constituted by determinate elements or positions and relations, directly supporting a difference-role. Some structures include asymmetric order; many do not. Their abstract stability does not by itself amount to temporal persistence or physical bearing. Upgrading the mathematical roles to T and Φ therefore requires a realization premise. Shapiro's account of structures as patterns whose positions are individuated by their relations to other positions in the same structure is a description, in the mathematical case, of the distinctness, ordering, and persistence that [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names. The reply is not that Shapiro is wrong about mathematical structure; the reply is that Shapiro's account of mathematical structure describes what [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names. The structural-conditions account is, on the present reading, structuralism extended to non-mathematical reality, the same insight applied to the wider domain of which mathematics is one structured region.

*Third.* The naturalized form (Maddy, Quine, Putnam) drops the strong realism about abstract objects and holds instead that mathematical objects are whatever the indispensability argument requires, the entities that are quantified over in our best scientific theories. The ontological commitment is to whatever is needed to make the science work; the metaphysics of the entities is left open.

The naturalized form does not aim to exhibit a counterexample to the structural account; it aims to deflate the metaphysical question. As deflation, it is irrelevant to the structural reply: whatever the indispensable mathematical entities turn out to be, they will be whatever the science requires, and the science requires distinctness, ordering, and persistence of mathematical facts. If the naturalist insists on a stronger reading (that mathematical entities have some metaphysical status that exempts them from the structural conditions) then the reply to the classical Platonist applies. If the naturalist remains deflationary, then the position is not in tension with the structural account.

*Fourth.* Plenitudinous Platonism (Balaguer) holds that every consistent mathematical theory describes a real domain of mathematical objects: the universe is mathematically plenitudinous, with every possible mathematical structure instantiated somewhere. This is meant to dissolve the access problem: we do not need a faculty for picking out particular abstract objects, because every consistent description picks out something.

Plenitude is a stronger claim than the classical Platonist makes, and the structural reply applies more straightforwardly. The plenitude of mathematical structures is not itself a further structured object but a description, at maximal extent, of what the structural conditions afford. To speak of the totality of consistent theories is to describe how such theories stand: individuated by their consistency conditions, ordered by relations of inclusion or interpretation, stable across all considerations of which structures exist. Each of those is a description of the distinctness, ordering, and persistence any possible structure would have, not a Time, Space, or Substance instantiated by some super-object 'the totality.' If the present account is right, plenitudinous Platonism is its mathematical correlate, not its refutation.

A kindred move is the divine-intellect Platonism: the abstract objects exist in God's mind, and their atemporality is the atemporality of the divine intellect. The reply combines the present reply with [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1) (the changeless-ground reply): the divine intellect that contains the structured realm of abstracts is itself structured, and the structuredness is what [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names. The classical theist's Platonism-plus-theology faces the structural reply twice over.

The modal-structuralist position (Hellman) is, on the present reading, not one more Platonism to absorb but the closest mathematical statement of the reply itself: mathematics is not about actual abstract objects but about possible structures. That is precisely the account given here: *7* is the structure of any possible seven-membered collection, and arithmetic is the study of what such possible structures are like. The only adjustment is the ground: the modality is not a primitive realm of its own but is fixed by the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6), which govern the whole space of the possible ([§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6)). Mathematics describes the possible; the possible is structured by Time, Space, and Substance; so mathematics, far from naming exceptions to the conditions, is one of the most general descriptions of what they afford.

*What converges.* Four forms and none exhibits the counterexample the position needs: classical Platonism's particular abstract objects resolve into descriptions of structured possibility, not exceptions to it; structuralism's structures are constituted by exactly the relational facts the account names; the naturalized form is either deflationary (and not in tension) or stronger-than-deflationary (and faces the classical reply); and plenitudinous Platonism is the most extensive description of what structure affords, not a counterexample to it. Across the four forms, no mathematical view by itself supplies a counterexample to the necessity of structure in concrete change-realizing worlds. The stronger nominalist conclusion, that mathematical objects are not objects at all but descriptions of possible structure, remains one proposed interpretation, not a result forced on Platonism by [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) alone.

Sibling counter-constructions: the changeless-ground objection, on which a timeless being grounds the structure from outside, is [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1). The B-theoretic block objection, on which the temporal manifold is a static four-dimensional reality, is [§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6). The McTaggart objection, on which time itself is unreal, is [§4.2.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-5).

What the Platonist tradition genuinely captures is worth preserving. There is a sense in which mathematical truths are not merely conventional, not merely useful, not merely about marks on paper or sounds in the air. The persistence of mathematical truth across cultures and millennia, the convergence of independent investigations on the same theorems, the resistance of mathematical structure to revision in ways that empirical theories are revised, each speaks to something real about the subject matter of mathematics. The account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is consistent with that sense. Mathematical structures are real structures; their reality is the reality of what the structural conditions afford, the count and pattern of every possible collection, described maximally and changelessly. The Platonist who reads the changelessness as exemption from [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) has misread the changelessness; what does not change is not a timeless object floating free of the conditions but the description of what every possible collection, every possible structure, would be, and that description does not change because the possibilities it describes do not. The stability is the stability of the possible, not the serenity of an abstract object.

Frege's *Grundlagen* (1884) was printed on paper that has decayed in the intervening century and a half. The arithmetic he was investigating did not decay. What did not decay, on the present reading, is not a timeless object exempt from [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) but a truth about every possible collection: that seven of anything is the successor of six of it. The number 7 is not somewhere because it is not the kind of thing that could be anywhere: it is the count any seven-membered plurality has, and pluralities are where their members are. It does not move or decay because descriptions of what is possible do not move or decay; the possibilities they describe are fixed by the structural conditions that govern the possible. The Platonist's number is not a counterexample to the present account, and it is not a hidden instance of it either. It is a description of what reality, under the conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6), makes countable.

### 4.2.5 The Unreality of Time {#sec-4-2-5}

In 1908 J. M. E. McTaggart published a paper in *Mind* titled "The Unreality of Time." The argument is short, the conclusion is shocking, and the influence has been deep. Time, McTaggart claims, is unreal. The paper became one of the most cited works in twentieth-century philosophy of time, with well over a century of subsequent literature responding to it. If McTaggart was right, the present account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) has, in its first condition, named something unreal, and the bidirectional identity collapses on the temporal side.

The argument is concise enough to state in a paragraph. McTaggart distinguishes two ways of describing temporal events: the A-series (past, present, future, with the present moving) and the B-series (earlier than, simultaneous with, later than, fixed across the manifold). Time, McTaggart argues, requires the A-series: without becoming, there is no genuine temporality, only a static array of events with relations of earlier and later. But the A-series is contradictory. Every event is past, present, and future (these properties are mutually incompatible) and any attempt to remove the contradiction by relativizing (event E is future relative to time t1, present relative to t2, past relative to t3) generates a regress: the relativizing times are themselves events, each of which is past, present, and future, and so on. The A-series is incoherent; the B-series alone is insufficient for time; therefore time is unreal.

The argument has divided the philosophy of time ever since. Broad's *An Examination of McTaggart's Philosophy* ([-@broad1938]) gives the first sustained reply, defending A-series becoming against the contradiction charge; the moving-spotlight theory (the view that a four-dimensional manifold of events is timelessly arrayed and a privileged 'now' moves across it) is the image Broad had earlier introduced in *Scientific Thought* (1923) only to reject it. Prior's *Past, Present, and Future* ([-@prior1967]) develops tense logic to formalize A-series claims. Mellor's *Real Time* ([-@mellor1981]) and *Real Time II* ([-@mellor1998]) accept the contradiction in the A-series and develop a B-theoretic alternative on which tensed claims are reduced to tenseless truth-conditions. Tooley's *Time, Tense, and Causation* ([-@tooley1997]) defends a growing-block theory (on which the past and present are real but the future is not, with the block growing by accretion as time passes). Dummett ([-@dummett1960], in *Truth and Other Enigmas*) reads McTaggart as a reductio of the assumption that the description of reality must be perspective-independent. Dainton (*Time and Space*, 2nd ed. [-@dainton2010]) gives the standard survey. The contemporary positions (presentism, eternalism, growing-block, moving spotlight) are largely structured by which side of McTaggart's argument they accept and which side they reject.

The target of the present reply is McTaggart's conclusion: that time is unreal. The A-series/B-series question, at the level it operates within the philosophy of time, is largely orthogonal to the present account. The dispute is already bracketed at the structural level by §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7: the present account requires temporal ordering of states sufficient to support change, and [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2) develops the composition view that resolves the dispute by holding A-series passage and B-series dimension together as two features Temporality requires rather than rival specifications of one. The reply here is narrower: McTaggart's argument, granting its details, does not establish what its conclusion claims. It establishes at most a thesis about how to describe time, not a thesis about whether the structural conditions of temporality obtain.

Three forms of the move develop the position at three depths: the strict-unreality form, the A-series-incoherence form, and the perspective-dependence form. Each fails for the same structural reason at increasing levels of refinement.

*First.* The strict-unreality reading: McTaggart's argument shows that time itself is unreal, full stop. There is no time, only the appearance of time, generated by some non-temporal feature of reality. This is the most extreme reading and the one McTaggart himself sometimes seems to endorse.

McTaggart's writing and publication occurred within the apparent temporal order, so the performance of the argument instantiates temporal structure at the act level. The 1908 paper is itself an event with structural conditions: it is distinct from the 1907 draft and from the 1909 reception (S), it stands in temporal relations to those events (T), and it persists as a paper across the century of subsequent commentary (Φ). Its publication in *Mind* presupposes that the paper was first written and then published, not that the writing and the publication are non-temporally co-present in some atemporal mode. What that establishes is narrower than the date 1908 might suggest: the argument cannot dispense with temporal representation in its articulation. It does not by itself refute an error theory on which the apparent order is grounded in non-temporal reality. The object-side account must be tested separately, and the burden it carries is to explain the indispensable structure without real time.

The deeper structural point: the A-series/B-series dispute is internal to the analysis of T. If one of the two series is incoherent, then T must be analyzed in terms of the other series, or in terms of some third structure. McTaggart's own C-series (the permanent, direction-neutral ordering of positions that survives the A-series' collapse) is one such third structure, and the structural account partially vindicates it: the C-series' bare ordering is real, the genuine residue of McTaggart's positive view. What the structural T-role adds is precisely what the C-series withholds (asymmetric direction) supplied not by the contradictory A-series but by the self-exclusion the account grounds independently. So the affinity is the ordering and the difference is the asymmetry: the account preserves McTaggart's positive residue while supplying the direction his negative argument leaves ungrounded. What the dispute does not show is that T fails to obtain. The structural condition T (directed ordering of states) is satisfied by either an A-series tensed analysis or a B-series tenseless analysis or some combination, and the choice between them is the topic of the philosophy of time, not a refutation of the existence of T.

*Second.* The A-series-incoherence form is the more defensible reading. McTaggart's argument shows only that the A-series is incoherent, and a B-theoretic analysis of time is the proper response: time consists in the B-series, and the apparent reality of becoming is to be explained as a perspectival or psychological feature rather than as a metaphysical fact. Mellor's *Real Time II* develops this position with full rigor.

The retorsion-from-1908 above closes the strict-unreality reading only; the serious B-theoretic tradition (Mellor, Williams, Sider) operates at this level and is engaged here and at [§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6). The B-series (earlier than, later than, simultaneous with) supplies the dimension feature of Temporality. The four-dimensional manifold of B-series events is distinguishable into events (S), ordered (T), and persists across the manifold as a unified four-dimensional whole (Φ). On the composition view at [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2), Temporality requires both the dimension and the passage; the B-theorist who supplies the dimension cleanly and reduces passage to indexical content gives one feature where the composition requires two, and the disagreement lives there. The Mellor reading is one specification of Temporality's dimension feature, not the complete metaphysics of T.

*Third.* The perspective-dependence reading (Dummett, Sider, the early-twentieth-century Cambridge reading) takes McTaggart's argument as showing not that time is unreal but that any complete description of reality must be from no perspective (perspective-independent in the strong sense) and that the A-series, which is irreducibly perspectival, cannot figure in such a description. This is a thesis about the metaphysics of description rather than about the metaphysics of time directly.

The perspective-dependence reading is structurally interesting and partly correct. The A-series claims are perspective-dependent in a sense the B-series claims are not: 'the present moment' picks out different moments depending on when the claim is made; 'earlier than 1908' picks out the same moments regardless of when the claim is made. What the present account requires is that whatever specification of T is offered, the structural fact of directed ordering obtains. Whether the metaphysical description that captures the ordering is perspectival or perspective-independent is a separate question. The B-theorist offers the perspective-independent version; the A-theorist offers the perspectival version; both supply T. McTaggart on the present reading, like Dummett, raises a question about the metaphysics of description; the question is genuinely open, and the present account is consistent with either resolution.

A kindred move is the radical eliminativism (some readings of Parfit, some readings of Buddhist analyses): time is unreal because the relations it requires (between selves, between events, between moments) are themselves unreal. The reply combines the present reply with [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8) (the momentariness reply): the relations are exactly the structural facts [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names, and their elimination either collapses on its own description or relabels the structural facts under another vocabulary.

Another kindred is the McTaggart-via-presentism position: only the present is real, and the past and future are not, so the A-series cannot generate the contradiction because there is only the present moment. Presentism is a metaphysical thesis with its own challenges (the truthmaker problem, the cross-time relations problem, the problem of historical reference); the present account is consistent with presentism in the sense that the structural conditions can be specified at each present moment as a fact about what reality contains. Whether presentism is the right metaphysics of time is a separate question that the present account does not adjudicate.

*What converges.* Three forms clarify the dispute: strict unreality faces an act/object burden because its argument uses temporal representation but may still propose a non-temporal ground of appearance; A-series-incoherence is consistent with the present account, which admits B-theoretic specification of T; and perspective-dependence is a thesis about the metaphysics of description, not about whether T obtains. Across the three forms, McTaggart's argument either fails on its own terms or is consistent with the present account.

Sibling counter-constructions: the B-theoretic block universe is treated separately at [§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6). The temporary-intrinsics objection, on which apparent change is the difference of intrinsic properties at different times rather than change of a single intrinsic, is [§4.2.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-7). The momentariness objection is [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8).

McTaggart's argument belonged to a broader idealist program, and the natural worry is that the present account's necessary, empirically unencounterable structure is itself a covert idealism rather than a neutral structural claim. The question is taken up directly at [§4.3.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-5): whatever is taken as fundamental (a cosmic mind included) instantiates T, S, and Φ once it is structured enough to do the work the position needs of it, so the structural conditions are mind-compatible without being mind-derived. The idealist setting is engaged there, not set aside here.

What the McTaggart literature genuinely establishes is worth preserving: the conceptual analysis of time is harder than the pre-analytic vocabulary suggests, and the relation between A-series description and B-series description is one of the deepest structural questions in metaphysics. The present account does not adjudicate that question. It makes a weaker claim: the structural fact of directed ordering obtains, with the A/B dispute resolved by the composition view of [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2). Hybrid views (growing-block and moving-spotlight) and presentism each carry the structural conditions in different vocabulary, with the metaphysical commitments developed there. McTaggart's contribution to twentieth-century metaphysics is to have sharpened the question of how T is to be specified. The contribution does not extend, on the present analysis, to dissolving T altogether.

The 1908 argument survived its tradition: the British Hegelian idealism that gave it its broader setting was largely abandoned by the 1920s, but the distinction between A-series and B-series became a permanent landmark of analytic philosophy of time. The argument survives because the question it raises is real, even if the conclusion it draws is not. Time is real. Its analysis is hard. McTaggart helped make the analysis harder, and the present account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is, on the present reading, one beneficiary of the long literature his paper provoked.

### 4.2.6 Block Universe {#sec-4-2-6}

The B-theorist of time (Mellor, Smart, Williams, Sider) holds that the world is a four-dimensional manifold in which all events, past, present, and future, are equally real. There is no objective becoming; the apparent flow of time is a feature of conscious experience or of the indexical content of tensed claims, not a metaphysical fact about the manifold. The block-universe view is an influential metaphysical interpretation of relativity: the relativity of simultaneity makes a privileged present problematic, and the four-dimensional manifold is a natural setting for relativistic physics, though the interpretation remains contested. If the B-theorist is right, the present account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) must be reinterpreted: T is the temporal extension of the block, not the directed flow of becoming, and the structural conditions obtain across the block as a whole rather than as a feature of a moving present.

The move is influential and the position is widely held. Smart's "The River of Time" [-@smart1949] and *Philosophy and Scientific Realism* [-@smart1963] give the position its mid-century analytic articulation. Williams's "The Myth of Passage" [-@williams1951] is the canonical statement of the case against objective becoming. Mellor's *Real Time* [-@mellor1981] and *Real Time II* [-@mellor1998] develop the most careful contemporary defense, on which tensed claims are reduced to tenseless truth-conditions and the apparent flow of time is a perspectival feature. Sider's *Four-Dimensionalism* [-@sider2001] defends the block as the proper setting for ordinary objects, with persistence cashed out as having temporal parts at different times. Putnam's "Time and Physical Geometry" [-@putnam1967b] and Rietdijk's [-@rietdijk1966] argue that special relativity forces the block. Maudlin's *The Metaphysics Within Physics* [-@maudlin2007] defends time's fundamentality against the standard B-theoretic readings. Price's *Time's Arrow and Archimedes' Point* [-@price1996] argues for a thoroughgoing block view on which temporal asymmetry is a perspectival illusion.

The target of the present reply is the structural claim: that the block universe is a static four-dimensional manifold without genuine becoming, and therefore that the structural conditions [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names (if they obtain at all) obtain in a sense compatible with the absence of becoming, and possibly in a sense weaker than the present account requires. The reply is not that the B-theory is incoherent (it is not) but that the B-theoretic block instantiates the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) in the sense the account requires. The block is not a counterexample to the present account; it is one of the available metaphysics of how the structural conditions are instantiated.

Three forms of the move develop the position at three depths: the strict-static-block form, the relativistic form, and the perspectival-becoming form. Each is consistent with the present account at the level the account operates.

*First.* The strict-static-block reading: the four-dimensional manifold is static in the sense that no genuine becoming obtains. The events of the manifold are timelessly arrayed, and the appearance of becoming is illusory. This is the most extreme reading and is sometimes endorsed by readers of Williams or by readers who take the relativistic argument to its eliminativist limit.

The strict-static-block reading must distinguish two senses of 'static.' In one sense, the block is static in that the manifold as a whole does not itself change: there is no super-time in which the four-dimensional manifold is arrayed and across which it evolves. In this sense, 'static' is correct and uncontroversial. In a second sense, 'static' would mean that the events within the manifold do not stand in temporal relations: that no event is earlier or later than any other event, that there is no directed ordering. In this second sense, the block is not static; the temporal extension of the manifold is what makes it a four-dimensional manifold rather than a three-dimensional one. The events within the block stand in B-series relations (earlier than, later than, simultaneous with) and these relations supply the directed ordering T requires. The B-theorist who denies becoming in the metaphysical sense (no objective A-series flow) does not deny temporal relations in the structural sense (B-series ordering across the manifold). The present account requires the latter, not the former.

The events within the block are distinguishable from one another (S). They stand in temporal relations of earlier and later (T). The manifold is a unified four-dimensional whole, but it does not itself persist through a further time. Within it, worldlines, temporal parts, or other cross-time relations may realize the bearing and continuity role associated with Φ. The block's unity should not be redescribed as temporal persistence of the whole. The B-theoretic block instantiates the dimension feature of T cleanly. On the composition view developed at [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2), Temporality requires both the dimension and the passage as two features held together; the block-only reading without objective passage gives one feature where the composition requires two. The B-theorist who reduces passage to indexical content (Mellor, Williams, the perspectival-becoming form below) is in disagreement with the composition view on the metaphysical status of passage rather than consistent with it; the disagreement lives there. The B-theorist who allows objective passage through the manifold is the composition view in B-vocabulary.

*Second.* The relativistic form is the central motivation for the block. Special relativity's relativity of simultaneity is incompatible with a privileged objective present: different inertial frames disagree on which events are simultaneous, and there is no frame-independent fact of the matter. The four-dimensional manifold of Minkowski spacetime is the natural setting; events stand in the light-cone structure (causal past, causal future, elsewhere) rather than in a frame-independent A-series (the tensed past/present/future ordering with the present moving); the block is what relativity gives us.

The relativistic argument is correct as far as it goes, and the present account accommodates it without revision. T (directed ordering of states) does not require a frame-independent global present. It requires that events stand in temporal relations sufficient to support change, and the light-cone structure of Minkowski spacetime supplies exactly that: every event has a determinate causal past (events that can have influenced it) and a determinate causal future (events it can influence). The ordering is partial rather than total (events in each other's elsewhere do not stand in a determinate temporal relation) but partial ordering is sufficient for the present account. Change is local; the structural conditions [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names are conditions on local processes of change, not on the existence of a global frame-independent present. Relativity makes the present account more careful, not less correct.

A note on the contested status of the inference itself. The move from special relativity to the four-dimensional block is not a settled physics result. Neo-Lorentzian interpretations, @bell1976, Maudlin's *Quantum Non-Locality and Relativity* [-@maudlin2002, ch. 7], and Craig's *Time and the Metaphysics of Relativity* [-@craig2001] most directly, preserve a privileged frame consistently with the empirical content by treating Lorentz contraction and time dilation as dynamical effects on rods and clocks rather than as features of the spacetime structure itself; the Putnam–Stein exchange [@stein1968; @stein1991] and Balashov–Janssen [-@balashovJanssen2003] press the orthodox four-dimensionalist reading against these alternatives. The dispute is genuine, and the present account does not contest either reading: on the orthodox reading T is supplied by light-cone partial ordering across the manifold, on the neo-Lorentzian reading T is supplied by a privileged dynamical frame, and on either reading the directed ordering the structural conditions [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) name is instantiated.

*Third.* The perspectival-becoming form (Mellor's mature position; Williams's "Myth of Passage"; Price's perspectival arrow) accepts the block at the metaphysical level and locates becoming at the perspectival level: the apparent flow of time is a feature of conscious experience, of indexical content, of the perspective of an observer embedded within the block, not a fact about the manifold itself.

The perspectival reading is consistent with the present account on the dimension feature of T and in tension with it on the passage feature. The structural conditions are instantiated by the manifold; the Mellor account preserves the dimension feature of T (B-series ordering), preserves S (event-distinctness), preserves a cross-time continuity or temporal-parts structure capable of realizing the Φ-role, and offers a story about how perspectival experience of becoming arises from the structural facts. On the composition view at [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2), the passage feature of Temporality is metaphysically real rather than indexical, and Mellor's reduction is what the composition view declines. The story about perspectival becoming is consistent with the present account where it explains how the metaphysically-real passage registers from within a configuration that tracks its own position; it is not consistent where the becoming is the whole of what passage names. The disagreement is local to the passage feature; the rest of the Mellor architecture stands.

A kindred move is the growing-block theory (Tooley, Broad's earlier position): the past and present are real, the future is not, and the block grows by accretion as time passes. Growing-block is structurally a hybrid: it accepts B-series relations among the past-and-present events, accepts a privileged present (the leading edge of the block), and posits an objective process of accretion. The present account is consistent with growing-block in the sense that the growing block instantiates T (across the past-and-present), S, and Φ; the disputes between growing-block and the strict-block (and between both and presentism, on which only the present moment is real, the past having ceased and the future not yet existing) are internal to the metaphysics of which structures are instantiated, not whether the structural conditions obtain.

Another kindred is the moving-spotlight theory (Cameron, Skow): the block is timelessly there, and a privileged present moves across it. The present account is consistent with the moving-spotlight in the sense that the spotlight obtains within an already-structured block; the spotlight is one structural feature among others, supported by the underlying structure.

*What converges.* Three forms and each is consistent with the present account at the level it operates: the strict-static-block reading distinguishes two senses of 'static' and yields the structural conditions in the sense the account requires; the relativistic form replaces a global present with light-cone structure and supplies T as a partial ordering; and the perspectival-becoming form locates becoming in conscious experience while preserving the structural conditions at the metaphysical level. Across the three forms, the B-theoretic block instantiates T ∧ S ∧ Φ, sometimes more cleanly than the A-theoretic alternatives.

Sibling counter-constructions: the McTaggart-unreality objection is [§4.2.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-5). The temporary-intrinsics objection, on which apparent change is the difference of intrinsic properties at different times rather than change of a single intrinsic, is [§4.2.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-7). The emergent-time objection, on which time is derivative rather than fundamental, is [§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3).

A consequence for the Kalām engagement ([§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2)). On the composition view at [§7.2.2](nature-alone.html#sec-7-2-2), the passage feature of Temporality is metaphysically real; *began to exist* therefore has determinate structural content. What the composition view marks is two readings of the begin-question: a quantitative reading (how far back the passage runs along the dimension) engaged at [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2) and a categorial reading (a moment-prior-to-T from which T began) foreclosed by Parasitic Negation. The strict-B-theoretic reduction of passage to indexical content is a separable issue that does not absorb the begin-question in the way Craig's pressure assumes; the composition view's commitment to objective passage is what the [§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2) engagement runs on.

What the B-theoretic literature genuinely establishes is worth preserving: it gives powerful reasons to question naïve assumptions about a frame-independent present, objective passage, and the metaphysical privilege of the present moment. B-theorists commonly locate apparent flow and presentness in conscious experience or the indexical content of tensed claims; A-theoretic and neo-Lorentzian rivals contest that interpretation. These are live philosophical disputes, and the present account is designed to state what it preserves across them. What the present account adds is that the four-dimensional manifold the B-theorist describes is not an alternative to T ∧ S ∧ Φ but a particular specification of it. The events of the manifold are distinct (S), the manifold has temporal extension (T), and the manifold's structure underwrites the cross-time identity of objects (Φ). The block is what the dimension feature of T looks like when it is described by the metaphysics of relativistic physics.

The block is the standard backdrop now in a way it was not in McTaggart's day. The present account, on the present reading, is what the block is when it is described not as a metaphysics of time but as a metaphysics of the structural conditions that any time must instantiate. The block's events are distinct and ordered, and its cross-time structure bears the persistence Φ names; that is what the block consists in, and that is what [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names.

### 4.2.7 The Problem of Temporary Intrinsics {#sec-4-2-7}

David Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds* [-@lewis1986]) names the problem of temporary intrinsics; a simple case makes it vivid: a banana is green at t1 and yellow at t2, and the banana cannot be both green and yellow simpliciter (in the unqualified, unrelativized sense), since those properties are incompatible. Some way of relativizing the predication is needed, and the analysis one chooses for it is largely determinative of one's metaphysics of persistence and change.

The problem is sharp because the available solutions all carry costs. Presentism (only the present is real) avoids the contradiction by holding that the banana is yellow simpliciter at t2 (t2 is the present) and there is no greenness for the contradiction to obtain with. But presentism faces difficulties about cross-time relations and historical truth. Four-dimensionalism (perdurance) holds that the banana is a four-dimensional object with temporal parts; the t1-stage is green, the t2-stage is yellow, and there is no contradiction because the green and yellow are properties of distinct stages. But four-dimensionalism faces the standard objection (Lewis himself raises it) that ordinary objects do not seem to have temporal parts in the way they have spatial parts. The relational-properties account holds that 'green at t1' and 'yellow at t2' are time-relativized properties that the banana has wholly and simpliciter; the contradiction is dissolved because the properties have time-indices built in. But the relational-properties account makes intrinsic properties relational, which Lewis argues is to misdescribe what 'intrinsic' means.

The target of the present reply is the structural claim that the temporary-intrinsics analysis, in any of its three forms, undermines the account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6). The argument the objector might run: change, on every available analysis, turns out to be either the difference of intrinsic properties at different times (presentism, with cross-time relations as a separate problem), or the difference of intrinsic properties of different temporal parts (perdurance), or the relational property of the same object at different times (relationalism). On none of these analyses is change a single thing standing in different conditions across time, the picture [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names. So the present account is, at best, a description of one of these analyses, and likely a description of none of them.

The reply is that the present account is consistent with all three analyses of temporary intrinsics, and indeed is the structural fact each of them is an analysis of. The structural conditions [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names, Time (T), Space (S), and Substance (Φ), generating the structural features of ordering, distinctness, and persistence, are at a level above the metaphysics of how persistence is realized; they are conditions any analysis of persistence must satisfy. Each of the three analyses satisfies them in a distinct way. The dispute among the three is internal to the metaphysics of persistence; the present account is what the disputes are disputes about.

Three forms of the move develop the position at three depths: the presentist form, the perdurantist form, and the relationalist form. Each is consistent with the present account.

*First.* Presentism (Prior, Bigelow, Markosian) holds that only the present is real. The banana is yellow simpliciter at the present moment t2; the banana was green at the past moment t1, but that past moment is not now real, only its having-been-real is now real. Tensed truths are taken as primitive: 'the banana was green' is true now, but its truth-maker is not a present-tense fact about a past entity but a primitive past-tense fact.

Presentism is consistent with the present account at each present moment. The banana at t2 is distinct from the seed it grew from and from the compost it will become (S). Presentism cannot straightforwardly relate the present banana to presently nonexistent past and future stages. It instead invokes primitive tensed facts, ersatz times, or another truthmaking account. Those resources may realize the ordering role, and the reply assumes no literal relations to non-real relata. The banana persists across changes (the banana that is now yellow is the same banana that was green) and the persistence is the structural fact that the cross-time identity obtains, however the metaphysics of cross-time relations is specified (Φ). Presentism's specific contribution to the metaphysics of temporary intrinsics is to hold that the cross-time relations are tensed primitives rather than relations to wholly-real past or future entities.

*Second.* Four-dimensionalism (Lewis, Sider, Heller, Hudson) holds that the banana is a four-dimensional object with temporal parts. The t1-stage of the banana is green; the t2-stage of the banana is yellow; the four-dimensional banana itself, the whole, is partly-green-and-partly-yellow in the way a striped flag is partly-red-and-partly-white. There is no contradiction because the green and yellow are properties of distinct temporal parts.

Four-dimensionalism is structurally a maximally clean specification of T ∧ S ∧ Φ. The temporal parts are distinct (S). They stand in temporal relations of earlier and later (T). The four-dimensional whole does not endure from one time to another; it has temporal parts at different times. Its perdurance and the relations unifying those parts offer one realization of the Φ-role, but calling the timelessly extended whole persistence in the strongest sense would beg the question against endurantism. The four-dimensionalist has not eliminated persistence; they have given the most explicit possible analysis of it.

*Third.* Relationalism (Mellor, Lowe in some moods, Wasserman) holds that 'green' and 'yellow' are not strictly intrinsic but covert relations to times: 'the banana is green-at-t1 and yellow-at-t2.' The contradiction is dissolved because 'green-at-t1' and 'yellow-at-t2' are compatible properties; the banana has them both wholly and simpliciter, in the way it has the property of being-three-feet-from-the-window and the property of being-five-feet-from-the-door wholly and simpliciter without contradiction.

Relationalism is consistent with the present account. The relations to times require times for the relations to be relations to (T). The relations distinguish the banana's condition at t1 from its condition at t2 (S in the relational structure). The persistence of the banana (the same banana having both relations) is the structural fact that one entity stands in both (Φ). The relationalist's specific cost (making intrinsic properties relational) is a cost internal to the metaphysics of properties, not a cost to the structural account.

A kindred move is the adverbialist account (van Inwagen, in "Four-Dimensional Objects"): the banana is green at t1 in the sense of being t1-ly green, where 'green' is modified adverbially by the time. The adverbialist hopes to keep intrinsic properties intrinsic by relocating the time-relativization from the property to the manner of having the property. The reply is that the structural conditions are satisfied either way: the manner of having the property at t1 is distinct from the manner of having the property at t2 (S in the manners), the manners stand in temporal relations (T), and the entity persists across the manners (Φ).

Another kindred is the soft-presentist combination (Crisp, Markosian's later work): only the present is real, and tensed truths are primitive, but the structural fact that the world has been and will be in determinate ways is itself a primitive feature of present reality. The reply is that the structural facts the soft-presentist takes as primitive are the structural facts [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names, taken as primitive. The present account is consistent with primitivism about the structural facts.

*What converges.* Three forms and each instantiates the structural conditions of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) at a level the account operates above. Presentism instantiates them at each present moment with cross-time relations specified by tensed-fact primitivism. Four-dimensionalism instantiates them in the timelessly-extant four-dimensional manifold. Relationalism instantiates them in the relational structure of properties indexed to times. Across the three forms, the temporary-intrinsics problem is a problem about the metaphysics of persistence, and the present account is what the metaphysics is the metaphysics of. The level-above placement is a deliberate trade, worth stating in Lewis's own cost-benefit idiom. What it buys: neutrality, the structural conditions are secured without adjudicating the persistence dispute, and what all three rivals share is made explicit rather than left implicit. What it costs: discriminating power, the account does not, and does not try to, settle which of presentism, perdurance, or relationalism is correct, and it commits to structural facts of ordering, distinctness, and persistence whose own individuation is specified at [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) rather than here. For the present argument the purchase is the right one: the thesis of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) needs only what every analysis of persistence must satisfy, so buying neutrality at the price of adjudication costs the argument nothing it required and secures exactly what it did.

Sibling counter-constructions: the changeless-ground objection, on which a timeless being grounds the structure from outside, is [§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1). The B-theoretic block, on which the four-dimensional manifold is a static reality, is [§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6). The momentariness objection, on which persistence is illusory, is [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8). The McTaggart-unreality objection is [§4.2.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-5).

What the temporary-intrinsics literature genuinely establishes is worth preserving: ordinary change is harder to analyze than the pre-analytic vocabulary suggests. The banana that ripens is not in the simplest possible relation to its earlier self; the relation requires either a metaphysics of temporal parts, or a metaphysics of relational properties, or a metaphysics of tensed primitives, or some other specification of how cross-time identity is sustained. The present account does not adjudicate among these. It makes a weaker claim: whatever specification of cross-time identity is correct, the cross-time identity itself is a structural fact of the kind Φ names. The banana that ripens is analyzed differently across the views: as one enduring object, as a four-dimensional whole with differently qualified parts, or as appropriately related stages. What survives neutrally is an ordered continuity structure, not strict numerical identity on every account. The present account is the level at which the same is sameness regardless of which specification is correct.

Lewis introduced the temporary-intrinsics problem in 1986, in the brief passage on endurance and perdurance in *On the Plurality of Worlds* (pp. 202–204) that has occupied subsequent metaphysics for decades. Lewis's own resolution was perdurance, but the problem outlived his answer; presentism, perdurance, and relationalism remain the three dominant analyses, and the dispute among them is one of the central debates of contemporary metaphysics of persistence. The banana ripens, on the present reading, by being one banana standing in successive conditions across an ordering of times, with the metaphysics of how the standing-across is realized to be specified separately. The standing-across is the structural fact. The metaphysics of its specification is the topic of the dispute. The former is named by [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6); the philosophy of persistence elaborates the latter.

### 4.2.8 Stage Theory {#sec-4-2-8}

What if there is no persistence? What if the world is a sequence of momentary flashes: each instant a complete fact unto itself, each one followed by another that is not it, each connected to the next by nothing but resemblance and causal succession? The Yogācāra Buddhists call this *kṣaṇabhaṅga*, momentary destruction. The contemporary analytic version is stage theory, or four-dimensionalism with temporal counterparts. Different traditions, different vocabularies, one structural proposal: persistence is illusory, and what we call a continuing thing is a series of distinct stages bound only by relations of similarity and causal continuity.

The move is radical and the consequences are drastic. If it succeeds, the structural account of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) collapses at Φ, the persistence condition. Without persistence, there is nothing across which Change can occur. Without persistence, the bidirectional identity of change-permission and T ∧ S ∧ Φ has no third leg to stand on. The classical theist, sensing the opening, sometimes adopts a momentarist line: God's relation to the world is a sequence of momentary creative acts, each instant freshly produced, with no need for persistence running through them. Pratītyasamutpāda (dependent origination) supplies the metaphysical scaffolding. Sider supplies the contemporary analytic version. The objection deserves a careful answer.

The Yogācāra school of Mahāyāna Buddhism develops *kṣaṇabhaṅga* most rigorously: every existent (*bhāva*) is a *kṣaṇa* (momentary instant), arising and ceasing in the same instant, replaced by a successor that is causally continuous but numerically distinct. Vasubandhu (4th–5th c.) and Dharmakīrti (7th c.) elaborate the doctrine; the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) and the *bhāva-santāna* (continuum of being) provide the explanatory work that ordinary persistence would otherwise do. Nāgārjuna's *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* presses the analysis further: nothing has *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), and *śūnyatā* (emptiness) is the proper analysis of every apparent persistent.

In analytic philosophy, the structurally similar position is stage theory: Sider (*Four-Dimensionalism* [-@sider2001]) develops the most rigorous version, on which ordinary objects are momentary stages bound by genidentity (Lewin's term, taken up by Carnap and Reichenbach, for cross-time identity-by-causal-continuity rather than strict numerical identity) or counterpart relations. Hawley (*How Things Persist* [-@hawley2001]) defends a closely related view. Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds* [-@lewis1986]; *Philosophical Papers* II [-@lewis1986b]) supplies the perdurantist framework. Quine's stage-theoretic readings of ordinary objects in *Word and Object* ([-@quine1960]) and Russell's logical-construction program are ancestral. Heller (*The Ontology of Physical Objects* [-@heller1990]) and Hudson (*A Materialist Metaphysics of the Human Person* [-@hudson2001]) develop the position in different directions.

The target of the present reply is the structural claim: that the world is a sequence of momentary stages bound by external relations only, with no persistence operating across them. The philosophical opponents of stage theory, endurantists like van Inwagen (*Material Beings* [-@vanInwagen1990]), Wiggins (*Sameness and Substance* [-@wiggins1980]), Lowe (*The Possibility of Metaphysics* [-@lowe1998]), who hold that ordinary objects are wholly present at each moment of their existence rather than composed of momentary stages, have written extensively against perdurance. The present reply is narrower than their full case: it locates the structural commitment that any momentarism must make to be the position it claims to be, and shows that the commitment instantiates the structural roles the position is defined as denying.

Three forms of the move develop the position at three depths: the strict-momentarism form, the causal-continuity form, and the counterpart-theoretic form. The reply argues that each fails for the same structural reason at increasing levels of refinement.

*First.* Strict momentarism (the cleanest form of the doctrine) claims that each instant is a complete fact unto itself, with no relations to any other instant. Each *kṣaṇa* arises and ceases in the same instant, and what we call succession is a cognitive imposition on what is in fact a sequence of unrelated complete facts.

Strict momentarism cannot describe its own claim. To say that there are many *kṣaṇa*s, in succession, is to relate them, and the relation of succession is exactly what is being denied. The position requires either that the *kṣaṇa*s be related or ordered, in which case a cross-stage structural fact is admitted, or that they be wholly unrelated, in which case the theory cannot recover succession. Wholly unrelated plurality does not literally collapse to one fact, but it cannot constitute a sequence without an ordering relation. The strict-momentarist version of the doctrine collapses on its own description: either the position is false because succession obtains, or the position is empty because nothing in it can be a succession of anything.

*Second.* The causal-continuity form weakens the claim: each moment is distinct, but moments are bound by causal relations. The *bhāva-santāna* (the continuum of being) is a causal stream, not a persistence condition; the appearance of a continuing self or object is the cognitive trace of the causal continuity, not the deliverance of an underlying substance.

A causal relation between distinct *kṣaṇa*s requires a structural fact connecting them. That supplies directed dependence and cross-stage bearing, but it does not by itself establish numerical identity or persistence of one bearer. The momentarist may accept causal continuity while denying strict persistence; the structural account must therefore distinguish the thin Φ-role from an endurantist persistence type. *Bhāva-santāna* names what Φ names: the structural condition that makes A's effect on B a real relation rather than a coincidence of pattern. If the doctrine is read as eliminating Φ, then the causal continuity it appeals to has nothing to run on and no force; if the doctrine is read as preserving Φ under a different name, then it has not eliminated persistence, only relabeled it. The Yogācāra commentators are aware of this tension; the elaborate apparatus of *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness as the carrier of karmic seeds across instants) is precisely the structural persistence the strict doctrine forswears, smuggled back in to do the explanatory work the strict doctrine cannot do without. The relabeling is honest about the explanatory need; what it does not show is that the structural role has been eliminated.

*Third.* The counterpart-theoretic form goes deepest: stages are momentary, but the genidentity relation (or the counterpart relation, or the appropriate cross-time similarity-plus-causation relation) ties them into the unified entities ordinary discourse names. The claim that this stage is the same person as that earlier stage is true under genidentity even though strict numerical identity does not obtain. Sider develops the position with full rigor; the technical apparatus is sophisticated and the resulting metaphysics is internally coherent.

The genidentity or counterpart relation is one proposed surrogate for persistence, not strict persistence under another vocabulary. For genidentity to obtain between this stage and that earlier stage, there must be a structural fact (not internal to either stage, since each is momentary, but extending across them) that makes the relation hold. Whatever fact it is, it is a structural fact spanning instants, and that *is* what Φ *consists in*. Sider's own stage theory is more precisely distinguished from perdurance: stages are not temporal parts of a four-dimensional whole but the primary objects, with persistence analyzed as a counterpart relation among numerically distinct stages (*Four-Dimensionalism* [-@sider2001, [§4.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3)]). On stage theory, the persistence structure is the counterpart-genidentity relation itself, which may realize the thin Φ-role as cross-stage continuity. Stage theory nevertheless denies that the later stage is numerically the same entity as the earlier stage; the relation supports survival-talk without restoring strict identity. On perdurance, the persistence structure is the four-dimensional whole of which stages are temporal parts. Both posit a structural fact spanning instants; they differ on whether that fact is a relation among stages or a whole of which they are parts. The question of which is more fundamental is not settled here and need not be: either description preserves Φ. The reply is not that perdurance or stage theory is incoherent (neither is) but that neither is a refutation of Φ: each *is* Φ in a different decomposition. The endurantist holds that a thing wholly present at each moment persists; the perdurantist holds that a thing has temporal parts at each moment and the four-dimensional whole persists. Both posit a structural fact spanning instants. Where they differ is on the metaphysics of the parts, not on whether persistence (in the structural sense [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names) obtains.

A kindred move is the bundle theory variant: the world is a bundle of tropes or property-instances, with no underlying substance. Each instant is a co-presence of tropes; the apparent persistence of an object is the resemblance and causal connection between successive bundles. The reply is structurally identical: either the bundles are unrelated (no succession, no persistence, no anything) or related (the relations are the structural facts [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) names). The bundle theorist who gives accounts of cross-time identity at all gives an account of structural persistence under another name.

Another kindred is the radical Heraclitean: nothing persists; everything is in flux; the river is never the same river twice. The reply is the same. To say that the river is in flux is to say that something stands in the relation of being-the-changing-pattern across the flux: the bed, the volume, the channel, or the whole spatiotemporal manifold of the river-event. Without structural persistence of some kind, 'flux' has no subject and the claim has no content. Heraclitus needs more structure than his slogan announces, and the more careful presocratic readings (Kahn, *The Art and Thought of Heraclitus* [-@kahn1979]) acknowledge as much.

*What converges.* Three forms and none lets the structural elimination stand. Strict momentarism collapses on its own description: succession is the relation it denies. Causal-continuity smuggles Φ back in under the name *bhāva-santāna* or its analogs; the explanatory need is met only by reintroducing exactly what the strict doctrine forswears. The counterpart-theoretic form is internally coherent but is not a refutation of Φ; it is Φ in a different decomposition, with the counterpart-genidentity relation (or, on perdurance, the four-dimensional whole) as the persistence analog. The endurantist and the perdurantist agree on the structural fact; they disagree on its metaphysics of parts. The question of which description is more fundamental (the four-dimensional whole, the momentary stages in counterpart relations, or the wholly-present enduring object) is a question within the structural framework and answerable within it. It does not bear on whether Φ obtains. Sider's stage theory is a fundamentality proposal within a structurally committed metaphysics: it specifies how the persistence structure is best analyzed, not whether it exists. The meta-position held here is that fundamentality questions of this kind are downstream of the instantiation question: once Φ is established as a necessary structural condition, further questions about its realization (by temporal parts, by counterpart relations, or by simple endurance) remain open to metaphysical investigation without threatening the structural conclusion.

Sibling counter-constructions: emergent-time positions, on which time itself is derivative rather than fundamental, are [§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3). The Shoemaker objection, on which time can obtain without change, is [§4.2.2](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-2). The temporary-intrinsics objection, on which apparent change is the difference of intrinsic properties at different times rather than change of a single intrinsic, is [§4.2.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-7).

The deepest form of the momentarist insight is one the structural account preserves rather than denies: there is something importantly correct about the observation that nothing in the world is fixed, that every object is in some sense an event, that what we call a thing is the persistent pattern of its becoming. The structural account names that pattern Φ (the persistence condition) and locates it as one of three structural roles whose joint instantiation is what change consists in. The momentarist who pushes the insight to the elimination of Φ has gone too far: persistence is not a substance behind the pattern but *is* the pattern itself, the structural fact that there is a pattern at all rather than a sequence of unrelated fragments.

### 4.2.9 Existential Inertia {#sec-4-2-9}

Two traditions agree that things persist and disagree about why. The classical theist holds that no contingent thing keeps itself in being for an instant: existence must be conserved, moment to moment, by a being that holds it there, on pain of annihilation. The existential-inertia theorist denies the dependence: a thing that exists tends to remain in existence on its own, absent a sufficient destroyer, and needs no concurrent sustainer to persist. This book sides with the inertialist's conclusion and rejects the inertialist's ground. Nature is not held in being by anything outside it; there is no concurrent divine sustainer to invoke. But neither does it persist by brute default. It persists because Φ (the retention of identity across an interval) is what persistence consists in. The conservation debate is conducted over a gap the structural account closes from below.

The conservationist case is Thomist in origin. Aquinas holds that God's causality is required not only to bring things into being but to keep them there: creatures stand to God as the air stands to the sun's illumination, ceasing the instant the influx ceases (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.104.1]; *De Potentia* [-@aquinas1932, q.5 a.1]). Freddoso ("God's General Concurrence with Secondary Causes," [-@freddoso1991]; and the 1994 sequel [-@freddoso1994]) reconstructs the medieval taxonomy, mere conservationism (God conserves things in being but creatures produce their own effects), concurrentism (each created effect is produced by God and creature together), and occasionalism (God is the only real cause, creatures mere occasions for his acting), and defends the concurrentist reading on which divine sustaining is required for every created effect. Feser (*Aquinas* [-@feser2009]; *Five Proofs of the Existence of God* [-@feser2017]) presses the demand through act and potency: a thing's existing at each moment is a potency that must be actualized by something already actual, terminating in Pure Act. Against the demand stands the existential-inertia thesis. Beaudoin ("The World's Continuance: Divine Conservation or Existential Inertia?" [-@beaudoin2007]) and, in its most developed form, Schmid ("Existential Inertia and the Aristotelian Proof," [-@schmid2021]) and Schmid and Linford (*Existential Inertia and Classical Theistic Proofs* [-@schmidLinford2022]) argue that persistence is the default state of concrete objects and that the conservationist owes a positive argument the tradition has not supplied. Kvanvig and McCann ("Divine Conservation and the Persistence of the World," [-@kvanvigMccann1988]) hold the conservationist line with the sharpest form of the counter-challenge: what grounds a thing's continuing to exist from one moment to the next, they ask, if not a sustaining cause? The structural account answers that question without adopting either side's location for the ground.

*First.* The conservationist argument runs on a hidden premise: that continued existence is a kind of change, a fresh actualization at each moment, a coming-to-be repeated. Feser's act/potency version makes the premise explicit: existence-now is a potency, and a potency requires a concurrent actualizer. Grant the framework and the conclusion follows; the demand is only as strong as the premise that persistence is a transition. It is not. A transition is a passage from one state to another. Mere continued existence need not be a fresh transition, although a persisting thing may undergo many qualitative changes while remaining the same thing. The conservationist must therefore argue that existing at a later time is a continuously derived effect, not simply infer that persistence as such is the absence of all change. The act/potency machinery earns its concurrent cause where there is becoming to account for; applied to mere continuation it manufactures a becoming that is not there and then requires a cause to sustain the manufactured becoming. Continuation is not continuous becoming. Nothing crosses from potency to act in a thing's simply remaining what it is, and so nothing is required to drive the crossing. The sun-and-illumination analogy (*ST* [-@aquinas1947, I.104.1]) imports exactly this picture (a continuous effect requiring a continuous cause) and holds only if continued being is an effect of the relevant kind. Illumination is a process; existence is not. (The simultaneous-causation machinery the Thomist offers to make the sustaining concurrent rather than prior is taken up at [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3); the point here is upstream of it: there is no sustaining-effect to make concurrent.)

This defeats the act/potency form of the demand, but not every form of it. The concurrentist need not say that persistence is a becoming at all. Freddoso's continuous-creation reading ([-@freddoso1991]; [-@freddoso1994]) treats created existence as a continuously-derived *effect*: dependent at every instant on a sustaining cause, yet with no transition, nothing crossing from potency to act, no becoming to drive. So construed, the demand never leans on the transition premise and survives its denial, but it survives as a demand for a *ground*, in virtue of what the thing exists now, not for a cause of change, and a grounding demand is met below rather than here. Two replies converge on it. The ground the concurrentist places in an external sustainer is supplied one level down by Φ (third move): once continued existence has a structural analysis, a continuously-deriving sustainer is not thereby shown redundant. Excluding the sustainer requires an additional argument that the constitutive account exhausts the relevant explanatory demand. And independently, as Chapter 6 will argue ([§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)), no candidate is available to do that work: a being answering to the classical specification (atemporal, aspatial, immaterial) is ∅ under that description and could derive nothing, so even a sound continuous-derivation demand would have nothing to name as the deriver. The transition form fails here; the continuous-effect form is answered downstream, not waved past.

*Second.* Conceding that persistence is not a transition does not end the matter, and the most precise opponent presses past it. Schmid's question is not "what changes a persisting thing?" but "in virtue of what does it persist rather than not?", a demand for a ground, not for a cause of change. Schmid and Linford ([-@schmidLinford2022]) are right that the demand cannot be waved off: a thing's continuing to exist is a fact about it, and facts about what is have grounds. The existential-inertia theorist who answers "it just does: persistence is the default" has named the explanandum (the fact to be explained) and called it an explanation. The structural account does not take that exit. Φ provides a constitutive analysis of persistence: persistence consists in the relevant retention or continuity of identity across an interval ([§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)). That answers what persistence is. It does not, merely by definition, answer the conservationist's distinct explanatory question of why this particular thing continues rather than ceases; treating the constitutive analysis as a sufficient sustaining explanation would beg that question. This is deeper than any contingent disposition the object carries (deeper than a tendency-to-persist that might be present or absent, masked or triggered) because Φ is the condition under which the object is a determinate something at all, at either moment. The conservationist is right that persistence is grounded and not brute; the inertialist is right that the ground is not God. Both put the ground outside the persisting thing: the theist in a sustaining cause, the inertialist's critics in a missing one. It is one level down, in the structural condition any persisting thing already instantiates by being a thing across time. This is the book's inversion performed at the site of conservation: the feature the tradition reaches for (a sustaining ground beneath contingent existence) is real, and is not what the tradition takes it to be.

*Third.* Schmid's modal-collapse instinct supplies the sharpest reply available to the opponent. If persistence is grounded in Φ, and Φ is necessary (the book argues exactly this) then is the persistence of every particular thing necessary too? If the ground cannot fail, and the ground is what holds the thing in being, then the thing cannot fail to persist, and the contingency of the world collapses into necessity. The worry is the existential-inertia analogue of the modal-collapse argument Schmid presses against divine simplicity, and it is the one objection a structural ground must answer or forfeit the field.

It does not go through, and the reason is a distinction the book has already drawn. The necessity of Φ is the necessity of the condition (that whatever persists does so by retaining identity across an interval), not the necessity of any particular persister's retaining it. The level-distinction is fixed at [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4): that the conditions of contingency are necessary does not make the contingent facts they condition necessary; the framework within which things come and go cannot itself come or go, while the things within it still do. L9, the non-propagation of constitutive grounding ([§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9)), is the grounding-theoretic statement of that same distinction rather than a second defense: a constitutive ground hands its modal status to the *condition* it grounds, never to the particular actualizations that satisfy it. L9 is earned at [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) for the necessity of change: there □(T∧S∧Φ) and □◇C are not ground and grounded but one fact under two readings, so the necessary possibility of change carries its necessity by identity, not by transmission across a grounding relation. What the conditions ground *constitutively, not productively* are the particular changes, with the necessity propagating to none of them (□◇C, not □C). The persistence case runs that constitutive half of the schema once more, with one shift worth marking: at [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) the constitutive ground bears on each particular change, whereas here it bears on persistence under a constitutive *condition*, leaving the contingent de re fact (*that any particular thing persists*) outside the reach of the necessity.

Φ grounds persistence *constitutively*, not productively: it does not produce each thing's continuation as an effect produces its output, which is the only way necessity would propagate Spinoza-fashion; it is what continuing-to-be *consists in*, the identity-retention condition any persister instantiates simply by being a thing across the interval.

So the □ attaches to the conditional, read de dicto (a claim about the proposition, not the thing), □(if x persists, x persists by Φ): necessarily, whatever persists does so by retaining identity across an interval. It does not attach to the de re □(x persists): no particular thing's continuing is thereby made necessary. Φ's being necessary no more makes this oak's persistence necessary than the necessity of the conditions of value makes any particular thing valuable of necessity. The oak persists by Φ while it persists, and ceases when its identity-retention fails. Modal collapse is blocked not at two joints but at one stated twice: the level-distinction of [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4) and L9 of [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9) are the same non-propagation seen from the side of levels and from the side of grounding.

*The nearest neighbors.* Three positions also locate persistence in what the thing is, and the account must not blur into any of them. Dispositional essentialism grounds persistence in a first-order power to persist: a disposition the object carries, one that could be present or absent, masked or triggered. Φ is not such a power: a disposition is a further feature of an already-individuated thing, whereas Φ is the condition under which there is an individuated thing at all, at either end of the interval, to bear features.

Beaudoin's naturalist inertia ([-@beaudoin2007]) reaches the right conclusion (no sustainer) by treating persistence as a brute default; it differs from the structural account exactly as the brute inertialist of the second move does, by leaving ungrounded what the structural account grounds.

And Spinozist necessitarianism grounds persistence in the necessity of substance, paying for it with the collapse just blocked: it runs the ground's necessity straight into the persister, making every continuation necessary. The structural account takes the necessity of the ground together with the level-distinction, so the ground is necessary while the persister is not. The difference from each neighbor is one difference told three ways: Φ is a condition, not a first-order feature; the ground is structural, not brute; and the necessity in play is the necessity of that condition, not of whatever satisfies it.
