*Third, information.* Chalmers’s later work (*Reality+* [@chalmers2022]) and the simulation literature [@bostrom2003] press a related thought: perhaps the world is a simulation and what is fundamental is information or computation, not matter. Taken from the information-theoretic side, this is engaged at [§4.1.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-5); what this section adds is that information is itself a structural notion. It requires distinguishable states (S), transitions between them (T), and a substrate that carries them (Φ). A simulated world exhibiting T, S, and Φ is a world exhibiting T, S, and Φ, and the simulator’s own substrate is structured in turn. The regress ends at the conditions, not before them.

*What the position actually buys.* Analytic idealism’s deepest attraction is that it dissolves the hard problem of consciousness: if experience is fundamental, the question how non-experiential matter generates experience cannot arise, there being no non-experiential matter to do the generating. That dissolution is genuine — taking experience as primitive is no more illicit than any account’s taking its own ground as primitive. But the hard problem doesn't retire here — it trades, and the trade is asymmetric in kind. Physicalism owes a cross-category derivation, the experiential from the non-experiential, which is the hard problem proper; idealism owes only an intra-category one, the structuring of what is already experiential. That asymmetry is the one place the comparison stops mirroring, and it falls to idealism: unlike a parsimony tally, which runs both ways, this debt is lighter on the idealist side.

How much lighter is worth pressing, because the intra-category debt is not small. Idealism must say why the fundamental consciousness is differentiated and structured at all, dissociated into alters and articulated into a lawful world, rather than an undifferentiated field. Set beside the hard problem this looks like the easier question, an internal shaping rather than a category crossing, and it is easier only in category, not in force. The move from an undifferentiated substrate to a structured world of alters is a move from no T, S, or Φ to all three; it is the appearance of articulated structure from a ground said to have none, which is a structural analogue of the hard problem run one level down. The analogy should not be overstated: both terms stay within the experiential, so this is not the phenomenal-generation gap itself, and to that extent idealism’s dissolution of it is genuine. What recurs is the gap’s form, not its content: an unexplained passage from the homogeneous to the differentiated, and that formal debt is discharged only in T, S, and Φ. Idealism has not dissolved the problem of how structure arises; it has renamed the terrain on which that problem is posed, from matter-and-experience to substrate-and-differentiation. And its own answer, when it gives one, must credit the substrate with the power to differentiate, to persist, and to unfold in time — with exactly T, S, and Φ. The generation question is won; the differentiation question is inherited; and the differentiation question is answered only by the conditions whose fundamentality the position set out to deny. What experience positively is, the identification with self-modeling structure, is Chapter 8’s work, resting on the substrate-neutral ground supplied at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8); the point here is only that the differentiation debt is structural.

The same lineage makes a second appeal, to parsimony: idealism posits only experience, where physicalism posits experience and non-experiential matter and still owes the passage between them. The general reply is at [§5.1.4](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-4) — comparative parsimony cannot adjudicate between structure and an alternative to it in either direction, because the count presupposes the very conditions (distinguishable posits set against a common measure) it would use to decide. Here the count that makes a single field look simpler omits the differentiation the field must undergo to appear as a world of alters, and that differentiation just is T, S, and Φ at the level of the cosmic mind. Entered on the ledger it is no saving: the apparent economy is bought back exactly where the work is done. Parsimony cannot select idealism over the structural account, because what it would economize on is what idealism must keep.

*One objection cuts across all four forms.* The reply to every idealism has the same shape, that whatever is made fundamental turns out to be structured, and that very uniformity invites the charge that the argument is unfalsifiable: no matter what the idealist names, the section will declare it structured enough, so the thesis rules nothing out and says nothing. The charge would land if the conditions were imposed by stipulation. They are not, and the section accepts the burden the charge identifies. There is a way for idealism to win: specify a fundamental that hosts a world of appearance while instantiating none of T, S, or Φ (no distinction among its contents, no order to their succession, nothing that persists to bear them), and the argument fails. The claim is not that such a posit is forbidden but that every attempt to specify it collapses into ∅, the state that on examination is no state at all ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7), [§2.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-8)). The idealist is owed that opening and has it; what the idealist lacks is a filling for it. Conceded, then, is just what the symmetry objection concedes against the cosmological tradition elsewhere in the book ([§5.1.2](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-2)): the reply earns no victory by fiat. It earns it only because the unstructured fundamental, pressed for content, keeps turning out to be nothing.

*The dispute is downstream of the conclusion.* Step back from the four forms and the shape of the whole engagement comes into view. Idealism and physicalism are two redescriptions of one skeleton. Subtract the words *mental* and *physical* from each, and what remains on both sides is the same thing: distinguishable items held in an ordered succession by something that persists — T, S, and Φ carrying the explanatory load. Their dispute is over which vocabulary the skeleton wears. The book’s positive conclusion is a claim about the skeleton, not the vocabulary, and it is therefore settled before the mental-versus-physical dispute is even joined. This is why the argument need not defeat idealism to reach its end. It need not choose between idealism and physicalism to establish its positive conclusion (that conclusion holds whatever the ground’s metaphysical character turns out to be, as established at [§2.2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-3)); and it need not defeat idealism to overturn classical theism (the inversion holds under idealism as readily as under physicalism, as established at [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1)). What it requires of idealism is only what idealism, on examination, always grants: that whatever is fundamental be structured.

*What converges.* Idealism in its four forms (Berkeleyan, transcendental, phenomenological, analytic) shares with the structural account a single refusal: it will not derive consciousness from antecedent non-conscious matter. The four part company over what is fundamental (divine perception for Berkeley, the conditions of possible experience for Kant, the constituting ego for Husserl, cosmic consciousness for Kastrup), and the book’s reply is one and the same across them, distributed over [§2.2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-2-3), [§6.1](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-1), and this section: whatever is put at the bottom, if it is structured enough to do the work the position needs, it instantiates T, S, and Φ. The conditions are conditions on anything that hosts process, and a mind is one kind of host. So the structural conditions are mind-compatible without being mind-derived: consistent with consciousness being widespread and substrate-independent (the substrate-neutral ground is supplied at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), life as multiply realizable closure-plus-throughput, and the consciousness identification that rides on it is carried in Chapter 8), and consistent with its being fundamental in a sense the argument need not adjudicate. What the argument is not consistent with is the one claim idealism would need and never establishes: that what is fundamental is unstructured, that it lacks T, S, and Φ. That claim, examined, identifies nothing.

### 4.3.6 The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics {#sec-4-3-6}

Riemann's 1854 habilitation lecture generalized geometry beyond Euclidean space and introduced the conceptual machinery later developed into Riemannian curvature. Roughly sixty years later, Einstein, working with Grossmann and others, used differential geometry to formulate general relativity and describe effects including the bending of light. Sophus Lie's 1873 transformations answer to no force or particle known at the time; sixty years later, the symmetry groups he catalogued become the structural language in which the strong and weak interactions are written. David Hilbert worked out the theory of infinite-dimensional function spaces in the 1900s as part of a program in pure functional analysis; by the late 1920s Hilbert-space methods became a central formulation of quantum mechanics, though later algebraic, path-integral, and other formulations show that no single notation should be called uniquely indispensable. The pattern is not one anecdote or two. It is, as Wigner said, unreasonable.

Wigner (*The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences*, 1960) gave the observation its classical statement and left the explanation open. Hamming (1980) restated the puzzle in a working mathematician's voice and left it as unresolved as Wigner had. Steiner (*The Applicability of Mathematics as a Philosophical Problem*, 1998) pressed the quantitative version: specific anticipations, each precise, cumulatively demanding an explanation a naturalist cannot easily supply. Plantinga (*Where the Conflict Really Lies*, 2011) developed the theistic interpretation rigorously: if reality and mathematics share a common rational origin, the fit is intelligible; the designer who authored the world also authored the minds that describe it. Tegmark (*Our Mathematical Universe*, 2008, 2014) pressed the radical inversion: the universe is a mathematical structure, and applicability is identity. Against the theistic reading stand naturalistic explanations of varying depth: Pincock (*Mathematics and Scientific Representation*, 2012) developed a 'mapping account' on which mathematics applies when the abstract structure models the concrete; Bueno and French (*Applying Mathematics*, 2018) pushed a partial-structures version; Colyvan (*The Indispensability of Mathematics*, 2001) defended the Quine–Putnam line as a foundation for mathematical realism without theistic auxiliaries. The present reply sits closest to the structural realists (Ladyman and Ross 2007) in treating applicability as a fact about shared structure rather than about correspondence between two independent domains, and specifies what the bare position does not: which structure is shared. It is equally not Tegmark's Mathematical Universe Hypothesis: applicability is here grounded in the instantiation of the T∧S∧Φ architecture, not in Level-IV plenitude or an identity of physical reality with abstracta, while [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4) leaves robust Platonism and uninstantiated abstract structure as live positions rather than identifying them with ∅. The agreement of mathematics and physics is one instantiated structure recognized twice, not reality being mathematical; the full structural-realism-versus-MUH non-equivalence is developed at [§4.3.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-7).

The challenge bears directly on the Triconditional Identity of [§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10) and on the Necessity of Nature of [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5). The applicability theorist replies that the precise correspondence between a priori mathematical structures and a posteriori physical reality is a positive fact about the world that the structural roles do not explain, and that the best explanation appeals to an authoring mind whose rational character underwrites both. If the explanatory ask is well-founded, either Nature is not self-sufficient (against [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5)) or the structural roles do not exhaust what a complete account must specify (against [§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)).

A clarification before the moves. The puzzle is not merely that mathematics is useful. Utility is a weak notion that any formal tool might satisfy. The puzzle is that specific mathematical structures, derived for internal reasons decades or centuries before any physical application, turn out to match the physical world with high precision: Riemannian geometry (smoothly curved manifolds generalizing Euclidean surfaces to arbitrary curvature), Lie groups (continuous symmetry groups indexed by smooth transformations), and Hilbert spaces (infinite-dimensional state spaces equipped with an inner product), each arriving years before the physics that needed them. Three forms of the move press that specificity at three resolutions (the general observation, Steiner's anticipation argument, and the precision claim), and the space they cover is the space the applicability theorist occupies. The replies test whether any form can preserve the external/internal gap it requires to get started.

*First.* The unreasonable-effectiveness move holds that mathematicians develop structures for internal reasons (elegance, generality, formal consistency) and those structures turn out to describe physical reality. The fit is not accidental; it is evidence physical reality and mathematical structure share a common origin. A common origin is most naturally a rational mind.

Mathematics is not a script the universe follows from outside. It is a description of the structure of the medium itself, produced by cognitive faculties that are themselves configurations of that same medium. The mathematician's reasoning proceeds under the same constraints that govern the physical world, because both mathematician and world instantiate T, S, and Φ. There is no gap between the describer and the described requiring a bridge. What looks like pre-established harmony between two domains is a single necessary architecture recognized from two locations within itself.

*Second.* Steiner's anticipation argument presses from another angle. Pure mathematics, developed with no physical application in view, repeatedly anticipates the deep structure of physical reality. Riemannian geometry existed sixty years before general relativity needed it. Group theory existed decades before particle physics needed it. Anticipation is the point: mathematics is not merely consistent with physics; it arrives first. Arriving first requires explanation.

The anticipation dissolves when one asks what the mathematician was doing. Riemann developed his generalized geometry by following the logical consequences of letting curvature vary freely, by asking what relational structures are possible given Space's constraints at a certain level of abstraction. Lie developed his groups by asking what transformations preserve structural identity across a manifold: the same question Space asks at higher generality. The mathematician is not transcending the structural roles to anticipate them from outside. The mathematician is mapping T, S, and Φ from inside, following the logical consequences of what the roles necessarily permit. When physics later needs those structures, nothing has been pre-tuned. Both the mathematical investigation and the physical phenomena were already constrained by the same necessary architecture. The anticipation, on this reading, is not external fit but two independent descriptions meeting at their point of shared necessity.

*Third.* The specific-precision move appeals to high resolution. It is not merely that mathematics is applicable: it is that the specific mathematical structures match the specific physical phenomena with astonishing exactness. Hilbert spaces are exactly what quantum mechanics requires. SU(3) (the special unitary group of 3×3 matrices, parameterizing the color-charge symmetry of quarks) is exactly the symmetry group of the strong force. Riemannian geometry with Lorentzian signature is exactly what general relativity needs. The precision is too exact to be coincidence. It suggests a designer who chose both.

Specific precision is what structural necessity looks like at high resolution, though the examples should not be overstated as if each formalism were uniquely forced independently of theory. Lie groups capture the transformation-structure physics repeatedly needs when asking what preserves structural identity across a manifold. Riemannian geometry becomes the right language for general relativity once extension, curvature, and causal distribution have to be represented together. Hilbert spaces provide the standard formalism for quantum mechanics when states are represented so as to preserve superposition, transition amplitudes, and unitary evolution. The specific structures are not tuned to fit the physics from outside; they are mathematical vocabularies that repeatedly articulate the same structural roles at different levels of the architecture. The precision, on this reading, is the signature of shared structure recognized from two directions rather than a sign of external authorship.

A word is owed on the probabilistic register Plantinga and Steiner share. Plantinga's inference is abductive (the fit is more probable given a common rational origin than given naturalism), and Steiner's is cumulative: each precise anticipation is individually unlikely, the conjunction far more so. Both ledgers presuppose that the fit is a contingent datum whose probability theism raises and naturalism leaves low. The structural reading does not compete on that ledger; it contests how much contingency the ledger has to score. The shared structural architecture can explain why mathematics is broadly applicable, but T, S, and Φ are too coarse to necessitate the particular success of SU(3), Hilbert-space quantum theory, or Lorentzian geometry. Those high-resolution fits depend on contingent physical laws, theory selection, and the richness of mathematics. The applicability puzzle is therefore reduced at the general structural level, not dissolved as a single necessity. The independence Steiner's cumulative case needs (each anticipation a separate low-probability event whose improbabilities multiply) is the first casualty: the cases do not multiply because they are not independent coincidences but the same architecture surfacing again. The comparison is narrowed rather than conceded: what remains contingent is the particular physics, not a further mathematics–world harmony standing over it, and a residue of that shape is not a datum theism explains better than naturalism.

A kindred move drops Plantinga's theistic framing for mathematical Platonism: the Quine–Putnam indispensability arguments (Quine 1948; Putnam 1971) treat mathematical truths as abstract facts physics cannot dispense with, and the explanatory puzzle reduces to correspondence between Platonic abstracta and concrete physics. The Platonic challenge is engaged at [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4); the version here assumes its result: no mathematical view by itself supplies a counterexample to the structural conditions in concrete change-realizing worlds, and the structures mathematicians apply to the world are structural roles described under mathematical vocabulary.

The information-theoretic ontology that treats reality as fundamentally informational is [§4.1.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-5); the mathematical-universe hypothesis, that reality is itself a mathematical structure, is [§4.3.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-7). The hard problem of consciousness, which presses a different mode of non-structural residue, is [§4.3.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-1). The contemporary-physics challenges (Bell non-locality, Everett, and the quantum-field-theoretic dissolution of the particle concept) are [§4.3.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-8).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms collapses the external fit it required to get started. The unreasonable-effectiveness move treats mathematics as a script the universe follows from outside, when it is a description of the medium itself produced by cognitive faculties that are themselves configurations of that medium. Steiner's anticipation dissolves once the mathematician is located inside the architecture: Riemann and Lie were mapping T, S, and Φ from within by following the logical consequences of what the roles necessarily permit, not anticipating them from outside. The specific-precision cases show that mathematical formalisms can capture physical structure at high resolution. The structural roles help explain why such mapping is possible, but they do not uniquely derive those formalisms or exclude alternative mathematical representations. External authorship is therefore not forced, yet neither is the detailed fit exhausted by the thin triad alone.

Wigner delivered *The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences*: a physicist asking why mathematicians' work kept arriving in his hands before he knew he needed it. He offered no explanation. He named the fit unreasonable and let the word do its work. On the structural account, the word does less work than it was originally asked to carry. Riemann developed his geometry under the constraint of a mathematical practice conducted in Space and Time by a persisting Substance: Riemann himself, alive, thinking. Lie developed his groups by asking what transformations preserve structural identity across a manifold: the question Space itself asks at higher generality. Hilbert built his spaces out of relations between states, which is what Space builds at every level. The applicability the theist reads as the signature of external authorship is, on the present account, the signature of shared necessity. The 'unreasonable effectiveness' recedes once math is recognized as the internal grammar of Time, Space, and Substance. The mathematician who marvels at applicability is marveling that structural descriptions describe.

What answers Wigner's unreasonable, on the structural account, is that the word named a surprise the architecture does not in fact support: the world *is* what the architecture looks like when a part of the architecture describes the whole.

Put in the vocabulary of Modal Pressure ([§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10)): mathematics *is* what Modal Pressure looks like when attended to in the notation built to track inference, and physics *is* what Modal Pressure looks like when attended to in the notation built to track state transition. Both notations are tracking the same running structure. Their agreement is not pre-established harmony between two domains. It is one pressure, recognized twice.

### 4.3.7 Mathematical Universe Hypothesis {#sec-4-3-7}

Tegmark (2008, 2014) defends the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis: physical reality is a mathematical structure. Not modeled by a mathematical structure, identical to one. Every mathematical structure exists in the same sense; the one we inhabit is the one whose internal observers detect themselves as inhabiting it. The hypothesis is meant to be the most parsimonious possible ontology: nothing exists but mathematical structures, and the question why our particular structure exists has no answer because every structure does.

The MUH is the clearest contemporary alternative ground to the present argument's T-S-Φ (the three structural conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance). It deserves direct engagement.

A mathematical structure, on the standard account Tegmark relies on, is an isomorphism class of relations on a set. As pure mathematics, it may instantiate abstract relations without temporal succession, spatial extension, or causal persistence. The present argument concedes that much.

The issue begins only when Tegmark identifies a structure with **physical reality** and invokes internal observers. A structure that realizes observerhood, state evolution, and actual physical processes must supply more than an abstract isomorphism class: it must realize succession, differentiation, and bearing at role-resolution, and its physical realization must meet the further type-level burden developed in the book. The reply is therefore conditional on the MUH's identity thesis. Pure mathematical structure is not refuted; a mathematical structure proposed as the complete physical realizer does not escape the structural roles.

Read in the present argument's terms, the MUH looks less like an alternative to T, S, and Φ than a vocabulary for them: the mathematical-structure ontology specifying in pure mathematics what the present argument specifies as necessary conditions. But an equivalence asserted from one side is not yet an engagement. Tegmark's thesis is an identity claim (physical reality *is* a mathematical structure), not the weaker claim that mathematics supplies one vocabulary among others for a Nature specified independently; and he would resist the redescription as flattening a substantive metaphysical thesis into a notational variant. The thesis must therefore be met on its own terms. Taken there, it does not escape the conditions. Any mathematical structure identical with an observer-containing physical reality must have differentiated positions or states and support an internal ordering adequate for observer-processes. Invariance under isomorphism is a criterion of structural identity, not temporal persistence or Substance. The Φ-role requires a further account of how determinate capacities or continuities are realized inside the structure. Tegmark may still call this a redescription rather than a discovery, but the resistance cannot consist in denying that his structure has distinguishable elements, persists, and carries succession, for a structure without these could not be the one we inhabit. The identity thesis does not bypass the structural conditions; it presupposes them.

A second pressure. Tegmark argues that *every* mathematical structure exists. The claim is comparative: the structure we inhabit is one of an infinite plenitude. The plenitude is not posited idly: its motivation is anthropic. The apparent fine-tuning of our universe's constants needs neither a designer nor brute luck if every mathematical structure is equally real, since observers necessarily find themselves in one of the life-permitting members of the ensemble. This is the selection-within-an-ensemble strategy the fine-tuning argument meets directly ([§5.1.5](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-5)), and that verdict carries over here with one addition proper to the MUH. Even granting the ensemble, a structure can house observers who detect themselves only if it has distinguishable elements, persistence, and internal succession, so anthropic selection does not select away from T, S, and Φ; it ranges only over structures that already satisfy them. The plenitude universalizes the structural conditions rather than relieving them. And it faces a difficulty in its own right. Our reasoning about the plenitude is an act within a structured world, but that act-side fact does not determine the object-side ontology of the other structures. The sharper objection is whether Tegmark has supplied a clear, non-equivocal sense of physical existence applying equally to observerless and observer-containing mathematical structures. Anthropically selected structures must realize the roles required for observers; the plenitude as a whole need not.

*What converges.* What the MUH offers is a mathematical formalization of the necessary ground, not an alternative to it. Its parsimony is real (nothing exists but mathematical structure), but the structure it cannot do without is the structure the present argument names. The argument’s conclusion that T, S, and Φ are necessary is, translated into Tegmark’s vocabulary, the claim that mathematical structure is necessary; within his own hypothesis, T, S, and Φ are the conditions any structure must meet to be the one we inhabit. Read either way, they are not what the hypothesis leaves behind; they are what it cannot be stated without.

### 4.3.8 Non-Locality, Branching, and the Particle Concept {#sec-4-3-8}

In 1964, John Bell wrote down an inequality any local hidden-variables theory of quantum mechanics must satisfy. Eighteen years later, Alain Aspect's team confirmed experimentally that the inequality is violated in the actual world. Bell's theorem, together with the experiments, rules out local hidden-variable accounts satisfying the theorem's auxiliary assumptions, including the relevant independence conditions. It does not by itself select one metaphysical interpretation of quantum mechanics. That was one door. Everett's 1957 proposal had already opened another: the quantum state never collapses but branches, with each measurement partitioning reality into decoherent branches, each of which contains a copy of the measuring apparatus and the measurer. And in the relativistic extension of quantum mechanics, as Doreen Fraser and David Baker pressed across the 2000s, the particle concept itself loses its frame-invariant referent. Three results. Three places where a piece of the classical metaphysical picture has had to give ground to the mathematics.

The contemporary literature on these three loci is well-developed. On Bell non-locality: Maudlin's *Quantum Non-Locality and Relativity* (3rd ed. 2011) gives the most sustained metaphysical analysis; Wallace's *The Emergent Multiverse* (2012) develops the Everettian alternative frame. On Everettian branching: Wallace 2012 stands as the systematic contemporary defense; Saunders, Barrett, Kent and Wallace's *Many Worlds?* (2010) is the standard anthology; Albert (*Quantum Mechanics and Experience*, 1992) and Maudlin (*Philosophy of Physics: Quantum Theory*, 2019) press the major objections. On QFT: Fraser (2008) and Baker (2009) give the philosophical case against Fock-space particle ontology; Wallace ('In Defense of Naiveté,' 2006) and Ruetsche (*Interpreting Quantum Theories*, 2011) develop field-interpretive alternatives. The structural reply does not enter these debates as a rival position. It accepts the most demanding reading of each result and asks what the structural roles look like once that reading is incorporated.

The challenges so far in [§4.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3) have come from philosophy of mind and philosophy of mathematics. This final cluster comes from physics itself. Three questions press the account from contemporary physics: one from Bell's result on correlations, one from Everett's branching, one from QFT's treatment of the particle concept. Bell non-locality appears to threaten Space's relational non-identity: distant regions are correlated in ways no local structural description admits. Everett multiplies worlds in a way that appears to threaten Substance's persistence and Time's unique directed succession. QFT appears to remove the thing Substance was meant to name: particles, as well-defined countable objects, do not survive the relativistic formalism. If any of these is taken at face value, the Necessity of Nature of [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5), supported by the Triconditional Identity of [§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10) (the result that Time, Space, and Substance, the bearers of the three structural Conditions Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality, must be co-instantiated for any concrete existent), faces a counterexample from physics: the kind of counterexample a metaphysical argument has to address directly.

*First.* Bell non-locality holds that quantum correlations between spatially separated outcomes outrun local hidden-variable accounts. Bell (1964) proved a limit on correlations between spatially separated measurement outcomes that any local hidden-variables theory must respect. Experimental violations of that limit, Aspect et al. (1982), followed by the loophole-free experiments of the 2010s (Hensen et al. 2015; Giustina et al. 2015), establish that quantum correlations outrun local common causes. Maudlin (*Quantum Non-Locality and Relativity*, 3rd ed. 2011) has pressed the philosophical consequence with the most clarity: the world, on the best reading of the evidence, contains non-local dependencies between spatially separated events. If Space guarantees relational non-identity (if distinct positions are ontologically distinct loci) Bell's result seems to show that distinctness is weaker than the argument requires. The outcomes display correlations incompatible with local hidden-variable factorization, while the no-signalling structure prevents their use for superluminal communication. Describing this as instantaneous causal influence would add an interpretation the experiments alone do not establish.

Non-locality refines Space's specification without dissolving it. Bell's inequality is a constraint on what kinds of correlations are possible between spacelike-separated outcomes; it is not a denial that spacelike-separated outcomes are distinct. The correlation presupposes the distinction: Alice's measurement and Bob's measurement are two measurements, at two locations, with two outcomes, and the correlation Bell quantifies is the relation between those two. What Bell rules out is a specific metaphysical picture: local hidden-variable determination. What survives is a richer structural picture in which non-identity is preserved but the relations binding non-identical positions exceed signal-bounded causation. Maudlin's own preferred reading (non-locality as a fundamental relational feature of the world) is Space specified at higher resolution, not Space refuted. The argument has never required that all spatial relations be mediated sub-luminally. It has required that distinct positions be distinct. Non-locality leaves that requirement intact and tells us what else is true at its level. A sharper version of the worry does not stop at the correlations. If the entanglement-geometry program in quantum gravity is right — if spatial separation is itself emergent from entanglement structure, as the ER=EPR conjecture and allied approaches propose — then Spatiality is pressed one level below distinctness: the reply above secures that the outcomes are two, not that the spatial gap between them is fundamental. The structural answer runs parallel to the emergent-time handling at the QFT locus below. The S-role never required that spatial extension be fundamental, only that real differentiation be realized; a proposal on which space emerges from entanglement must still ground an order of real differences, and the role then attaches to whatever grounds the emergence — entanglement structure included, which is itself a structure of distinct, differently related relata. Whether any emergent-spacetime program succeeds is a live physical question, an alignment matter for the framework rather than something this survey derives; what no such program can deliver is differentiation from no differences at all.

*Second.* Everettian branching holds that the quantum state never collapses but forks into decoherent branches at every measurement. The Everett interpretation (Everett 1957; Wallace, *The Emergent Multiverse*, 2012) holds that the quantum state never collapses. Measurement interactions branch the universal wave function into decoherent branches, each containing a copy of the measurement and a copy of the observer. On Wallace's mature development, branching is continuous and ubiquitous, the branches are real, and the classical world is one branch's-eye view of a structure larger than any single branch. Time's unique directed succession appears to split. Substance's persistence appears to fork. The Triune architecture, specified at the level of a single temporal-spatial-substantial flow, appears to meet a physics in which that flow is one trajectory among indefinitely many.

The Everettian picture, at its clearest, does not dissolve Time and Substance. It multiplies them. Each branch instantiates the structural roles. Branching itself requires what any differentiating operation requires: distinct outcomes (Space), distinct directions of succession within each branch (Time), and the maintenance of causal capacity within each branch (Substance). On a realist Everettian reading, the universal wave function and its decoherent branch structure are taken as physically real. Whether branches are exact ontological loci or emergent, approximate patterns is part of the interpretation and should not be settled by the structural vocabulary alone. The argument's claim that existence requires T, S, and Φ (Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality) is satisfied within every branch. That there are many branches speaks to the scale of the structural commitment, not its nature. The Everettian owes the argument one answer: does the universal wave function, considered as the whole of reality, itself instantiate the structural architecture the argument requires? For T and S, it does. Unitary evolution and decoherence supply an ordered dynamical structure, while decoherent branch-patterns become distinguishable for practical purposes. Whether the universal state supplies the Φ-role as a persisting physical entity or only as mathematical state structure depends on the ontology adopted. Everett multiplies the domain across which the architecture is instantiated without replacing the architecture itself.

A qualification on dialectical scope is owed before proceeding. The preceding reply works on Wallace’s (2012) mature Everettianism, granting the branching structure and showing that it instantiates T, S, and Φ. Maudlin’s own position is not Everettian; he is among the interpretation’s most sustained critics. His principal objections concern branch individuation (the formalism provides no physical criterion for individuating branches, leaving the probability calculus without a derivable foundation), the Born-rule problem (recovering the Born-rule probabilities from branching ratios requires a notion of branch weight that cannot be derived from the wavefunction alone without circularity), and the absence of primitive ontology (Everettianism specifies a formalism without saying what physically exists in spacetime — the universal wavefunction is not itself local, and no catalogue of local beables is provided). These objections press whether Everettianism should be granted in the first place, not whether, granted, it preserves the structural roles. The structural argument is therefore not adjudicating between Maudlin and Wallace. What it establishes is scope-neutral: whatever interpretation of quantum mechanics is adopted, Everettian branching, Bohmian mechanics (whose particle trajectories are paradigm local beables instantiating S, Φ, and T directly), GRW collapse theories (whose flash or matter-density ontologies similarly supply local Φ-realizers), or algebraic approaches, the structural roles must be satisfied by whatever the interpretation countenances as its primitive ontology. Maudlin’s local-beable insistence is, from this vantage, a demand that the Φ-role be explicitly realized by something in spacetime; the structural argument agrees, and adds that every serious candidate for that something satisfies the role.

*Third.* The QFT particle-concept problem holds that the relativistic formalism dispenses with frame-invariant particles. Quantum field theory in its relativistic form dispenses with the classical particle concept. Fraser ("The Fate of 'Particles' in Quantum Field Theories with Interactions," 2008) and Baker ("Against Field Interpretations of Quantum Field Theory," 2009) develop the philosophical consequences. In interacting relativistic QFT there is no Fock-space particle description invariant across frames, no particle-number operator that commutes with the full Hamiltonian, no countable thing whose identity persists across the field's evolution. Particles, as well-defined individuals, do not survive the mathematics. What survives, depending on interpretation, is a structure of fields, algebraic observables, excitations, state-transition constraints, or some more austere QFT ontology. If Substance was meant to name particle-persistents, QFT has removed its referent.

Substance was never specified as particle-persistence. Substance is defined at [§1.4.3](groundwork.html#sec-1-4-3) as the maintenance of causal capacity across transitions, leaving open what realizes the maintenance. Particles were one candidate: the nineteenth-century candidate, inherited by the early twentieth. Fields are another. The reply does not simply trade particles for fields as if field ontology were uncontested. Whether the preferred interpretation speaks in terms of fields, local algebras, excitations, gauge-invariant structures, or state-transition constraints, the structural point is the same: the formalism preserves determinate capacities across transitions. There are states or observables that can differ, rules or constraints governing their transformations, and stable relations across which those transformations are specified. That is the role Substance plays here. QFT refines the realizer of Substance (perhaps beyond both particles and naïve fields) rather than eliminating the role.

Maudlin’s primitive-ontology insistence bears directly here: an unspecified disjunction of realizers (fields, algebraic states, excitations, gauge-invariant structures) is not yet an ontology, and a role-claim ungrounded in a specified ontology is, on his methodological view, physics-as-decoration. The structural argument’s response is not to choose among the candidates but to explain why the choice can be deferred at this level without losing force. The Φ-role specifies what any acceptable realizer must do: make a determinate physical capacity available to the ordered regime in which a real difference can occur. When the ontology is fundamentally dynamical, that is the maintenance of causal capacity across transitions. When a proposal treats time as emergent, it need not posit a fundamental clock-time; it must instead show how its fundamental constraints or states ground an emergent order in which determinate capacities can be carried and made effective. A proposal that denies any such capacity-and-order story has not yet supplied a realizer of change, rather than having supplied a counterexample to it.

This is a division of roles, not a collapse of Φ into T. T supplies the order of before and after; Φ supplies what can remain determinate and make a difference through that order. The present survey does not decide whether any timeless quantum-gravity program successfully supplies the required emergence account. That is a live physical question, and the framework's use of the role here is abductive rather than a result it certifies in advance. Committing to one realizer would narrow the claim without strengthening it; remaining at the role level preserves the comparison across the live interpretive options. Where Maudlin’s demand is directed at physical theory (QFT owes a primitive ontology) the argument agrees, and defers to that ongoing debate on its own terms.

*What converges.* Each of the three questions finds the physics specifying the structural roles at higher resolution than the classical picture anticipated. Bell's inequality is a constraint on what kinds of correlations are possible between spacelike-separated outcomes, not a denial that the outcomes are distinct; the correlation presupposes the distinction, and non-locality refines Space's non-identity rather than dissolving it. The Everett multiverse multiplies the domain across which the architecture is instantiated without replacing the architecture: every branch instantiates T, S, and Φ, and the universal wave function supplies the ordered, differentiated structure at its own level. QFT refines the realizer of Substance beyond the classical particle concept without eliminating the role: the maintenance of causal capacity across transitions survives the loss of the particle concept. None of the three tells us the roles are dispensable. Physics, pressed to its contemporary frontier, leaves the structural roles intact: each result refines rather than dissolves a Time in which things happen, a Space in which things are distinct, and a Substance whose causal capacity persists across the happening.

Fraser and Baker have pressed the philosophical consequences of interacting quantum field theory that the physics literature more often takes up as technical rather than metaphysical questions. What contemporary physics finds at its frontiers is, on the present reading, the structural architecture itself rather than the classical picture specialists grew up pressing against.

### 4.3.9 Structural Realism {#sec-4-3-9}

In a 1989 paper in *Dialectica* titled "Structural Realism: The Best of Both Worlds?", John Worrall proposed that what survives across theory change in physics is not the entities science postulates but the structural relations encoded in its mathematics. The Fresnel equations survived the abandonment of the luminiferous ether; what was preserved was the structure, not the substance. Worrall's epistemic structural realism (we can know the structure but not the natures of the relata) became, over the next two decades, the most discussed form of scientific realism. James Ladyman pressed the position further. In "What is Structural Realism?" (1998) and then with Don Ross in *Every Thing Must Go* (2007), structural realism turned ontic: there are no relata with intrinsic natures awaiting our knowledge of them; reality is structures all the way down. Steven French's *The Structure of the World* (2014) gave the position its most systematic book-length defense. Michael Esfeld and Vincent Lam developed a moderate version on which objects are retained as nodes within the structure but stripped of independent intrinsic natures (Esfeld 2004; Esfeld and Lam 2008). Anjan Chakravartty's *A Metaphysics for Scientific Realism* (2007) defended a semirealist alternative: structures and detectable causal properties are real, with dispositional natures grounding the causal properties. The position now occupies a continuum: epistemic structural realism (Worrall) at one end; moderate ontic structural realism (Esfeld, Lam) in the middle; eliminativist ontic structural realism (Ladyman, Ross, French) at the other. The challenge to the present account is that the trio T, S, Φ (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) may be a parochial selection from a much richer relational fabric the position describes, and the argument's necessity claim of [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5) (Necessity of Nature), supported by the Modal Identity and Triconditional machinery of §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7, may be the wrong claim about the wrong feature.

The challenge sits closer to the present account than to its standard rivals, and the reply is correspondingly cooperative. The present argument does not posit T, S, and Φ as objects with intrinsic natures; it identifies role-level conditions of genuine change-realizers. OSR's claim that the world is fundamentally relational is compatible with directed order, relational differentiation, and real bearing. Whether a given physical relational fabric also realizes temporal succession, spatial extension, and causal persistence is a further type-level question, not something settled merely by calling every relation Time, Space, or Substance. The disagreement concerns both the modal status of the roles and the step from roles to their realizers. OSR is typically silent on whether the relational structure it describes is necessary or contingent; the present argument fills in the modal claim. Three forms of the position sharpen what it can commit to and what each commitment costs.

*First.* The eliminativist form (Ladyman and Ross 2007; French 2014) eliminates objects entirely. There are no things; there are only patterns of relation. The challenge: any pattern of relations could constitute a world, and the trio T, S, Φ is a parochial choice from the space of relational fabrics. The reply runs through §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7: any pattern of relations capable of supporting a configuration (any pattern offered as a realizer of change) must include the three roles at the appropriate resolution. Bare obtaining directly supports determinacy or difference, but does not by itself entail temporal extension or causal persistence. Those stronger types require the separate change-realizer arguments. French's careful development in *The Structure of the World* makes the point sharper, not weaker. The relations he identifies as fundamental (group-theoretic symmetries, gauge structures, permutation invariance) are relations among distinguishable items or positions (S). In familiar dynamical formulations, they are also articulated through an order of states or events (T) and through constraints or capacities that hold determinate physical difference in place (Φ). But a thoroughgoing atemporal-structure reading need not concede that the formal parameter in an equation is fundamental time. It owes a different account: how the atemporal structure grounds an emergent order in which real differences can occur, and how determinate capacities are available within that order. Merely redescribing the base as structure does not discharge those obligations; neither does the present argument certify that every timeless structural proposal meets them.

The division matters. T is the order of before and after; Φ is the determinate capacity or bearing condition that is exercised in that order. They are mutually required for real change but not the same role. The eliminativist version therefore does not by itself undermine the role-level claim. It reformulates ontology in relational terms and can resist intrinsic-nature-bearing objects. But it remains a live challenge at the type level: an eliminative structuralist may deny that relations require persistent causal bearers in the book's richer sense. The present account can reply that a relational fabric proposed as physical reality or as a realizer of change must meet the relevant type arguments; it does not treat eliminative OSR as defeated merely because relations are named. T, S, and Φ are roles; the configurations satisfying the roles need not be intrinsic-nature-bearing objects in the sense OSR rejects.

*Second.* The moderate form (Esfeld 2004; Esfeld and Lam 2008) retains objects as nodes within the structure but denies them independent intrinsic natures. The position is straightforwardly consistent with the present account: configurations are nodes within the structural fabric, and T, S, and Φ are the relational roles the fabric must include for any node to obtain. Esfeld's central claim (that nodes are exhausted by their relational profiles) itself requires the relational profiles to be temporally extended, relationally distinct, and persistent across the relations they enter into. The moderate OSR theorist and the present account converge: both deny that fundamental ontology requires intrinsic-nature-bearing objects; both affirm that fundamental ontology requires relational structure with the features the present account names. The disagreement, if there is one, is about whether the relational structure described by current physics (group symmetries, gauge invariance) exhausts what is fundamental, or whether the structural roles T, S, Φ are necessary at a level prior to physics. The present argument takes the second view and offers [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) for the Modal Identity result and the mutual-requirement / Triconditional machinery, and [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) for the collapse of the unstructured alternative: the three roles mutually require one another and cannot be reduced to a more primitive base.

Ladyman’s Principle of Naturalistic Closure gives the modal claim its sharpest methodological challenge: no metaphysical hypothesis should be accepted unless it serves to unify well-confirmed hypotheses from more than one specific science. The necessity of T, S, and Φ satisfies this constraint in an unusual but genuine way. The three structural roles are not a hypothesis derived from one science and then applied to others; they are the conditions on which any scientific inquiry operates. Temporal succession is presupposed by every state-evolution formalism in physics; it is equally presupposed by the experimental design structures in cognitive science, economics, and biology. Relational extension is constitutive of field theory, topology, and network science alike. Causal persistence is what conservation laws, developmental biology, and institutional economics each track, in different vocabularies, at different scales. The claim that T, S, Φ are necessary is not a physics claim that chemistry must accept on physics’s authority; it is a claim about conditions that each science independently instantiates whenever it describes anything at all. In Ladyman's own terms, this is a unification claim (identifying the structural joints across all sciences, not merely within one). And it is warranted not by rationalist intuition but by the demonstration in §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7, specifically [§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7) (Triconditional Cross-Entailment), where the physics-facing case is made that any nomological structure requires T, S, and Φ as co-instantiated, that the three roles mutually require one another and are jointly presupposed by any coherent structural description. The Principle of Naturalistic Closure rules out free-floating neoscholastic machinery; the present claim is not free-floating but confirmed at every juncture where a science describes structure, which is to say at every juncture where science operates.

*Third.* The semirealist form (Chakravartty 2007) retains both structure and detectable causal properties, treating dispositional natures as the ground of causal-property detectability. The position is the most ontologically committed of the OSR family and the most consistent with the present account. Chakravartty's detectable causal properties are configurations of T, S, and Φ at the level at which physics meets phenomena: dispositions are temporally extended (manifesting over time), relationally specified (manifesting in relation to other dispositions or stimulus conditions), and causally persistent (carrying their manifestation profile across the relations). The present account does not adjudicate between Chakravartty's dispositionalist commitments and the more austere ontologies of moderate OSR; what it requires is what all three positions concede when fully developed: the relational fabric instantiates the structural roles.

A kindred move worth marking. The structuralist tradition in philosophy of mathematics, Resnik (*Mathematics as a Science of Patterns*, 1997), Shapiro (*Philosophy of Mathematics: Structure and Ontology*, 1997), runs a parallel argument in the mathematical case: mathematical objects have only relational properties, and the structures themselves are what is real. The reply parallels the OSR reply: a mathematical structure contains distinguishable positions or relational differences, directly supporting the S-role. Stability across mathematical instances is not automatically physical persistence, and the temporal course of our inquiry is an act-side feature rather than a property of the abstract structure. Mathematical structuralism therefore supports the thin relational point while leaving T- and Φ-realization open. The argument's modal claim is consistent with both.

Two adjacent positions live elsewhere. The Tegmarkian "mathematical universe" hypothesis (Tegmark 2008, 2014) runs a parallel ontological-monism move with mathematics rather than relational structure as the fundament; it is engaged at [§4.3.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-7). The information-theoretic ontology that treats reality as fundamentally informational is engaged at [§4.1.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-5).

*What converges.* The present account converges with each of three forms of OSR (eliminativist, moderate, semirealist) at increasing levels of ontological commitment. Eliminativist OSR rejects intrinsic-nature-bearing objects, which the present account does not require. Moderate OSR retains nodes as structurally exhausted, which the present account already affirms. Semirealist OSR retains dispositional natures, which the present account is consistent with without requiring. The disagreement, where there is one, is about whether the trio T, S, Φ is necessary at a level prior to the relational fabric current physics describes, or merely one description among others of that fabric. The case for the prior-necessity reading is given at §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7, with [§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7) (Triconditional Cross-Entailment) providing the physics-facing demonstration that any nomological structure requires T, S, and Φ as co-instantiated, and OSR theorists who reject it owe a counter-argument, and what the literature has produced (group-theoretic symmetries, gauge invariance, permutation structure) does not yet supply one. What it supplies is rich confirmation that the relational fabric, however described, includes the structural roles.

Structural realism was proposed to reconcile the no-miracles argument for scientific realism with the pessimistic meta-induction from theory change. Two decades after Worrall, Ladyman and Ross gave the position its fullest ontic form. Two more decades later, French and Esfeld and Chakravartty have populated the space between epistemic and eliminativist with positions that disagree about objects but converge on structure. The present argument takes the convergence seriously. Whatever the relational fabric of fundamental physics turns out to be, T, S, and Φ are the conditions on its being a relational fabric at all.

### 4.3.10 Bundle and Trope Theory {#sec-4-3-10}

Bundle theory, developed in different forms by Hume, Russell, and more recently by Paul (2017), holds that objects are bundles of properties without underlying substrates. Trope theory, developed by Williams (1953), Campbell (1990), and Maurin (2002), holds that properties are particularized (this redness here, that hardness there) rather than universals shared across instances. Both positions challenge the substance role of Φ (causal persistence across temporal change, the third structural Condition alongside T and S, borne by Substance just as T and S are borne by Time and Space): if there are no underlying substrates, what does causal persistence inhere in? If properties are particularized tropes, what bundles them into the persisting configuration the structural account requires?

The reply distinguishes the metaphysics of property-bearing from the structural role of Φ. The substance role is the role of causal persistence across temporal change: whatever obtains in such a way that the same configuration is causally connected from one moment to the next. Bundle theory and trope theory are accounts of how property-bearing works at a fine grain; they are not denials that something persists. A bundle that persists across time is, for the present argument, an instance of Φ. A collection of compresent tropes (tropes co-occurring at the same location) that maintains its compresence across temporal succession is, for the present argument, an instance of Φ. The present argument is not committed to the substrate metaphysics that bundle and trope theories deny; it is committed to the structural role those metaphysics still have to fill, however they fill it.

Two finer questions the bundle and trope theorist press do not change this. The first is Bradley's old regress: if the tropes are bound into one bundle by a relation, and that relation is itself a trope, it requires its own binder, and the bundle never closes. The regress is a real pressure on bundle theory's internal economy. Renaming compresence as S holding across Φ does not by itself solve it; the bundle theorist still owes an account of what unifies the tropes, whether primitive compresence, a non-relational tie, or another device. The structural account can remain neutral on that account while requiring any successful proposal to realize differentiation and continuity. Whatever the bundle theorist settles on (a primitive compresence relation, a non-relational tie, a brute fact of togetherness) the structural roles are what that settlement must instantiate, not a rival to it. The second is whether the bundle endures, wholly present at each moment, or perdures through distinct temporal parts. Φ is neutral between them: it asks only that the configuration be causally connected from one moment to the next, a demand the endurantist meets through identity and the perdurantist through genidentity among temporal parts. The persistence-metaphysics dispute (pressed in its perdurantist form at [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8)) settles how Φ is realized, not whether it is.

*What is established.* The reply matches the reply to ontic structural realism ([§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9)) in shape. The present argument identifies the roles any configuration must instantiate; metaphysical accounts of how the roles are filled are downstream of the necessity claim. Bundle theory, trope theory, substance theory, and process theory are competing answers to a question that arises only after [§2.6.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-8) has specified the Φ / Physicality role and [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) has shown how that role belongs to the Conditions-as-Nature structure.

### 4.3.11 Mereological Nihilism {#sec-4-3-11}

Van Inwagen's *Material Beings* (1990) defends the most precisely formulated version of mereological nihilism the analytic tradition has produced. There are no chairs, no tables, no planets, no stones: only simples arranged chair-wise, table-wise, planet-wise, stone-wise. The single exception is living organisms, whose self-maintaining causal activity Van Inwagen takes to ground a unity mere arrangements lack. The position shrinks the ontology where Lewis's plurality ([§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)) multiplies it, and it does so with the same systematic care. Sider's "Against Parthood" (2013) presses one step further: even the organism exception is rejected, and what remains is only simples in arrangements.

Mereological nihilism (also called compositional nihilism or compositional eliminativism) has a precise lineage. Classical mereology (Leśniewski 1916; Tarski 1929) supplies the formal vocabulary of parthood, and Lewis's *Parts of Classes* (1991) systematizes the contemporary defense of unrestricted composition the nihilist most directly opposes. Van Inwagen (*Material Beings*, 1990) develops the organism-exception version with the most systematic care. Merricks's *Objects and Persons* (2001) extends Van Inwagen's exception to persons and presses the overdetermination argument against composite objects more broadly. Sider's "Against Parthood" (2013, *Oxford Studies in Metaphysics* vol. 8) develops the strictest nihilist version: no composites at any level, organisms included. Dorr's "What We Disagree About When We Disagree About Ontology" (2005) defends compositional nihilism through paraphrase: nihilist and non-nihilist sentences can be made truth-conditionally equivalent. Cameron's "Truthmakers and Ontological Commitment" (2008) develops a kindred deflationary line. Against the nihilists: Markosian's "Brutal Composition" (1998) treats composition as a brute fact admitting no further criterion; Schaffer's "On What Grounds What" (2009) and the monist literature (Schaffer 2010) defend the cosmos as the fundamental composite from which parts derive; classical mereology (Goodman 1951; Simons's *Parts*, 1987) defends unrestricted composition. The structural account sits closest to the moderate-OSR line of [§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9) in being neutral on composition while specific about what any arrangement must instantiate.

The nihilist pressure bears on Φ specifically and on the [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) architecture more generally. If composite objects do not exist, then the persistent configurations the argument has been describing (patterns of features held together as one substantial bearer across temporal succession) have no bearer to inhere in. T and S might survive as relational facts among simples, but Φ, the persistence of structured pattern, would require a pattern that is something over and above its constituents. The nihilist position, in its strict form, dissolves the Substance role into arrangements of underlying simples and denies that the arrangement composes anything further.

A clarification before the moves. The nihilist is not denying that the world contains the arrangements ordinarily called "chairs" and "tables." Van Inwagen and Sider both grant the arrangement-facts; what they deny is that the arrangements compose further objects. "Simples arranged chair-wise" describes a real configuration on every nihilist account; what it does not describe, on the strict version, is a chair as an additional ontological item. The question turns on whether the structural argument requires composite objects beyond the arrangements, or whether the arrangements themselves carry the structural roles. Three forms of the move press that question at three resolutions: the basic eliminativist version, Van Inwagen's organism-exception version, and Sider's strict version. Each reads the structural argument as requiring composite objects and replies by denying them. Each misreads what the argument requires.

*First.* The basic eliminativist move denies composition wholesale. There are no composite objects (chairs, tables, planets, organisms), only simples in various arrangements. The structural argument, in describing the persistence of configurations across time, has been describing composites the nihilist rules out. Without composites, no Φ; without Φ, the Triconditional fails.

The argument does not need composites in the sense the nihilist denies. What it needs is that the arrangements themselves instantiate the structural roles. A pattern of simples arranged chair-wise that persists across a temporal interval instantiates Φ at the level of the arrangement, whether or not the arrangement composes a further object called "the chair." Persistence is a feature of the pattern, not a posit beyond it. The nihilist who grants that the arrangement obtains, and obtains across time, has granted the structural role; what they have refused is the additional ontological commitment to a composite as a further item. The argument is neutral on that further item. T, S, and Φ specify what arrangements consist in, not what arrangements compose. Compositional nihilism leaves the structural roles where they are.

*Second.* Van Inwagen's organism exception holds that living things compose but artifacts and inanimate aggregates do not. The criterion is unity: the activities of an organism's parts are coordinated in service of the organism's life in a way that the parts of a chair are not coordinated in service of the chair. Living things therefore qualify as composites; chairs and tables do not. The structural argument, on this reading, gets purchase only where Van Inwagen's exception holds.

The criterion Van Inwagen invokes is itself Φ at the appropriate resolution. Causal persistence of a configuration across temporal change, where the configuration's persistence is constitutively maintained by its internal causal activity: that is what Substance names in the structural argument, and it is what Van Inwagen identifies as the mark of organic unity. The argument generalizes the criterion rather than restricting it. Any arrangement whose obtaining is constitutively maintained across time by its own causal activity instantiates Φ; the question is whether the maintenance is real, not whether the arrangement is biological. Crystalline lattices maintain themselves through electromagnetic binding; weather systems maintain themselves through fluid dynamics; the argument applies wherever maintenance obtains. Van Inwagen draws the line where the maintenance is most conspicuous; the argument follows the maintenance wherever it goes.

*Third.* Sider's strict version denies even Van Inwagen's exception. There are no composites at any level, organisms included; only simples in various arrangements, including the arrangements ordinarily described as living. The arrangement-facts obtain (Sider does not deny that simples are arranged organism-wise), but no further composite organism exists. The structural argument, on this version, must run entirely on arrangement-facts, without the resource of any composite bearer.

The recasting is the right one for the strict nihilist, and the reply is correspondingly cleaner. Arrangement-facts that obtain across time, with patterns maintained by causal activity among their constituents, instantiate the structural roles whether or not they compose further objects. The argument operates at the level of what arrangements consist in. Sider's strict version concedes the arrangement-facts; it denies the further composite. T, S, and Φ are specifications of what arrangement-facts must be like to be the kind of facts they are: temporally persistent, relationally distinct, causally maintained. The argument's necessity claim runs at the arrangement-fact level. Whether the additional composite is also there is a separate ontological question the structural argument leaves open. Sider's nihilism, taken at its strictest, is compatible with the structural argument: it constrains the inventory of composites without contesting the structure of arrangements. Sider's nihilism is only one of two commitments he brings to bear here; the other (his joint-carving structuralism, on which the live question is whether T, S, and Φ belong to the fundamental ideology rather than sit above a deeper structure) is the subject of [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7), where that question is engaged on its own terms.

A kindred move runs through priority monism (Schaffer 2010). Where the nihilist denies composites by eliminating them, the monist denies composites as fundamental by absorbing them into the cosmos: only the whole cosmos fundamentally exists, and the apparent composite objects are derivative aspects of it. The reply runs in the same direction. Whether the cosmos is fundamental and its parts derivative, or the simples are fundamental and the apparent composites eliminated, the structural argument operates at the level of the arrangements that obtain (at whatever ontological level the arrangements are located) and on the structural conditions any obtaining arrangement must instantiate. The composition question is orthogonal to the structural-role question. The same applies to the bundle/trope alternatives canvassed in [§4.3.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-10): those answers, like nihilism, address what the inventory contains rather than what the inventory's items must be like to obtain.

*What converges.* Each of the three forms misreads what the argument requires. The basic eliminativist move denies composites the argument does not need; the structural roles attach to the arrangements, not to the composites the arrangements may or may not constitute. Van Inwagen's organism-exception invokes a unity criterion that just is Φ at the level of organic maintenance; the argument generalizes the criterion to any arrangement constitutively maintained by causal activity. Sider's strict version concedes the arrangement-facts while denying the composites, and the arrangement-facts are exactly where the structural argument operates. Nihilism, at every resolution, leaves the structural roles where they are.

One clarification of scope is owed, because Van Inwagen's signature pressure is not compositional but modal-epistemic. His deeper question (how one knows that T, S, and Φ are *necessary* rather than merely pervasive, given how far that claim sits from the conceptual and near-by possibilities the modal faculty handles reliably) is not answered by the compositional reply above, and is not meant to be. That pressure is upstream of this section, and the book's answer to it is methodological rather than intuitive: the necessity verdict is claimed as the output of the derivation of §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7, not of a modal intuition about distant scenarios, which is precisely the non-intuitive line Van Inwagen's own modal skepticism leaves open. This section discharges the compositional half of the Van Inwagen inheritance; the modal-epistemic half is engaged on its own terms at [§4.1.13](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-13), and paid where the necessity is derived, not where composition is discussed.

What Van Inwagen saw clearly, and Sider sharpened, was that the modern compositional tradition had multiplied entities far past anything the world's structure demanded. The classical-mereology pedigree (from Leśniewski's plenitudinous parthood through Lewis's *Parts of Classes* to contemporary unrestricted-composition defenses) produced an inventory the nihilist was right to refuse on grounds of austerity. What the nihilist tradition has not always seen as clearly is that the world's structure does not consist in that inventory either. It consists in what arrangements (composite or not) must be like to obtain. The composition debate is real; it runs on a level the structural argument leaves open. Wherever simples are arranged in patterns that obtain across time, are distinct from other patterns, and are maintained by causal activity, T, S, and Φ are there. The argument is for the structure of what obtains, not for the inventory of what composes.

### 4.3.12 Haecceitism {#sec-4-3-12}

Haecceitism holds that the facts about which individual is which are not exhausted by the qualitative and relational facts: two situations can agree on every qualitative and relational property and still differ over which individual is which. Adams's *Primitive Thisness and Primitive Identity* (1979) gives the position its canonical analytic statement: a thisness is the non-qualitative property of being this very individual, grounding numerical identity prior to and independently of any qualitative or relational characterization. The motivating case is older: Black's "The Identity of Indiscernibles" (1952) describes a symmetric universe of two qualitatively indiscernible iron spheres, two and not one, with nothing qualitative to tell them apart. Lewis's *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986) is the locus of the contemporary debate, rejecting non-qualitative differences between worlds in favor of a counterpart-theoretic treatment, on which an individual figures in other possible situations not literally but through its qualitatively closest counterparts there, so that qualitative character fixes all there is to fix. The subsequent literature (Skow 2008) separates a deflationary form, which grants haecceitistic possibilities without positing primitive thisnesses, from the robust Adamsian form, which grounds them in genuine non-qualitative properties. What unites the family is the refusal to reduce individuation to qualitative or relational structure.

The position bears on the spatial Condition directly. Positional distinctness is grounded in relational extension at [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7), which states the load-bearing Constitutive Premise: genuine non-identity at the positional level just *is* relational non-identity, distinctness constituted by a traversable interval, not by intrinsic difference. Haecceitism is the most direct denial available. If a primitive thisness grounds the distinctness of two items independently of any relation between them, then distinctness need not be relational, and the premise on which the derivation of Spatiality turns is false. The relationalist pressure on that same premise, Dasgupta's *Individuals: An Essay in Revisionary Metaphysics* (2009), which [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7) already engages, pushes from below, holding individuals to be less fundamental than structure; haecceitism presses from above, holding thisnesses to be more fundamental than any structure they enter into.

Grant the position at full strength. Haecceitism may well be the correct account of individuation as such. Black's symmetric universe is a real difficulty for any view that grounds all numerical distinctness in qualitative difference, and the obvious relational repair (distinguishing the spheres by their distances from things) cannot break a symmetry in which every relational description one sphere satisfies is satisfied by the other. The concession should be larger still. The consideration sometimes pressed against the haecceitist (that even a primitive thisness must be picked out as *this* rather than *that*, and so already trades on a contrast) does not by itself settle the matter, because how a thisness must be *referred to* is a fact about representation, not about what the thisness *is*. A haecceitist who locates the individuating work in the order of being while assigning the contrast to the order of description has not thereby been refuted. The reply does not run through that bridge.

What the structural argument requires is narrower than the thesis the haecceitist denies. The derivation does not need every numerical distinctness to be relational; it needs the distinctness that *change* crosses to be relational. Spatiality is the Condition movement presupposes, and movement is displacement across an interval: a crossing. The distinctness at issue in [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7) is therefore positional distinctness specifically: the non-identity a displacement traverses. Primitive thisness, whatever else it grounds, does not by itself supply an interval to cross. A thisness delivers a label (this individual, not that one), and a label is not a distance. Two items distinct in thisness alone, with no relational extension between them, are non-identical in just the way red is non-identical to blue: distinct, with nothing between them that anything could move across. That is exactly the line [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7) draws between a difference of contents or names and a distinctness of positions. The haecceitist's primitive grounds *that* the items are two; it does not make their twoness *positional*.

The flagship case confirms the premise rather than threatening it. Black's two spheres are positionally distinct, and they are positionally distinct because a relational interval separates them: a distance something could cross, the very feature the Constitutive Premise names. What the case withholds is a *qualitative* ground of distinctness; it does not withhold the interval. The distance in Black's original case suffices for positional distinctness while leaving the spheres qualitatively indiscernible.
