It does not prove that distance is necessary for numerical plurality: a robust haecceitist may posit co-located indiscernibles. Black's universe is therefore compatible with relational individuation of position, but it does not by itself refute primitive thisness. The haecceitist is right that the distinctness is not qualitative, and right that no description breaks the symmetry; what follows is that the distinctness is relational-extensional, which is what Spatiality is.

A defender might press the harder case: two indiscernibles with no interval between them, co-located, or differing only in which is which across possible worlds. If such distinctness is genuine, it is distinctness without a crossable interval, and the premise fails. The case divides, and neither half reaches the spatial claim. Where the two are co-located with no interval between them, there is nothing a displacement could traverse from the one to the other; whatever makes them two, it is not a positional distinctness, and the argument never held that primitive thisness fails to ground individuation of a non-positional kind. Where the distinctness is the trans-world question of which individual is which, it concerns identity across worlds, not the distinctness of positions within Reality, and the spatial claim is about the latter. Neither half exhibits a positional distinctness across which nothing could move: the one thing the Constitutive Premise rules out.

*What converges.* The robust Adamsian thisness, the deflationary haecceitistic possibility, and Black's symmetric universe all press one point: that distinctness is not qualitative. The structural argument grants it. What none of them supplies is a positional distinctness without a crossable interval, and that, not the reduction of all individuation to relation, is what the Constitutive Premise asserts. Where a haecceitist case carries an interval, it instantiates the relational extension Spatiality names; where it carries none, it is individuation of another kind, which the argument leaves untouched. Haecceitism constrains what grounds identity; it does not displace what grounds position. Like bundle theory and mereological nihilism ([§4.3.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-10), [§4.3.11](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-11)), it answers a question about the inventory of individuals, not the question of what an interval must be for something to cross it.

## 4.4 Modal Variants and Extensions {#sec-4-4}

This cluster questions the modal machinery the argument rides on: necessity, possibility, and possible worlds. If the semantics of possibility differed, the canonical lift might not follow. The reply begins with a distinction. The argument's operator ◇ means *real possibility*: membership in one fixed global domain W, the complete range of ways Reality permits (§[§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1), 2.1). A theory may instead model local reachability, epistemic openness, or world-relative accessibility. Those are legitimate relative modalities, but variation in them does not by itself vary membership in W. The engagements below ask whether a rival has offered a different account of real possibility or only a different relation inside or alongside the same global domain.

The objections of [§4.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3) press whether the present account leaves something out: experience, intrinsic nature, mathematical applicability, mind itself. The objections of this section press the modal apparatus the argument runs on. If the modal logic is wrong (if necessity, possibility, and counterfactual reasoning do not behave as the argument assumes) then □(T∧S∧Φ) does not follow even if T, S, and Φ (Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality, the three structural Conditions the book's argument derives, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) are exhaustive.

The space of moves is well-charted. Lewis (1986) develops concrete modal realism, on which possible worlds are concrete entities of the same kind as the actual world; the actual world is just the world we inhabit. Williamson (2013) develops necessitism, on which everything that exists exists necessarily and the only contingency is qualitative rather than ontological. Counterpart theory (Lewis 1968) replaces transworld identity with similarity relations and changes what "the same necessary being" can mean across worlds. The Barcan formulae (named for Ruth Barcan Marcus's 1946 derivations linking quantifiers and modal operators) press whether quantification and modality commute, with consequences for whether necessary existents must exist in every possible world. Stalnaker (1976) presses the moderate realist line, on which possible worlds are abstract maximal properties or ways the world could have been. Kripke (1980) gives the standard picture against which the alternatives press their cases. Plantinga (1974b) develops a robust modal realism for theological purposes. The literature is dense, technical, and inconclusive on most of the central questions.

The argument's strategy across the section is to distinguish three questions that modal theories often run together: the global domain of real possibility, the semantics used to represent it, and the ontology assigned to worlds or domains. The canonical proof depends on the first, not on Lewisian concreteness, transworld identity, Barcan formulae, or a particular local accessibility relation. Structural roles enter only where a candidate world or ground is offered as a realizer of genuine change. A thin abstract representation need not instantiate temporal succession, spatial extension, or causal persistence; a theory that offers it as physical reality, a ground of experience, or a complete change-realizer inherits the richer burden. The sections below therefore test each framework at the resolution it claims.

### 4.4.1 Modal Realism {#sec-4-4-1}

David Lewis began with counterpart theory in the 1960s, added the analysis of counterfactuals in the early 1970s, and over the following decades built the most extravagant ontology any analytic philosopher has ever defended. When you say “I could have taken the other job,” Lewis holds, you are saying truly that somewhere, in a universe spatiotemporally isolated from this one, a person who resembles you in the relevant respects took that job. The universe is concrete: just as concrete as this one. It contains stars and tables and chairs. You will never causally interact with it. But it exists, full stop, in exactly the sense this one does. Modal language is not abstract after all. It is a report on a plurality, and the plurality is the ontology.

Lewis developed Modal Realism across two decades, in *Counterfactuals* (1973) and *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986), one of the most systematic books of late analytic metaphysics. The position remains his alone: its orbit has structured a generation of work on modality without persuading others to adopt the concrete plurality unchanged. Divers (2002) and Nolan (2002) develop Lewisian variants with modified commitments. Bricker (2020) gives the standard contemporary taxonomy of how Lewisian worlds individuate. Against the concrete variant stand the abstract or ersatz realists: Plantinga (1974b) defends worlds as maximal states of affairs; Stalnaker (1976, 1984) treats worlds as maximal properties; Adams (1974, 1981) as maximal consistent sets of propositions; Kripke (1980) operates with primitively stipulated worlds rather than discoverable ones. Van Inwagen (1986) presses the central internal critique: the plurality is ontologically exorbitant without being explanatorily adequate. Rosen (1990) develops modal fictionalism as an explicit alternative: the plurality as useful fiction, not reality. Armstrong (1989) pushes combinatorialism: possibilities are recombinations of actual constituents, no alternative universes required.

The present reply sits closest to Armstrong's combinatorialism in rejecting the concrete plurality, and adds what combinatorialism alone does not specify: which structural roles any recombination must preserve. Why they cannot be recombined apart is supplied not here but by the cross-entailment among the three roles ([§2.4.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-8), [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)): they are not distinct existences for recombination to separate.

Modal Realism presses directly against the necessity claim of the argument. What [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5) establishes is □(T∧S∧Φ): in every world within the fixed global domain of real possibility, the structural Conditions obtain. S5 is earned from the fixed-domain reading of real possibility ([§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)), not assumed as an axiom. Transition Closure is a narrower result about the onset of Change under structural accessibility; it is not an independent derivation of proposition-wise S5. If possible worlds are concrete universes, the question is what every concrete universe in that global domain contains. Lewis's plurality is the most permissive ontology of possibility ever defended: if any consistent-sounding description individuates a concrete world, worlds without structure might be among them. The argument's necessity claim is false if even one concrete world lacks T, S, or Φ. (ET) (the Exhaustion-of-Existence claim, that T, S, and Φ exhaust the forms of real existence) is false on the same condition.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute is not with Lewis's counterfactual semantics or with the usefulness of possible-world talk. The question is whether the concreteness criterion Lewis himself requires (the feature that distinguishes Lewisian realism from ersatz alternatives) permits radically sparse worlds to qualify as concrete. The move comes at several resolutions: the bare sparse-world move and its sharpened recombination form, the isolation-thesis variant, and the primitivist fallback. The space they canvass is the space Lewisian realism can occupy. The replies argue that each collapses concreteness back into structure before the plurality is assembled.

*First.* The sparse-world move holds that among the plurality there is a world w′ containing a single unchanging state: no succession, no spatial extension, no causal activity. Such a world is conceivable, and the move needs conceivability of a coherent description to entail concrete existence of the corresponding world. w′ contains no T, no S, no Φ, and it concretely exists.

For Lewis, worlds are maximal sums of spatiotemporally interrelated things, with worldmates unified by the relevant natural external relations. This gives Lewisian worlds a spatiotemporal criterion where such relations obtain, but it does not by itself prove that every world contains both temporal succession and spatial extension. A sparse or changeless world remains a live test of the book's independent type-level arguments. The present argument need not claim that every abstract representation of a world has those types; it claims that a concrete world proposed as a real change-realizer cannot lack them. A world with no temporal succession has no internal change that could individuate one world-state from another, which means no structural fact distinguishes “world w′” from “no world.” A world with no causal persistence has no bearer across which content could be sustained. A world lacking all three is not a sparsely furnished concrete world. It is not a concrete world at all. Lewis's own concreteness criterion forecloses the sparse-world move before the plurality is even assembled.

*The sharpened form: recombination.* The sparse-world move has a sharper version that does not empty the world at all: Lewis's principle of recombination. The principle permits extensive recombination of distinct existences, subject to its own constraints; it does not license every arbitrary description as a world. Recombination does not need the empty world; it needs only a selective deletion of what the Humean treats as distinct. Take a spatiotemporally extended world and deny necessary connections between its distinct local states; the resulting Humean mosaic retains Time and Space while rejecting a necessary productive connection between distinct existences. The issue is whether the mosaic can retain the structural work the present account assigns to Φ without thereby retaining Φ under another description.

The reply must not answer it by saying the mosaic "has no bearer," since whether a world requires a persisting bearer is precisely what the Humean denies; to assert it here would beg the question.

The reply turns instead on what the mosaic already grants. A mosaic is a distribution of local states across a spatiotemporal manifold: Lewis (1986b, pp. ix–xvi), introducing Humean supervenience in *Philosophical Papers, Volume II*, exempts the spatiotemporal relations from it and takes them as primitive, so the manifold is conceded, not constructed. The manifold grants differentiation and spatiotemporal arrangement. It does not follow merely from exclusion or Best-System regularity that a productive cross-interval causal operation exists: the Humean denies exactly that inference. The sharper question is whether the mosaic realizes Φ's broader bearing or continuity role without accepting productive necessary connections. A regular mosaic may remain a substantive rival at the type level rather than collapsing into ∅.

*Second.* The isolation thesis presses from a different angle. Lewis's worlds are spatiotemporally isolated from one another: no causal or spatiotemporal connections between them. A world in the plurality need not be internally rich; it needs only to be isolated from other worlds. A single unchanging state, isolated from all other such states, qualifies as a world by isolation alone.

Lewisian worlds are isolated in the sense that no spatiotemporal relations connect their inhabitants; isolation is not an additional between-world relation requiring a common surrounding manifold. The thesis therefore does not establish any particular world's internal richness. Whether a sparse candidate qualifies as a world turns on Lewis's worldmate criterion and the candidate's contents, not on reifying non-connection as a structural relation. The isolation thesis is a structural criterion applied to structured worlds, not an alternative to structure.

*Third.* The primitivist version goes boldest. Being a world is a primitive fact, irreducible to any further ontology. Worldhood is fixed by the modal role 'world' plays: as the primitive truthmaker for modal claims. This is a coherent rival semantic proposal, but it carries a cost: it declines a constitutive account of what makes a world concrete or a genuine realizer of change.

The present argument cannot close primitivism by retorsion alone. At most, it can show that any primitive world introduced as a concrete universe or as a realizer of change inherits the relevant role- and type-level burdens. A primitivist who treats worldhood as primitive while refusing those burdens has replaced structural explanation with an additional primitive. That is a theoretical cost, not a contradiction.

A further Lewisian pressure targets the Modal Identity directly rather than the concreteness of worlds. Lewis's counterpart theory denies strict trans-world identity. What you would have been had you taken the other job is your counterpart in another world: qualitatively similar, numerically distinct. The Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) (□(◇C ↔ (T∧S∧Φ)), where ◇C is the possibility of change) appears, under counterpart semantics, ambiguous between a claim about the same T, S, and Φ across worlds (requiring trans-world identity Lewis denies) and a claim about qualitatively similar structural roles in each world (a weaker claim counterpart theory permits but insufficient to ground the necessity the argument needs). Either the Modal Identity assumes identity Lewis rejects, or it retreats to similarity that cannot carry the argumentative weight.

The dilemma dissolves at what the Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) actually asserts. The Modal Identity does not claim a numerically identical token of T, S, or Φ recurs across worlds in the way ordinary individuals would have to for strict trans-world identity. It claims any world containing change contains the structural *roles* change requires: whatever plays Time's role in w and whatever plays Time's role in w′ are both instances of a single role-type. Role-type identity is not the kind of trans-world identity counterpart theory forecloses. Counterpart theory denies strict identity of individuals because individuals are, on Lewis's picture, worldbound particulars. Structural roles are not particulars; they are types any particular must instantiate to be the kind of thing it is. Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds*, [§1.5](groundwork.html#sec-1-5)) is explicit that properties are classes of their actual and possible instances: an across-world specification counterpart theory permits for types even as it forbids it for tokens. A structural role meets that specification directly: “whatever plays Time's role” picks out the class of its actual and possible role-players, which is just what a property is on Lewis's account. The role-type is therefore not a trans-world individual smuggled past counterpart theory but an abundant property in Lewis's own sense: identified, as every Lewisian property is, by its actual and possible instances across the plurality. The Modal Identity operates at the level Lewis's own semantics already allows, and the structural roles fit the property-class regimentation rather than being exempted from it. A second counterpart-theoretic pressure, aimed at the transfer principle rather than at the Modal Identity, runs through the chained-origin cases of Chisholm, Chandler, and N. Salmon; it is engaged at [§4.4.11](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-11).

A kindred move drops Lewis's concrete realism for Stalnaker's (1976) moderate realism: possible worlds are abstract maximal ways the world could be, not concrete alternative universes. The abstract-realist variant is closer to the Platonist challenge of [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4) and is answered there. The reply in the modal-realist vocabulary: abstract maximal ways can be distinguished and compared, directly supporting only a thin difference-role. They need not thereby instantiate temporal succession, spatial extension, or causal persistence. The richer roles apply when a way represents or realizes a concrete change-world, not merely because it is an abstract modal surrogate.

*What converges.* Each form collapses concreteness back into structure before the plurality is assembled. The sparse-world move founders on Lewis's own concreteness criterion: a world with no spatiotemporal structure is not a sparsely furnished concrete world but no concrete world at all. Its sharpened recombination form is not closed by definition: the mosaic's conceded manifold already grants differentiation and arrangement, and whether Best-System regularity can discharge Φ's bearing role without productive connections is the type-level question the mosaic remains answerable to. The isolation thesis is itself a structural relation: isolation is a spatiotemporal concept, and worlds can only satisfy the isolation criterion if they have spatiotemporal structure to be isolated with. Primitivism about worldhood does not escape the structural account so much as decline it: the refusal replaces structural explanation with an additional primitive, a cost the position carries rather than answers.

*A stronger reply: the unity of the frame.* The replies so far grant Lewis his plurality and show only that each member of it must instantiate the structure; a bolder reply presses the count itself, and it stands apart from the rest because it reaches further and leans on a premise Lewis is entitled to refuse. A plurality is a plurality only if its members are genuinely many, and genuine two-ness is not bare: for two concrete totalities to be two rather than one totality described twice, there must be a real interval in which their non-identity registers — an interval something could cross ([§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7), the Constitutive Premise; [§2.4.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-1), its world-level form). Lewisian worlds are by definition isolated, with no spatiotemporal relation and nothing crossable between them, so the distinctness they require is exactly the kind [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7) declines to grant: a difference with no interval, which is either relational after all — a shared structure, hence one connected order, and isolation is lost — or a bare thisness, “a label without an interval,” which does not make two. Isolation is the absence of a separator, not a mode of separation; “two isolated concrete worlds” asks the cardinal predicate to grip where nothing gives it purchase. The same pressure shows in the very act of pointing: to single out a world as *that* one is to set it off from *this* one, and this-and-that is here-and-there in other clothes. “That world” says “not here,” and “not here” asks after a where — either a location standing off from this one, which is a relation and undoes the isolation, or no where at all, in which case “that” has singled out nothing. The plurality cannot be so much as indicated without borrowing the frame it was meant to exceed.

A deeper tightening follows. The primitivist might concede the demonstrative point — that "that world" borrows the here-and-there it was meant to outrun — and insist instead that bare thisness simply is, at the level of being, prior to any pointing or description. The question that move cannot answer is what it is. A world must be a something: it must carry enough determinate content to be a world rather than its own absence. Bare thisness strips every qualitative, relational, and structural feature by design — that is what "bare" means. What remains when all content is gone is ∅, not a minimally furnished concrete world but the null case. "Bare thisness exists" and "nothing exists" are, on every dimension that could distinguish them, the same description. A posit indistinguishable from ∅ has not located bedrock below structure; it has dissolved into the null case — which is the absence of a world, not an instance of one.

Stated precisely, what this reaches is not the numeral "exactly one world" but the unity of the frame. Reality is not the winner of a headcount among possible many; it is a unity-of-structure — the one frame any configuration must instantiate, beyond number rather than one of a kind ([§6.2.2](relocating-greatness.html#sec-6-2-2)). “One,” said of Nature, is not a cardinality but that unity: positions within the one logic of here-and-there can be multiplied without end, but not the logic of here-and-there itself, which is no particular admitting duplication but the frame within which any “two” is sayable. On this reading the plurality is not outweighed but mis-formed — a cardinal count run at the one level where the cardinal predicate finds no grip.

The candor the rest of the book keeps is owed here too. This is not a deductive refutation of a determined primitivist. Lewis can plant precisely on the fault line [§2.4.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-7) marks: he can hold the numerical distinctness of concrete totalities to be primitive — needing no interval and no ground — and the reductio does not move him, because its load-bearing premise is the one he denies. What the reply secures against him is not formal contradiction but a convergent exposure: bare thisness dissolves into ∅, the absence of a world rather than an instance of one, and the cost of maintaining the posit against that dissolution is not confined to the cross-world case: the same bare thisness he plants on can no more make one being one across a change, absent continuous carrying, than it can make two worlds two absent an interval ([§2.4.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-1)). Nor can he discount that cost by making the distinctness merely numerical — the bare non-identity of two from three — for that is how abstract objects are told apart, and abstractness is the one price Lewis cannot pay: concreteness is what separates his realism from the ersatz alternatives he wrote against. He wants the numeral’s economy and the world’s concreteness together — a two with a world hung upon it — and they do not combine, since the entire content of concreteness is the here-and-there that a bare numeral forgoes ([§2.4.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-4-1); [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4)). His intervalless plurality is a positive existential posit with no access and no causal trace, carried for a modal-semantic payoff the structural account already supplies from a ground that is independently necessary ([§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5)). And the terrain the unity reading stands on is not an ad hoc anti-Lewis axiom but the oldest treatment of the one and the many — Plotinus’s source of number that is itself beyond number, mathematical structuralism, Spinoza’s single substance. The plurality remains sayable; what it has lost is its cheapness: distinctness-without-relation is the least defensible of the position's commitments, and the unity of the frame is what one reaches the moment that commitment is refused.

The cost ledger carries one more line, and it is quantitative. Grant the primitivist his bare distinctness, and the plurality still owes an answer no positive existential posit gets to waive: how much of it is there? Lewis’s own machinery cannot settle the question. Forrest and Armstrong (1984) showed that recombination, applied without restriction to the totality of worlds, generates a world containing duplicates of all the worlds — a world bigger than any world, itself included — so neither the aggregate nor the set of all worlds survives the principle’s own closure. Lewis’s reply (*On the Plurality of Worlds*, [§2.2](the-argument.html#sec-2-2)) restricts recombination by the proviso the principle already carries in its statement ([§1.8](groundwork.html#sec-1-8) of the same work), “size and shape permitting,” a qualification whose content he leaves unspecified; Nolan (1996) argues the restriction is unmotivated on Lewis’s own terms, and the alternative he defends, recombination unbound with more possibilia than any set can hold, concedes the point at issue here: the plurality has no determinate size. Either way the count never closes. A finite tally of concrete totalities would be arbitrary — nothing in the theory could say why that many and no more — and the infinite alternative cannot be stabilized at any cardinality. A posit whose quantity is in principle unanswerable carries exactly the mark the unity reading predicts: number failing at the level of totalities. What looks from inside the theory like a bookkeeping embarrassment is, read structurally, the same finding the interval argument reached from outside — there is no fact of how many, because how many is not a question the frame can answer about itself.

The shape of the mistake can be put more plainly. Each Lewisian world is internally rich — intervals throughout, a full spatiotemporal interior, exactly like the interior of a fiction, which stipulates its own distances freely. What carries no interval is the relation *between* worlds. That relation is a seam — world-to-world as fiction stands to reality — and every seam we have uncontested access to is interval-free precisely where it is non-concrete: there is no distance from Sherlock Holmes to Hamlet, not an unknown distance but no such fact. The photograph in your hand sits a foot away, while the person it pictures, held now as pictured, is at no distance from you at all; the only way to recover a distance is to switch back from the representation to the living worldline — from the seam to a concrete interior. Lewis is thus a concretist about each world and, without owning it, an ersatzer about the many: he imports the interior's concreteness across a seam that bears none of concreteness's marks. His plurality is a set of concrete relata related as if they were non-concrete. And the intuition that makes the picture feel forced — that the worlds are *obviously* many — leans on distinguishability, which is downstream of the structure and confers no actuality of its own: that two worlds can be told apart no more makes them two concrete existents than telling Holmes from Hamlet makes either one a man. The arrow runs from the Conditions to distinguishability, never back.

*On the Plurality of Worlds* defends concrete realism against what Lewis called “the incredulous stare”: the reaction he expected from any reader encountering the view for the first time, and which he thought no sufficient response to a working modal semantics. The reaction it provoked was not confusion about the view's coherence but a genuine ontological concern: one Lewis acknowledged and thought the modal semantics outweighed. What Lewis left behind is not the plurality but a diagnostic: any modal ontology powerful enough to do the work has to specify what makes a world a world, and whatever does the specifying instantiates the structure the argument names. Ersatz worlds individuate by property or proposition; concrete worlds individuate by spatiotemporal aggregation. Either specification is a structural fact. What the plurality purchased in modal expressive power it paid for in ontological commitment, and the ontological commitment, examined for what it requires, confirms the structural conditions the argument derives.

### 4.4.2 Linguistic Ersatzism {#sec-4-4-2}

Linguistic ersatzism (from German *Ersatz*, "substitute"), defended by Plantinga (1974b, 1976), Stalnaker (1976), and Adams (1974), holds that possible worlds are not concrete spacetime manifolds, à la Lewis's Modal Realism (on which every possible world is an equally concrete, equally real spatiotemporal manifold), but maximally consistent sets of propositions or world-state-descriptions. The actual world is the unique such set whose propositions are all true. Other worlds are abstract objects: surrogates rather than rivals. The position retains the modal apparatus while avoiding Lewis's ontological extravagance.

The label covers three importantly different positions, and the reply that follows must hold across all of them. Adams ("Theories of Actuality," 1974) is the version the "maximally consistent set of propositions" gloss fits most exactly: worlds are world-stories, maximal consistent sets of propositions, and the actual world is the set all of whose members are true. Stalnaker ("Possible Worlds," 1976) is a moderate realism on which worlds are not sets of propositions but abstract ways the world could have been (maximal properties it might have had), and his later *Mere Possibilities* (2012) refines this into a contingentist account on which there are no robustly existing merely-possible individuals to begin with. Plantinga (1974b, 1976) is the most ontologically robust of the three, and the only theistically committed one: worlds are maximal possible states of affairs, abstract objects that exist necessarily and, on Plantinga's wider view, have their being in the divine intellect. The differences are real and matter for the metaphysics of abstracta, but they are orthogonal to the point pressed here: propositions, ways, and states of affairs alike are distinguishable, content-bearing items standing in consistency relations, and the reply turns only on what any of them requires to be distinguishable and consistent at all.

The argument's relation to ersatzism is broadly friendly. Ersatzism does not require Modal Realism's commitment to a plenitude of concrete worlds; it does not commit the user of modal vocabulary to the existence of donkeys that talk in some other concrete reality. Ersatzism's worlds are abstract objects, and the question of what abstract objects depend on is a question for the metaphysics of abstracta, addressed in [§4.2.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-4) (Platonism) and adjacent.

Ersatz worlds contain distinguishable propositions, ways, or states of affairs standing in logical relations. This directly secures thin differentiation at the level of the representation. It does not make an abstract surrogate temporally successive, spatially extended, or causally persistent. Those richer burdens belong to the concrete world represented, or to any surrogate proposed as its physical realizer.

A second observation. On Adams's world-story version, actuality privileges the maximal consistent set all of whose members are true. Stalnaker's ways and Plantinga's maximal states of affairs require their own actuality relations rather than this exact set-theoretic formulation. In each case, truth or obtaining is assessed against how things actually are. How things are *is* Reality: with its T, S, and Φ. The actual world's privilege is parasitic on Reality being a particular way. Ersatz worlds are alternative description-sets relative to Reality; they are not ontological rivals to it.

*What converges.* Ersatzism is a successful theory of what we mean by talk of possible worlds. It is not a theory that displaces the present argument's necessary structure. The two operate at different levels: ersatzism at the level of modal semantics, the present argument at the level of the structural conditions any modal semantics describes.

### 4.4.3 Combinatorialism {#sec-4-4-3}

Armstrong (1989, 1997) defends a combinatorial theory of modality. Possibility, on this view, is the combinatorial space generated by recombining the actual world's fundamental constituents, particulars and universals (the concrete individuals and the repeatable properties they instantiate, in Armstrong's technical sense), in all possible ways consistent with their adicity (the number of argument-places a universal takes) and type. Possible worlds are not concrete (Lewis) or abstract (ersatzism); they are constructions out of actual elements. The space of possibility is wholly determined by what actually exists.

The combinatorialist's modality is grounded in the actual. The argument here is consonant with this in its commitment to the actuality of T, S, and Φ. Where the two part ways is on the source of the recombinatorial range. Armstrong takes the actual particulars and universals as primitive and lets recombination do the rest. The present argument identifies T, S, and Φ as necessary features of the actual, which means that recombination cannot generate worlds in which T, S, or Φ fail to obtain, since their failure is not a configuration of the elements but the absence of the conditions for any configuration.

This is a constraint on combinatorialism, not a refutation of it. Combinatorialism is consistent with the argument provided it acknowledges that the recombinations operate within the structural conditions, and that acknowledgement can be extracted from the combinatorial operation itself, without first granting the structural argument's conclusions. Combinatorial generation requires distinguishable constituents and admissible arrangements, so it directly presupposes a thin difference-role. But the modal construction is not itself a temporal process: possible combinations need not be produced one after another, and the constituents need not persist through an act of recombining. Temporal succession and causal bearing must be established within any concrete change-world represented by a combination, not inferred from the theorist's operation on the base. The structural conditions are therefore not items in the actualist base awaiting recombination: the difference-role is presupposed by any combinatorial generation, and the richer roles fall due wherever a combination is offered as a concrete change-world rather than a description.

A second observation. Combinatorialism faces a familiar pressure: it cannot easily generate alien properties, properties that no actual entity instantiates. If recombination is restricted to the actual, the modal range is narrower than most modal intuitions allow. Various extensions have been proposed (Armstrong himself, then Sider 2003): typically by admitting alien properties as primitive possibilities not generated by recombination, or by allowing modal primitives beyond the actualist base. The combinatorialist will call these workable refinements, but they are not free, and naming the cost precisely is what the objection requires. The appeal of combinatorialism was exactly its strict actualism (the thesis that only actually existing things exist, with no real merely-possible entities): the promise that the entire space of possibility is fixed by what actually exists, with nothing modal taken as primitive. An alien property admitted as a primitive possibility is, by definition, a possibility not fixed by the actual base, so the extension purchases modal adequacy by conceding the very reduction that made the position attractive. And the resulting view is no longer the actualist economy it advertised but a base of actual elements supplemented by free-floating modal primitives. The dilemma is stable: stay strictly actualist and the modal range is too narrow to capture ordinary modal intuition; widen it and the actualist motivation lapses.

Either horn is consistent with the present point, because T, S, and Φ are not candidate alien properties at all: not properties an entity might or might not instantiate, but conditions on there being entities, properties, or recombinations in the first place. The present argument does not turn on the resolution of this debate. What it offers is a fixed point: whatever combinatorialism includes or excludes, T, S, and Φ are not in the recombinable set. They are what the actual base must already instantiate for there to be anything to recombine.

*What converges.* Combinatorialism is, like ersatzism, a theory of how modal vocabulary is grounded. The present argument is a theory of what modal vocabulary describes. The two are compatible if the former locates its grounds within the structural conditions the latter identifies.

### 4.4.4 Modal Fictionalism {#sec-4-4-4}

Gideon Rosen's "Modal Fictionalism" (1990), a short paper in *Mind*, became one of the most discussed positions in the philosophy of modality by proposing a radical middle path: accept the expressive power of Lewis's plurality, reject its ontological commitment. When you say “I could have taken the other job,” Rosen holds, you are saying truly that according to the fiction of possible worlds, some world contains a counterpart of you who took that job. The fiction does its work without the worlds needing to exist. The plurality becomes a story we tell about modality, not a plurality we discover. Lewis built a universe of universes; Rosen borrowed it, used it, and handed it back.

Rosen's paper set the terms for two decades of debate. Brock ("Modal Fictionalism: A Response to Rosen," 1993) pressed the first major objection: fictionalism threatens to reduce modal claims to claims about what the fiction says, which presupposes a non-fictional fact about the fiction. Divers (*Possible Worlds*, 2002) and Nolan (*Topics in the Philosophy of Possible Worlds*, 2002) canvassed Lewisian and fictionalist variants side by side. Hale ("Modal Fictionalism: A Simple Dilemma," 1995) and Noonan (1994) sharpened Brock's dilemma. Sider (*Writing the Book of the World*, 2011) moved the tradition toward pragmatic deflation: modal talk as a useful tool whose commitments do not penetrate metaphysics. Woodward ("Is Modal Fictionalism Artificial?," 2011) defended Rosen's account against the charge that the fiction is hopelessly artificial; Rosen himself later partially distanced himself from the most extreme version of the view. What the literature preserves is a test case: how far can modal talk be deflated before the deflation undermines the level at which talk itself happens?

Modal fictionalism presses directly against the necessity claim of the argument. The current proof chain separates the relevant work. [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1) supplies Necessary Possibility / S5, [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) identifies the structural roles required by change, [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) gives the Modal Identity, and [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5) declares the Necessity of Nature: □(T∧S∧Φ), the necessary obtaining of the three structural Conditions borne by Time, Space, and Substance. On the fictionalist picture, that claim is true only insofar as the fiction of possible worlds licenses it. But the fiction is a story, not a feature of reality. If the argument's necessity claim is a claim about a story, its ontological weight dissolves. The argument has proved something about the fiction we use to talk about modality, not something about reality. The structural-exhaustion claim suffers in parallel: if exhaustion is fictional, no actual alternative was ever excluded.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute is not with the usefulness of fictionalist semantics for counterfactual reasoning. The question is whether the fiction can be told without the structural conditions the fiction is meant to deflate. If telling the story requires T, S, and Φ, the structure is not what the fiction is about. It is what makes the fiction tellable. Three forms of the move press the answer at three resolutions: the bare story-element move, the meta-level refinement, and the no-correspondence move. The space they canvass is the space modal fictionalism can occupy. Each concedes the structural conditions at the level the argument's claim applies.

*First.* The story-element move holds that modal claims are true according to the fiction, not true *simpliciter* (Latin: "absolutely," without qualification). “Possible world w₀ lacks T, S, and Φ” is a coherent story element; the story is part of the fiction; therefore the fictionalist can say w₀ is possible without committing to its ontology. The argument's individuation conditions for concrete possible worlds do not apply to story elements.

The relevant world-fiction must be disciplined enough to support the fictionalist's translation scheme, though fictional discourse can represent contradictions without thereby collapsing. The key question is not whether the act of telling is structured, but whether the fiction licenses the target modal claim under the adopted analysis. The question is whether the story of w₀ (a world lacking T, S, and Φ) can be coherently told. Telling the story requires individuating w₀ as distinct from other story elements (Space), attributing the property “lacks T, S, and Φ” to it (Substance, since attribution is a persistent relation between term and attribute), and unfolding the telling sequentially across moments of consideration as one element follows another (Time). The story about w₀ cannot be told without instantiating the roles w₀ is defined by the absence of. A fiction of a worldless world is a fiction written nowhere.

*Second.* The meta-level refinement concedes the first reply and still preserves the move. The fictionalist can accept that storytelling instantiates T, S, and Φ and still insist that w₀'s properties are fictional. The story requires structure at the meta-level; it does not require structure within the story. w₀ can lack structure as a story element even if the act of telling the story about w₀ requires structure.

The meta/story distinction blocks any inference from the structure of telling to the structure of the represented world. At most, the actual performance supplies act-side evidence that the actual world is structured. It does not establish that every real possibility instantiates the loaded types. The remaining dispute is therefore about the non-fictional modal resources needed to state which world-fiction is correct, not about storytelling as a cross-world proof. The story can contain any element the fictionalist wants (including structureless worlds), and the argument's claim about reality holds regardless. The fictionalist's modal claims reduce to claims about a story, and the reality in which the story is told instantiates the structural roles as the condition of the story being tellable. The deflation runs at the story level; the argument runs at the level that has to be there for stories to be told at all. This is Brock's dilemma (1993) arriving at the point of deployment rather than in the abstract. Fictionalism can state its modal truths only by presupposing a non-fictional fact about what the fiction says, and the meta-level refinement names that non-fictional fact outright, that reality instantiates T, S, and Φ as the condition of the story's being told. The refinement does not evade the dilemma; it is the dilemma realized at exactly the level the argument's claim occupies.

*Third.* The no-correspondence move presses the boldest version. Modal claims have no truth conditions beyond what the fiction specifies. There is no fact of the matter about whether w₀ is possible beyond what the story says. The argument's claim that w₀ is incoherent is itself just another story about stories: a meta-fiction whose ontological weight is no greater than the fiction it critiques.

The boldest version is unstable at the meta-level. If modal claims have no truth conditions beyond what the fiction specifies, the fictionalist still owes a non-circular account of the translation's correctness and of which fiction is privileged. The meta-claim about that semantics is not automatically itself modal, so self-defeat does not follow merely from its formulation. What the move cannot do is extend the no-truth-conditions treatment to that meta-claim itself: the account of the translation's correctness and of which fiction is privileged must hold non-fictionally, or the position dissolves into a fiction about fictions with nothing to recommend it. The escape is purchased by admitting a level of non-fictional fact. At the level at which the fictionalist's meta-position is coherent, it requires the structural conditions the argument identifies, each realized through its bearer: a reasoner (Substance) who evaluates fictions (Time) and distinguishes the meta-fiction from the fictions it describes (Space). The bold move does not escape structure. It demonstrates structure as the condition of its own coherence.

A kindred move drops full-blown fictionalism for Sider's (2011) pragmatic deflationism: modal talk serves practical purposes and carries no deep ontological commitment, but neither does it require a full-scale fiction. The reply follows the same path. Pragmatic deflation evaluates modal statements by their utility for reasoners whose reasoning instantiates the roles; the pragmatic frame is the structure's tool for its own modal reasoning. Deflation does not escape structure; it describes structure's modal practice from within.

The Lewisian concrete-worlds alternative is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). The modal-collapse worry, that necessary grounds propagate necessity through all of modal structure, is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9). Williamson's necessitism is [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6); Sider's structuralism is [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7). The Whiteheadian process ontology is [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8). The parody objection, that the argument's modal machinery licenses absurd conclusions, is [§4.4.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-10).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms concedes the structural conditions at the level the argument's claim applies. The story-element move fails because the fiction itself must be tellable: telling the story of a worldless world requires individuating it (Space), attributing properties to it (Substance), and unfolding the telling across moments of consideration (Time), a fiction written nowhere. The meta-level refinement saves the move only by conceding that the structural roles operate at the meta-level, which is exactly where the argument's claim applies. The no-correspondence move preserves its coherence only by admitting a non-fictional level: the account of which fiction is privileged must hold independently of any fiction, and at that level the structural conditions apply.

Rosen's paper was written at a moment when Lewis's plurality had begun to look, to many of its readers, like a *reductio* of the very modal realism it was built to defend. Fictionalism promised the semantics without the ontology: a way to talk about worlds without being committed to them. What the three decades of debate since have shown is that the promise could not be kept at the level the argument is concerned with. The fiction can dispense with the worlds; the storytelling cannot dispense with the storyteller, the time in which the story unfolds, or the space across which its elements are distinguished. Rosen's instinct (that modal talk does not commit us to a vast plurality) was sound. His conclusion mistook the target. That Rosen himself later drew back from the strongest version of fictionalism is not incidental to the case: he retreated under precisely the pressure these three forms exert, the recognition that the deflation cannot be carried all the way down without dissolving the level at which the deflating is itself done. What modal talk does not commit us to is the plurality. What it commits us to is the structural conditions any plurality, real or fictional, has to be told within.

### 4.4.5 Modal Expressivism {#sec-4-4-5}

Modal expressivism, defended by Blackburn (1986, 1993) and developed by Brandom (2008) and Thomasson (2020), denies that modal sentences express propositions about modal facts. Saying *necessarily, water is H₂O* is, on this view, expressing a stance (a commitment to a certain inferential pattern, a certain way of treating the claim) rather than describing a feature of reality. Modal vocabulary is a tool for organizing thought, not a window onto modal reality. The position parallels expressivism in ethics (Gibbard 1990, 2003) and in mathematics, and it aims to deflate modal ontology without giving up modal practice. We can keep saying *necessarily, P* while denying that there are modal facts for *necessarily, P* to be true of.

The argument's reply turns on what expressing a stance requires. Stances are states. They have content. They are distinguishable from other stances. They are sustained by a thinker who persists from the formation of the stance to its expression. The expressivist's framework operates on the structural conditions the argument identifies, and the operation is not a marginal feature of expressivism: it is the mechanism by which expressivism replaces descriptive ontology.

The Frege-Geach problem (Geach's 1965 sharpening of a worry traceable to Frege: how can sentences that merely express stances figure as components in logically valid inferences when embedded in conditionals and other complex contexts?) deserves full engagement. Modal claims figure in valid inferences (*modus ponens*, from *if P then Q* and *P*, conclude *Q*, and conditional reasoning more broadly) that look like inferences over propositions, not over stances. Schroeder (2008) gives the most sophisticated expressivist response, building stances out of “being for” attitudes (mental commitments toward propositional contents, treated as a basic stance-type with logical structure) whose logical relations are engineered to mirror propositional logic. Gibbard's quasi-realism (1990, 2003) takes a parallel line: the expressivist earns the right to talk as if modal sentences had truth-conditions by showing that stance-talk supports the same inferential structure realist talk supports.

Both responses are sophisticated. Their actual deployment requires structured agents and inferential practices, but this act-side requirement does not by itself establish that modal vocabulary describes mind-independent modal structure. Stance-composition requires that one stance be distinguishable from another, that combinations of stances yield further stances with determinate inferential properties, that the network of stance-relations is something a thinker can navigate over time. Schroeder's “being for” attitudes are themselves states with content, sustained by a subject, distinguishable from other states. The structural conditions are required by the resources expressivism uses to do without them.

Two variants of the family require engagement on their own terms, since neither rests its case on the stance-bearing the reply above targets. Brandom (2008) constitutes modal content not by a speaker's stance but by inferential role: the material inferences a claim licenses within a discursive practice, which modal vocabulary makes explicit. The Brandomian can grant everything said above about stances and still hold that content is fixed by inference, not by any condition on stance-formation. Actual inferring and deontic scorekeeping involve ordered acts, differentiated commitments, and continuing practitioners. That establishes the structural conditions of the discursive practice at act-side resolution. Inferential relations considered abstractly need not themselves be temporal processes or physical bearers, and the expressivist can still deny that modal sentences represent independent modal facts.

Thomasson, in *Norms and Necessity* (2020), locates modal claims differently again: neither stances nor descriptions but object-language expressions of the semantic rules constitutive of our concepts. Her normativism needs a distinct reply only in its bearer, not in its form. A rule meets the same three conditions even more plainly than a stance does: it is instituted and followed across cases, it discriminates correct from incorrect application and one rule from another, and it requires competent users who persist as the same rule-followers across applications. A rule just is a standing pattern applied over time by a community that endures to apply it, so the bearer changes but the structural demand does not. Whatever bears the modal (stance, inference, or rule) is sustained by the conditions the argument identifies.

A second front opens at the level of scope. Expressivism is most plausible as a localized thesis about a particular fragment of vocabulary: *this* part of language is expressive, *that* part is descriptive. The local form requires a fact about which sentences fall on which side, and the local expressivist is content to admit such facts at the metalinguistic level while denying them at the object level. Globalizing expressivism (the thesis that all assertion is stance-expression) generates a different problem. The claim *modal sentences express stances rather than facts* is itself either a fact about modal sentences (in which case expressivism has been falsified by the position's own articulation) or a stance about modal sentences (in which case the position lacks the descriptive force its proponents take it to have). Dreier (2004) names the “creeping minimalism” worry from the realist side: as expressivism succeeds in recovering the surface features of realist talk, it becomes harder to tell what the disagreement was about.

The present argument's intervention is orthogonal to that debate. It does not press the realist demand that modal sentences correspond to modal facts. It presses the prior point that any assertion (descriptive, expressive, or quasi-real) operates on T, S, and Φ. Local expressivism faces this point at its metalinguistic level, where the demarcation between expressive and descriptive vocabulary is drawn. Global expressivism faces it at every level, since the structural conditions are exhibited by stance-formation as decisively as by description.

*What is established.* Any stance (whether descriptive or expressive, whether about modality or anything else) operates on the structural conditions. T, S, and Φ are not what modal vocabulary describes; they are what any vocabulary requires.

### 4.4.6 Necessitism {#sec-4-4-6}

Timothy Williamson published *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* in 2013, a book whose title names exactly what the project is. His argument (developed across two decades of papers and consolidated in the book) is that modal logic is not a regional formalism for talking about possibility but the central apparatus of metaphysics itself, and that its quantifiers, when interpreted with the seriousness the formalism deserves, range over a constant domain across worlds. Necessarily everything is necessarily something. Whatever there is belongs to the same unrestricted domain at every world, including merely possible objects that are non-concrete at the actual world. Contingency concerns which objects are concrete and which properties they instantiate, rather than variation in the unrestricted domain itself. The Barcan formula and its converse, which together express the commutativity of quantification and modality, are validated. The view is the most ambitious modal-logical position currently defended, and the case for it draws on the simplicity, generality, and explanatory reach of constant-domain QML (quantified modal logic).

Williamson (*Modal Logic as Metaphysics*, 2013) is the systematic statement; "Bare Possibilia" (1998), "Necessary Existents" (2002), and "Everything" (2003) develop the apparatus. The position descends from Barcan Marcus (1946), who first proved the formula that bears her name in a quantified modal logic and pressed its philosophical consequences. Against necessitism stands a cluster of contingentist responses: Stalnaker (*Mere Possibilities*, 2012) defends the contingent-domain alternative by arguing that the apparent simplicity of constant-domain quantification is purchased at the cost of a domain populated by "merely possible" entities whose existence-status is obscure; Fine ("Necessity and Non-Existence," 2005) develops an essence-based account on which Socrates can be necessarily Socrates without necessarily existing; Adams ("Actualism and Thisness," 1981) defends actualism against the Barcan-formula consequences; Hale (*Necessary Beings*, 2013) develops a structured-necessity account on which different kinds of necessity have different scopes. Plantinga (1974b) had in effect pressed the objection in advance: such a position misreads modal claims about objects as modal claims about haecceities (individual thisnesses, the property of being *this very individual* and no other). The contemporary higher-order modal logic literature (Linnebo, *Thin Objects*, 2018; Linnebo and Rayo, "Hierarchies Ontological and Ideological," 2012) extends the dialectic into plural-quantification frameworks where the Barcan formula's status is again disputed.

The present reply sits closer to Stalnaker on the contingentist question and adds what Stalnaker alone does not specify: which contingencies the structural argument requires, and why those contingencies survive Williamson's framework whether or not constant-domain quantification is endorsed.

The challenge to the structural argument is double-edged. On one hand, necessitism would seem to make the necessary being trivially available: every possible thing exists necessarily, so the necessary being is among them. On the other hand, necessitism eliminates the explanatory work the necessary being is supposed to do. If everything exists necessarily, there is no explanatory contrast between the necessary being and contingent beings, because there are no contingent beings in the relevant sense. The argument's modal conclusion □(T∧S∧Φ) (the necessary obtaining of the three structural Conditions T, S, and Φ, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) lands trivially in a framework where everything is □ (necessary), which means it lands without distinguishing the structural conditions from anything else. Worse: the argument's premises require contingency the framework appears to deny. ◇C (the possibility of change) is defended in [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) as a substantive possibility-claim grounded in Cartesian phenomenal givenness: change is possible because change is occurring in the very act of doubt. If the framework reduces all contingency to qualitative variation across a fixed domain, the question is whether ◇C remains a genuine modal possibility distinguishable from □C, and whether the contingency of which world is actual (presupposed for the proof's stretch from □◇C to □(T∧S∧Φ) being non-trivial) survives at all.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute is not with quantified modal logic, the Barcan formula's formal validity in S5, or the ambition of modal logic to do metaphysical work. The argument shares with Williamson the commitment that modal logic is not a regional formalism but the apparatus through which metaphysical structure is articulated. The dispute is with whether the move from formal validity in constant-domain QML to ontological necessitism preserves the contingencies the structural argument requires for its premises to retain their force. Three forms of the move press that question at three resolutions: the constant-domain compatibility move, the Cartesian-Certainty preservation move, and the actuality-contingency preservation move. The space they canvass is the space necessitism can occupy. Each requires the structural roles its modal apparatus presupposes, and each leaves the argument's needed contingencies intact at the level the argument needs them.

*First.* The constant-domain compatibility move presses that the structural argument's modal conclusion lands trivially in Williamson's framework. □(T∧S∧Φ) is a necessity claim, and necessitism makes every existence claim a necessity claim. The conclusion is therefore consistent with necessitism but undistinguished by it. If the structural argument's distinctive contribution is the modal status of T, S, and Φ, and necessitism flattens all modal-status differences at the existence level, the argument has not earned anything Williamson's framework does not already deliver. The conclusion would be true but not informative.

The reply distinguishes the structural sense in which T, S, and Φ are necessary from the necessitist sense in which everything is necessary. Necessitism's necessity is *constant-domain*: the same things exist in every world. The structural argument's necessity is *constitutive*: T, S, and Φ are conditions any world must instantiate to be a world. The two are compatible but not equivalent. A necessitist can accept that the things which exist in every world include configurations satisfying T, S, and Φ, and the structural argument adds that the satisfaction of T, S, and Φ is what makes the constant domain a domain of any kind rather than a featureless plurality.

The Barcan formula and its converse, applied to the structural roles, yield exactly what the argument independently derives (every world's domain instantiates T, S, and Φ), but the formula does not by itself explain *why* every world's domain instantiates them. Appendix A's *Domain Semantics and the Barcan Question* records that the structural argument quantifies over Conditions rather than individuals, so Barcan and Converse Barcan are orthogonal to the proof's load-bearing claims at the structural level.

The structural argument proposes a metaphysical explanation Williamson's formal framework does not itself provide. This should not be attributed to a general truthmaker requirement on Williamson's part: the narrower point is that constant-domain semantics alone does not establish the book's constitutive account of T, S, and Φ. The structural account answers: the constitutive role of T, S, and Φ in any configuration is what makes the constant domain a domain, and the quantifier's range across that domain is the formal shadow of the constitutive fact. The constant-domain framework is exactly the framework the structural argument's conclusion describes, with the constitutive content filled in.

*Second.* The Cartesian-Certainty preservation move presses the harder version. The argument's central premise (◇C, the possibility of change) is defended in [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) as a substantive possibility-claim grounded in Cartesian phenomenal givenness: change is occurring in the very act of doubting, and that the doubting is a change cannot itself be doubted without instantiating it. ◇C must therefore mark a genuine modal possibility distinguishable from □C, the necessity of change. On Williamson's framework, the objector presses, this distinction collapses. Contingency is qualitative: which properties things have varies across worlds, but which things exist does not. If ◇C is read as the claim that change-events exist, necessitism makes that claim trivially necessary. If it is the claim that change-events possibly occur, the modal qualifier ◇ adds nothing beyond the qualitative-contingency level Williamson already permits. Either way, the Cartesian datum (that something *might* not have been changing) loses its modal weight, and the proof's first step is undermined.

The collapse does not occur, because the premise's modal weight does not sit at the level necessitism flattens. ◇C is not a claim about which entities exist in modal space; it is a claim about which configurations the structural roles permit. The Cartesian datum is not 'a change-event exists' but 'the act of thinking now occurring is itself a change', and the modal scope of the premise is over configurations of the roles, not over the existence of relata. Necessitism leaves the configuration-level intact: even if every entity exists necessarily, the question of which configuration any entity is in remains a qualitative-contingency question, and qualitative contingency is precisely what Williamson preserves. ◇C marks a substantive possibility at the level Williamson's framework licenses: configurations vary across worlds, the configuration-of-change is one configuration among others, and the Cartesian certainty is that *this* configuration is instantiated.

Stalnaker (2012) is the natural ally here; the contingentist alternative makes the same observation in a different idiom: even if necessitism is correct about domain-constancy, it is not correct that all modal weight collapses to the qualitative level, because configurations themselves carry modal scope. ◇C is a configuration-level claim and survives the necessitist reframing intact.

The explicit formalization is given at [§2.8.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-4): □F ∧ (◇p ∧ ◇¬p) for F = T∧S∧Φ records the configuration-level contingency the Cartesian datum requires while preserving structural necessity at the F-level. Fine's (2005) essence/necessity distinction sharpens the point: that change is occurring is a Cartesian datum about the actual configuration; that change-events exist necessarily (if Williamson is right) is a Williamsonian claim about the domain. The two claims are at different levels, and the structural argument's premise is at the configuration level the necessitist framework leaves untouched.

*Third.* The actuality-contingency preservation move presses the boldest version. The structural argument's modal line decomposes into four distinct elements rather than a single stretch. *P3* is ◇C, asserted in [§2.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-4) as a Cartesian datum about the actual world: change is occurring in the very act of doubt. *The S5 lift* from ◇C to □◇C uses the collapse of iterated modalities: once ◇C obtains, ◇C obtains necessarily, since possibility in S5 is itself a necessary feature of modal space. *The Modal Identity* of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) is the biconditional □(◇C ↔ T∧S∧Φ): the necessary equivalence between the possibility of change and the co-instantiation of the three structural roles. *The theorem-level conclusion* □(T∧S∧Φ) follows from □◇C and the biconditional by K-axiom closure under □. The objection's bite lands not on the validity of the closure but on its informativeness: if which world is actual is not itself contingent (if there are no worlds whose configuration includes change distinguishable from worlds whose configuration does not) the closure runs formally but the conclusion records no metaphysical fact the alternatives could have falsified. The argument needs it to be a substantive fact that we are in a world whose configuration includes change. On Williamson's framework, the objector presses, the contingency of which world is actual cannot be sustained. Necessitism plus constant-domain quantification reduces the difference between worlds to qualitative variation in property-distribution; the actuality of *this* configuration becomes a brute haecceitistic fact rather than a contingent one. If which world is actual is not genuinely contingent, the stretch from □◇C to □(T∧S∧Φ) loses its bite: the conclusion follows by necessity from premises that themselves cannot be modally distinguished from their alternatives.

The reply runs at the level the proof actually operates. The actuality-contingency the argument needs is qualitative-contingency, not ontological-contingency, and qualitative-contingency is exactly what Williamson preserves. The proof requires that *some* configuration is actual and that not every configuration is actual: both are qualitative-contingency claims about how the constant domain is configured, not ontological-contingency claims about what the domain contains. Necessitism endorses the first (every world has a configuration) and is silent on the second (it does not require that every configuration be instantiated). Indeed, necessitism *requires* qualitative-contingency to be substantive, since otherwise every world is qualitatively identical and the framework has no work to do. The actuality-contingency the structural argument requires is precisely the qualitative-contingency Williamson's framework treats as the residue of contingency that survives constant-domain quantification.

Adams (1981) is helpful here as a foil: Adams holds that the qualitative-contingency level is itself unstable, but his argument depends on the haecceitist reading Williamson explicitly rejects. Hale's (2013) structured-necessity account makes the cleaner point: necessities at different levels do different work, and the structural argument's necessity at the constitutive level is compatible with qualitative-contingency at the configuration level. The stretch from □◇C to □(T∧S∧Φ) is non-trivial because the configuration-of-change is one qualitative possibility among others, and the actual configuration's instantiation of that possibility is what the proof's first premise records.

Williamson's positive defense of S5 in *Modal Logic as Metaphysics* rests on considerations the structural argument finds hospitable rather than threatening. The present proof likewise derives S5 from fixed-domain semantics: real possibility ranges over one global domain W, so a witness to ◇P remains a witness at every evaluation point. This is distinct from Williamson's constant-domain thesis about **individuals**. A fixed domain of possible worlds does not by itself entail a constant domain of entities across those worlds.

The Brouwer axiom (p → □◇p) then follows for the present operator because any actual P is witnessed within W, and every world evaluates possibility over that same W. The Cartesian datum establishes ◇C through actuality; the fixed-domain account, not a prior claim that T, S, and Φ are everywhere instantiated, yields □◇C.

The disagreement is therefore precise. Williamson uses constant-domain QML to motivate ontological necessitism. The structural argument uses a fixed global domain of real possibilities to establish modal invariance, then separately derives the necessary Conditions that any world in that domain realizes. The shared formal result does not settle the ontological reading.

Fine, engaged as dialectical opponent rather than as authority, presses the structural argument from a complementary direction. Fine's "Essence and Modality" (1994) and "Necessity and Non-Existence" (2005) establish that necessity derives from essence: what makes a modal claim necessary is that it follows from the essence of some entity. Applied to the structural argument: what makes □(T∧S∧Φ) necessary? If it follows from the essence of T, S, or Φ themselves, the argument is circular: T, S, and Φ must already exist and have essences to generate the necessity, which is what the argument is trying to establish. If it follows from the essence of *change*, Fine will press that conceptual essence generates analytic necessity rather than unrestricted metaphysical necessity. The structural reply is that the argument's modality is neither essence-based in Fine's sense nor merely analytic. It is role-necessity: the necessity that anything being a *something* at all instantiates the structural conditions, grounded not in the essence of T, S, or Φ as entities but in the role-structure that any entity's being anything at all requires. The book proposes role-necessity as an alternative explanatory basis, but Fine's framework is flexible enough to ask whether structural roles themselves have essences or are grounded in more basic essences. The challenge therefore remains substantive: the book must defend the priority of role-structure rather than treating it as outside Fine's apparatus by definition.

A kindred move drops Williamson's necessitism for Linnebo's higher-order modal logic, where the Barcan formula is reformulated in plural-quantification terms and the necessitism/contingentism dialectic re-emerges at the level of pluralities rather than individuals. This is the sharpest form of the necessitist challenge, and it cannot be turned aside by the observation that the structural roles are conditions rather than individuals. The first-order replies bank configuration-level contingency as the residue necessitism leaves free, and they can do so because first-order necessitism rigidifies only the domain of individuals. Higher-order and plural necessitism rigidify properties and pluralities as well, and configurations live at exactly that level. Plural logic is not silent where configurations operate; it is a logic of that level. The reply must therefore be earned at the higher order, not asserted to lie beneath it.

It is earned by lifting Williamson's own distinction to the plural level. Necessitism already separates *being* from *concreteness*: whatever exists, exists necessarily, but what is concrete is contingent; a thing has its being in every world and is concrete in only some. Carried up to pluralities, higher-order necessitism rigidifies the *being* of configurations-as-possibilia, but its contingently-concrete machinery leaves which configurations are concretely actual contingent. That residue is precisely what the proof draws on. The first premise does not record that some plurality exists; it records that the configuration-of-change is the one concretely instantiated. The contingency at work is concreteness-contingency, and concreteness-contingency survives plural necessitism for the same reason it survives the individual case: Williamson's framework rigidifies being, not concreteness, at whichever order it is run. Linnebo's apparatus extends the dialectic to the level of pluralities; pressed there, it presses the structural conclusion no harder than at the level of individuals.

The Barcan-formula version of the modal-collapse worry, that any necessity at the existence level propagates to all existential claims, is engaged in its Spinozan-propagation form at [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9), where the constitutive/productive distinction does the work necessitism alone cannot do.

The Lewisian concrete-plurality alternative, which gives modal claims maximal ontological weight rather than minimal, is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). The modal-collapse worry, that necessary instantiation flattens all modal distinctions, is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9). Sider's structuralism, which deflates rather than embraces necessity, is [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7). The Whiteheadian process alternative is [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8). Modal fictionalism's attempt to deflate the whole apparatus is [§4.4.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-4).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms of the necessitist threat operates at a level the structural argument either accommodates or does not depend on. The constant-domain compatibility move is correct that □(T∧S∧Φ) is consistent with necessitism, but it underestimates what the structural argument adds: the constitutive account of what makes the constant domain a domain. The Cartesian-Certainty preservation move presses the strongest threat to the proof's first premise; ◇C survives because its modal weight sits at the configuration level Williamson preserves, not at the existence level Williamson flattens. The actuality-contingency preservation move presses the boldest version; the contingency the proof requires is qualitative-contingency at the configuration level, which is exactly what necessitism leaves intact, and which necessitism in fact requires if its framework is to do any work at all.

Williamson draws the conclusion that the formal apparatus deserves to be taken at face value: the quantifiers range over a constant domain, the Barcan formula and its converse are validated, and what looked like ontological contingency dissolves into qualitative variation across a fixed plurality. The structural argument shares the formal commitment and adds what Williamson's framework requires but does not specify: the constitutive role of T, S, and Φ in making the constant domain a domain. What Williamson left behind is not a refutation of the structural argument but a cleaner statement of the level at which the argument's necessity claim operates: not at the qualitative-contingency level where Williamson preserves modal variation, but at the constitutive level where the variation is hosted. Necessitism is the framework the structural argument's conclusion is most compatible with at the formal level, and the argument supplies the constitutive reading its formalism leaves underspecified.

### 4.4.7 Sider's Structuralism {#sec-4-4-7}

Theodore Sider published *Writing the Book of the World* in 2011, a book whose title names exactly what metaphysics ought to do. His argument is that the world has a privileged structure (a set of joint-carving notions) and that the project of metaphysics is to identify which notions those are. Existence quantifiers, mereological parthood, fundamentality, even logical operators: Sider is willing to ask of each whether it carves at the joints or merely tracks our practical interests. Modality is among the notions whose structural status Sider's methodology invites us to assess. His project should not be reduced to the blanket claim that necessity is merely a relation between structure and language. The sharper rival considered here is a Siderian or Humean extension on which modal ideology is not fundamental and modal truths supervene on non-modal joint-carving structure.

Sider (*Writing the Book of the World*, 2011) is the systematic statement; "Ontological Realism" (2009) is the methodologically central earlier paper.
