The position is part of a broader contemporary trend: naturalistic structural realism in philosophy of physics (Ladyman & Ross, *Every Thing Must Go*, 2007; French, *The Structure of the World*, 2014, both engaged at [§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9)), Quine's structuralism in philosophy of mathematics (1969, the view that mathematical objects are exhausted by their structural roles rather than possessing intrinsic identities), and the structuralist movement in philosophy of science going back to Russell and continuing through Worrall ("Structural Realism: The Best of Both Worlds?", 1989). Sider's contribution is to extend structuralism beyond philosophy of science into general metaphysics: not just physical structure is fundamental, but logical, mereological, and existential structure. Against Sider's structuralism, the contemporary literature includes Schaffer (*Monism*, 2010, on grounding-as-fundamental), Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds*, 1986, on modality-as-fundamental, engaged at [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)), Williamson (*Modal Logic as Metaphysics*, 2013, on modal logic as metaphysically central, engaged at [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6)), and Fine ("The Question of Realism," 2001, who develops a kindred structuralism with different commitments). The present reply sits closer to Sider on the empirical question (physics does carve at the joints in something like the way Sider claims) and presses the modal question: whether Sider's structure-without-modal-scope can deliver what the present account's predictions require.

Sider's structuralism presses the central claim of [§1.5](groundwork.html#sec-1-5) from a direction [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1), [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9), and [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6) do not. Lewis multiplies the modal ontology; Modal Collapse worries about its propagation; Williamson endorses its scope. Sider does something subtler: he deflates it. Modality, on his picture, is a way of speaking about what the privileged structure looks like through the lens of various linguistic frameworks, not a feature the structure itself possesses. T, S, and Φ (the three structural Conditions, borne by Time, Space, and Substance, the trio the book's argument derives) might be perfectly real, perfectly joint-carving features of the actual world without being necessary features in any deeper sense. The argument's necessity claim (□(T∧S∧Φ), read as "necessarily, T and S and Φ obtain together") is, on the structuralist's reading, a claim about how the structure looks under a particular modal idiom rather than a claim about anything the structure itself contains. The threat is precise: if modal scope is deflated, the cycle prediction ([§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6)), the consciousness-elsewhere claim ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)), and the foreclosure of absolute nothingness ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)) all lose the modal weight they were carrying. They become claims about this world's structure rather than claims about the structure of any world.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute is not with structural realism as a methodological program. The argument shares with Sider (and with Ladyman & Ross's naturalistic structural realism, engaged at [§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9)) the commitment that fundamental ontology is given by structural relations rather than by hidden quiddities. The dispute is with whether the structural ontology can be specified without modal scope. Three forms of the move press the deflation at three resolutions: the bare deflation move, the redundancy move, and the no-modal-realism move. The space they canvass is the space modal-deflationary structuralism can occupy. The replies test whether any form can deflate modal scope without requiring it to specify what the structure is.

*First.* The bare deflation move holds that modal claims are not joint-carving. There are facts about what is the case (Sider's privileged structure, the actual configuration of the world) and there are facts about what would have been the case, but the second class of facts is derivative. Possible-worlds talk tracks something useful; what it tracks is not modal reality but the relations between linguistic frameworks and the privileged structure. The argument's modal claims, on this reading, are linguistic claims with structural correlates rather than structural claims about modal space.

The deflation requires specifying what the privileged structure is. Sider's account answers in joint-carving notions: existence, parthood, fundamentality, identity, predication, plus whichever physical and logical primitives the final theory turns out to require. Two readings of joint-carvingness are available. On the first, joint-carvingness is exegeted modally: what the structure would recommend across counterfactual variation in our descriptive vocabularies. On the second, pressed most fully by the Sider–Fine–Schaffer hyperintensional-structuralism alliance (Fine, "The Question of Realism," 2001; Schaffer, "On What Grounds What," 2009), with Lewis's perfectly-natural-properties as the precedent for a non-modal structural primitive in even the arch-modal-realist's metaphysics, joint-carvingness is primitive structural-fundamentality, hyperintensional, not analyzable modally.

The argument's reply does not require the first reading. Grant Sider the second: joint-carving is primitive structural-fundamentality, ontologically prior to modal facts. The argument's modal scope is still required, but it comes not from the joint-carving exegesis; it comes from what the empirical predictions of [§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6), [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), and [§2.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-8) carry across substrates. The redundancy move next makes the empirical-predictions ground precise.

A note on Sider's positive view (*Writing the Book of the World*, §12). Sider's modal deflationism is not mere skepticism but a positive Humean account: modal facts supervene on the actual-world mosaic of non-modal joint-carving patterns. What makes a modal claim true is whether the pattern it describes is joint-carving in the actual mosaic. This is a richer position than bare deflationism: it grounds modal claims in structural fabric rather than dismissing them. The structural argument's reply takes the positive Humean account seriously and presses one question: does the mosaic's joint-carving character itself hold necessarily or contingently? If contingently (if a different cosmos could have had entirely different joint-carving patterns) then Sider's Humean modal grounding bottoms out in a contingent mosaic, and the structural argument's necessity claim is not captured by it. If necessarily (if the joint-carving patterns of any mosaic are the patterns any mosaic must have by virtue of being a mosaic at all) then Sider's positive Humeanism, fully developed, endorses the structural argument's conclusion rather than deflating it. The structural argument offers the second reading: what makes T, S, and Φ joint-carving across any cosmos is that they are conditions on any fabric having causal joints at all. Sider's positive Humeanism and the structural argument converge when the necessity of the structural mosaic is taken seriously rather than deferred.

*Second.* The redundancy move presses harder. Where the present argument makes modal predictions, the cycle ([§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6)), substrate-independence of consciousness ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)), the preclusion of absolute nothingness ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)), Sider's structuralism delivers them as descriptions of how this world's structure works, without requiring modal scope. The cycle is what the actual cosmic dynamics deliver; the argument's modal apparatus is metaphysical surplus. The substrate-independence claim is what neuroscience plus the physics of information processing delivers; the argument's "in any world where T, S, Φ obtain..." formulation is bookkeeping. The preclusion of absolute nothingness is what cosmological inflation plus the structure of quantum field theory delivers; the modal scope adds nothing physics cannot say more carefully without it.

The redundancy diagnosis fails at the kind of generality it claims to absorb. The distinction the argument needs is not between a local forecast and a falsifiable cross-substrate empirical prediction: the substrate-neutral structural definition at [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) (closure-plus-throughput as a structural stance) and the cycle at [§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6) are structural-necessity claims about what any cosmos with T, S, and Φ must instantiate, rather than prediction-candidates in the narrow falsificationist sense. The reply therefore does not hostage itself to the standing of those predictions. A reader who suspends judgment on whether the cycle recurs ([§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6)) or consciousness arises on other substrates ([§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8)) still confronts the type-distinction, which turns on what kind of claim each makes (a structural-necessity claim across cosmological variation) rather than on whether either is ultimately borne out.

The distinction is between two kinds of structural generality: the Humean joint-carving description says 'this universe's constants and laws produce this pattern, and the pattern is joint-carving in this actual mosaic'; the modal structural-recurrence claim says 'any cosmos hosting causal succession across a relational manifold will instantiate this structural pattern, because the pattern is what the structural conditions require, regardless of which particular constants or substrate produce them.' Sider's deflation can endorse the first kind of generality; it cannot endorse the second.

The across-substrate structural recurrence that [§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6) and [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8) deliver is a scope of generality that local-universe joint-carving cannot capture: it identifies which features of our universe are universe-invariant (structural-necessity claims) versus which are local products of our particular physical constants (contingent-mosaic claims).

Whether this broader generality matters depends on what the structural argument is for. If only our actual universe is at stake, Sider's deflation may suffice. If the structural conditions are genuinely necessary across any cosmos, as §[§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6)–2.7 argue, then the modal scope is not surplus but constitutive; it is the difference between describing what this world happens to do and identifying the conditions any world must satisfy to be a world at all.

*Third.* The no-modal-realism move presses the boldest version. Modal facts are not facts about modal reality; they are facts about how the privileged structure relates to descriptive frameworks. The structural argument's "necessarily, T∧S∧Φ" can be rewritten as "in the privileged structure, T∧S∧Φ are joint-carving features of the actual world's fundamental ontology," with no modal claim left over. The argument's content is preserved, its modal commitment dissolved.

The rewriting fails to preserve content. "In the privileged structure, T∧S∧Φ are joint-carving features of the actual world's fundamental ontology" is true if T, S, Φ obtain in the actual world and the structure carves at the joints. It does not entail that T, S, Φ obtain in any other world. But the argument needs the entailment. The cycle prediction, the consciousness-elsewhere claim, and the foreclosure of absolute nothingness ([§7.6](nature-alone.html#sec-7-6), [§7.8](nature-alone.html#sec-7-8), [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)) hold across worlds, not just within the actual one, and the structural ground is what licenses the across-world reach. Sider's rewriting eliminates the across-world reach. What it preserves is the actual-world structure; what it loses is the necessity that makes the structure structural in the load-bearing sense. Joint-carving features can be contingent; structural conditions of any cosmos are not. The bold rewriting trades the second for the first and calls the trade a translation.

A kindred move drops Sider's full structuralism for the more cautious naturalistic structural realism of Ladyman & Ross. NSR holds that physics gives us structural facts about the actual world without committing to whether those facts are necessary across worlds. The reply runs as it does at [§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9): NSR is a methodological constraint on physics that is silent on the modal question; it is not a positive metaphysical alternative to the present argument. The argument welcomes NSR's empirical structuralism and adds the modal architecture NSR's caution declines to address. The two positions are not competitors but layered.

The Lewisian concrete-plurality alternative, which gives modal claims maximal ontological weight rather than minimal, is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). The modal-collapse worry, that the argument's modal scope over-generates necessity, is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9). Williamson's necessitism, which licenses the modal scope at the type level, is [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6). The Whiteheadian process alternative is [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms of structural deflation requires the modal scope it deflates. The bare deflation move can be granted its non-modal joint-carving primitive; the modal scope the argument needs is then carried by the across-substrate reach of its structural claims, where the redundancy move takes it up. The redundancy move loses the across-substrate reach the argument's claims carry: the cycle, substrate-independence of consciousness, and the foreclosure of absolute nothingness are structural-necessity claims across cosmological variation, not local forecasts about our horizon's future. The no-modal-realism move trades the across-world reach for actual-world joint-carvingness and calls the trade a translation, but the argument's central claims hold across worlds, not just within the actual one.

The deepest agreement between Sider's structuralism and the argument is real and worth naming explicitly. The structural-realist insight that physics names the constraints rather than discovers properties hidden behind them is already endorsed at [§7.5](nature-alone.html#sec-7-5). The Triconditional Cross-Entailment of [§2.6.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-7) and the Ontological Identity of [§2.6.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-8) operate within a framework that is recognizably continuous with Sider's. What the argument adds (and what the present section makes explicit) is the modal floor under the structuralism. Joint-carving features can be contingent; necessary structural conditions cannot. The cycle, substrate-independence, and foreclosure claims have modal reach only if the prior necessity argument succeeds. Their empirical or explanatory usefulness cannot independently establish that reach without circularity. The book shares Sider's joint-carving ambition but adds a contested modal thesis. A non-modal structuralist can accept the actual structural roles while withholding their cross-world necessity; later predictions inherit, rather than independently prove, the book's answer to that dispute.

Sider's defense of joint-carving structuralism is the most sustained one the analytic tradition has produced in this century: that there is a privileged structure, that metaphysics aims to identify it, and that the identification is genuinely revisionary: that we discover what the structure carves at, rather than choosing among equally legitimate frameworks. The defense is offered against a backdrop in which general metaphysics had begun to look, to many of its critics, like terminological housekeeping rather than discovery. The argument shares the project entirely. What it adds is the level of modal commitment on which the argument's across-substrate claims depend: not just that this world has the structure it has, but that any possible cosmos must have at least this much structure to be a cosmos at all. Sider's joint-carving is the local form; the argument's modal necessity is the global form. The book of the world has more pages than one cosmos can fill.

### 4.4.8 Whiteheadian Process Metaphysics {#sec-4-4-8}

Heraclitus held that nothing ever is, that everything becomes: what looks like a persisting thing is really a pattern maintained across constant material turnover, no drop of water in a river the same from moment to moment, only the shape and rate of its flow persisting. Alfred North Whitehead, twenty-four centuries later, worked out the most technically developed version of that ancient thought. If the process philosopher is right, what classical metaphysics called a substance is always a river, always just the apparent persistence of a pattern across occasions that arise and perish. The argument of this book asks the opposite: that what flows is Substance in verb form, and that asking a persistence question of a pattern only has content because something is carrying the pattern.

Whitehead (*Process and Reality*, 1929, from his Gifford Lectures of 1927–28) developed the classical statement of process metaphysics after leaving mathematical logic for philosophy at Harvard in his sixties. The position has three generations of defenders: Hartshorne (*Creative Synthesis and Philosophic Method*, 1970) develops process theology as the natural extension; Cobb (*A Christian Natural Theology*, 1965) and Griffin (*Reenchantment Without Supernaturalism*, 2001) extend it into theology and philosophy of mind (the process-theology branch named here is engaged directly at [§5.3.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-3-3)); Ford (*The Emergence of Whitehead's Metaphysics*, 1984), Kraus (*The Metaphysics of Experience*, 1979), and Lango (*Whitehead's Ontology*, 1972) develop the technical machinery. Rescher (*Process Metaphysics*, 1996) generalizes it beyond Whitehead's specific terminology. Seibt (2017) gives the contemporary continuation, preserving process as primary while remaining silent on Whitehead's more specific commitments. Against the process tradition stands the substance-realist line: Armstrong (*A World of States of Affairs*, 1997), Lowe (*The Four-Category Ontology*, 2006), and Heil (*From an Ontological Point of View*, 2003) all defend ontologies in which enduring substance is ineliminable. The present reply sits closest to Heil on the ontological question and adds what substance-realism alone does not: that Substance and process are not rivals but aspects. What the process carries, and what carries the process, are the same structural role described under two grammars.

The Whiteheadian challenge presses the specification in [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) of what Change requires and the identification at [§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10) of those requirements as Conditions-as-Nature. The argument of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) is that succession requires temporal order, distinction requires extension, and exchange requires maintained causal capacity, with [§2.6.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-8) specifying the Φ / Physicality role. Whitehead accepts the first two and contests the third: causal transmission, on his view, occurs through prehension (Whitehead's term for the relational act by which one actual occasion takes account of and incorporates the character of a predecessor occasion) without requiring anything enduring. If prehension alone can do the work Substance does, the third role of [§2.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6) and the Conditions-as-Nature identification of [§2.6.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-10) are incomplete: T, S, and Φ (the three structural Conditions the book's argument derives, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) are not the three necessary structural roles; there are two, with the third replaced by a relational pattern among momentary occasions. This is a more refined threat than classical momentariness ([§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8)), which denied persistence outright. Whitehead concedes the datum persistence captures (character does transmit across change) and proposes to capture the datum without the ontology.

A clarification before the moves. The dispute is not with the datum process philosophy starts from. The world plainly does flow, occasions plainly do arise and perish, pattern plainly does transmit across change. The dispute is with the ontological claim that the flow is fundamental and persistence is derivative. Three forms of the move press that fundamentality at three resolutions: the prehension move (pattern transmits without substrate), the superject move (what perishes leaves efficacious traces), and the process-all-the-way-down move (process is the final category). The space they canvass is the space Whiteheadian ontology occupies. Each relocates Substance under another name.

*First.* The prehension move holds that actual occasions perish entirely, and what we call persistence is the inheritance of character from predecessor to successor through prehension. No enduring substrate is required. The pattern is transmitted across a sequence of discrete creative acts, each complete in itself.

For a new actual occasion to inherit the character of its predecessor, there must be a structural connection between donor occasion and recipient occasion that transmits the character across the transition. That transmission is a directed dependence from donor occasion to recipient and requires differentiation plus causal efficacy: the predecessor's character must genuinely condition the successor, not merely precede it. This directly realizes thin order, difference, and bearing roles. It does not by itself establish a spatial interval between occasions or a persisting substance; those loaded types require the separate role-to-type argument. This last requirement is where the prehension move must be met on its own terms rather than by positing a carrier it denies: the Whiteheadian is right that no occasion persists alongside the others to ferry the pattern across, but inheritance is not mere succession; an occasion that merely followed its predecessor without being causally conditioned by it would not have inherited anything. What makes prehension inheritance rather than succession is precisely that the donor's character is causally efficacious in the constitution of the recipient, and that cross-transition efficacy is what Φ names ([§2.6.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-8)): not a substance enduring through the interval, but the causal capacity the inheritance-relation must instantiate to count as inheritance at all. Whitehead's own account of prehension (the most technically developed account of how inheritance works) describes precisely this structural architecture. The prehensive relation does not float free of structural conditions; it instantiates them. The Whiteheadian account does not offer an alternative ontology to the structural picture. It offers an alternative vocabulary for the same structural facts. The roles are instantiated between occasions rather than within a persisting thing, but instantiated nonetheless.

*Second.* The superject move goes deeper. Each occasion perishes into what Whitehead calls the 'superject': a mode of being in which it becomes an object for future prehension. The superject is not a continuing subject but a contribution to subsequent occasions. The causal pattern is carried in the way the superject functions in the prehensions of its successors, not in any ongoing existence of the occasion itself.

Superject ontology relocates Substance rather than removing it. Even granted in full, objective immortality as a *relational-inheritance* fact rather than an entity persisting through an interval (the most thoroughgoing non-substantialist reading, parallel to the relational-availability move classical momentariness pursues at [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8)), the superject's contribution to subsequent occasions instantiates the structural roles at the level of the transition itself. The inheritance of character from O₁ to O₂ has direction (Time's asymmetry: from donor to recipient, not the reverse), differentiation (Space's distinction: O₁ and O₂ are distinguishable contributors and recipients), and causal efficacy across the transition (Φ's role, engaged as substrate at [§2.6.8](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-8) in the form the transition itself must take). The ontological burden Substance carries in the present account (being the carrier of causal efficacy across the transition) is carried by the inheritance-relation in the Whiteheadian account whether that relation is glossed as persistence-through-interval or as availability-for-prehension. What changes is the name. What does not change is the work the role does at the level of the transition structure. What is settled here is the bearer-*role*: inheritance instantiates cross-transition causal efficacy under whatever grammar names it. The step from that role to a *persistent causal being*, the Φ-*type*, is neither carried here nor needed here; it is the Stage-2 work of the realizer biconditional Φ ↔ (T∧S) ([§2.6.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-4)), secured at [§3.5.3](convergence.html#sec-3-5-3). The Whiteheadian who grants cross-transition efficacy while denying that any occasion persists is therefore met on the persistence-*type* question there, not in this section, which secures only that no process ontology escapes the role.

*Third.* The process-all-the-way-down move presses the boldest version. Prehension is insufficient as a final ontology; what is needed is process as the fundamental category. Reality is not events in prehensive relation; reality is process: the dynamic, self-organizing flow of becoming that constitutes all finite entities. There is no substance because there is no static layer at any depth. Process is ontologically basic.

'Process all the way down' requires exactly the three structural roles at every level. For reality to be process, there must be transitions, differentiated phases or occasions, and some determinate continuity or efficacy linking them. These support the three roles at thin resolution. Requiring in addition a distinct thing that is processed would beg the question against process ontology, which treats the process or relation itself as fundamental. The deepest Whiteheadian commitment (that reality is nothing but process) does not escape the structural roles. It makes them the content of what the process is. Process ontology *is* Substance ontology articulated in the grammar of verbs rather than nouns. What the process *consists in* and what carries the process *are* the same structural role under two descriptions.

A kindred move drops the Whiteheadian apparatus for Bergson's (*Creative Evolution*, 1907) *élan vital* (French: "vital impulse"): reality is not composed of substances but of a creative evolutionary impulse, *durée* (French: "duration", lived time as continuous flow rather than discrete instants), whose continuous becoming precedes any static ontology. The reply is the same in French vocabulary. Creative becoming requires differentiation of the created (S), asymmetric direction of the creation (T), and continuity of the creating impulse across its acts (Φ). Bergsonian duration *is* the structural roles rendered in the grammar of flow.

The classical momentariness objection is [§4.2.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-8). The emergent-time objection, that temporal flow is a derived feature, is [§4.2.3](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-3). The modal-collapse worry that necessary process propagates necessity everywhere is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms relocates Substance under another name rather than replacing it. The prehension move describes the structural architecture of inheritance, direction from donor to recipient (Time), differentiation of donor occasion from recipient (Space), and causal efficacy across the transition that makes inheritance more than mere succession (Substance), under alternative vocabulary. The superject move relocates Substance's work into objective immortality: what the superject is and what it continues to do is exactly what Substance names, in non-substantialist grammar. 'Process all the way down' requires the three structural roles at every level (transitions, differentiated phases, and determinate continuity or efficacy linking them) with process ontology revealed as Substance ontology articulated in the grammar of verbs rather than nouns.

Whitehead delivered the lectures at Edinburgh in a form dense enough that the eventual book is read more often in commentaries than in the original. *Process and Reality* is the last great systematic metaphysics of the twentieth century. What it offers is a grammar (a way of redescribing the world under the verb rather than the noun), not an alternative to what the world structurally is. The Whiteheadian who argues that each occasion perishes entirely sustains the argument across multiple cognitive occasions, each thought inheriting the reasoning of its predecessor, carrying the argument forward to its conclusion. That inheritance is Substance described in verb form: the structural role persistence names, operating through the very transmission the argument describes.

Heraclitus said no one steps in the same river twice; the observation is acute and has never been refuted. But stepping, river, and twice are themselves structural descriptions: Substance moving through Time across Space. The flux Heraclitus saw and the structure Parmenides saw are one thing seen from inside and from outside; their dispute was over which vocabulary tracks it, not over which was illusion.

### 4.4.9 Modal Collapse Objection {#sec-4-4-9}

The modal-collapse objection holds that a necessary ground generates necessary outputs: an argument that makes the structural conditions of reality inescapable thereby makes everything that happens within them inescapable too. Spinoza reached this conclusion by tracing out the consequences of substance monism, and drew it as a triumph: every mode follows with the force of geometrical demonstration, and the appearance of contingency is a mark of ignorance. Most of his successors reached the same conclusion and tried to find a way to block it. The present account, the objector presses, appears to rebuild the same trap from a different direction: with T, S, and Φ (the three structural conditions the book's argument derives, borne by Time, Space, and Substance) in the place of *Deus sive Natura* (Spinoza's identification: "God or Nature") and the history of the world in the place of the modes.

The modal-collapse objection has a long lineage. Spinoza (*Ethics* [-@spinoza1677]) drew it as a positive conclusion: substance is necessary, its modes follow with geometrical necessity, and contingency is an illusion of perspective. Leibniz (*Theodicy* [-@leibniz1710]) reached a softer form: God necessarily chooses the *best possible world*, and the specific history of this world is therefore fixed with a necessity one step removed from Spinoza's. Modern defenses: Pruss (*The Principle of Sufficient Reason* [-@pruss2006]) presses the Leibnizian version against necessitarian accounts of grounding. Van Inwagen (*An Essay on Free Will* [-@vanInwagen1983]) sharpens the deterministic relative, the Consequence Argument: if the laws and the past are necessary, the future is necessary too. Rasmussen (*How Reason Can Lead to God* [-@rasmussen2019]) applies the modal-collapse worry to necessitarian alternatives to classical theism. Against the collapse, the contemporary literature runs thick: Plantinga (*The Nature of Necessity* [-@plantinga1974b]) deploys the de dicto/de re distinction in ways that block various propagation moves; Swinburne (*The Christian God* [-@swinburne1994]) defends a libertarian space within theism; the open theists (Hasker, Sanders) reject the collapse by denying the necessity of the antecedents. The contemporary grounding literature establishes the framework the present reply uses. Fine ("Guide to Ground," [-@fine2012]) and Rosen ("Metaphysical Dependence: Grounding and Reduction," [-@rosen2010]) set out grounding as a relation of constitutive determination and defend the principle that a full ground necessitates what it grounds; Schaffer (*On What Grounds What* [-@schaffer2009]; *Monism* [-@schaffer2010]) and Dasgupta [-@dasgupta2014] develop the apparatus the present reply turns on: above all the distinction, owed to Fine, between full and partial ground. The structural account sits closest to Dasgupta's line on grounding and adds: the specific grounds at issue are T, S, and Φ, and their necessity is compatible with the contingency of what they ground because they are only a partial, structural ground of any particular change, never its full ground.

The objection bears on two of the argument's central theses. The Modal Identity is established at [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6): the necessity of the structural conditions (□(T∧S∧Φ)) entails □◇C, the necessary *possibility* of change, not □C, the necessity of change itself. The Necessity of Nature is then established at [§2.8.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-8-5): the specific character of the natural order is constrained by, but not reducible to, the structural conditions. If the modal-collapse objection succeeds, one of two things goes wrong: either the distinction between □◇C and □C dissolves (collapsing the stage into the play), or the grounding relation between structure and specifics is productive (collapsing the contingent specifics into the necessary structure). Both collapses entail Spinozism. The argument would have generated, by a different line, the very view Hume thought Spinoza's necessitarianism reduced to absurdity.

A clarification before the moves. The objection is not that contingency is difficult to square with the argument: it is that contingency is incompatible with it. Three forms of the move press that incompatibility at three resolutions: the deterministic version, the Leibnizian best-of-all-worlds version, and the Spinozan propagation version. The space they cover is the space in which modal collapse could be forced. Each misreads what the argument establishes and misreads what grounding does.

*First.* The van-Inwagen-style propagation move presses the deterministic version. Necessary laws plus necessary initial conditions yield necessary outcomes. If T, S, and Φ are necessary, and the laws of physics follow from the structural roles, the laws are necessary too. Necessary laws plus a fixed past fix the future, so every event is necessary. The Consequence Argument delivers the collapse.

The Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6) draws a line the objection ignores. What the argument establishes is □◇C (the *possibility* of change is necessary), not □C (change occurs necessarily). Structural necessity fixes what is structurally possible, not which possibilities are actualized. A necessary stage does not script the contingent play. The necessity of T, S, and Φ constrains the *type* of physical law (any law must be expressible as a structural relation among the roles), but it does not fix the specific content. Which symmetry groups govern, which constants obtain, which particles compose the physical domain: these are contingent facts within the necessary architecture. Quantum theory supplies interpretations on which token history is genuinely open, but deterministic interpretations remain live. The modal-collapse reply does not depend on settling that dispute: the structural roles do not by themselves fix laws, initial conditions, or outcomes, so modal collapse does not follow from their necessity alone. The Consequence Argument targets determinism. The present account is not committed to determinism.

*Second.* The Leibnizian best-possible-world version goes deeper. A necessary, perfectly good ground must produce the best possible outcome. If the structure is necessary and it generates a universe, that universe must be the best possible one. Anything less contradicts the ground's perfection. So the specific universe is necessary after all. Modal collapse returns through the back door.

The Leibnizian move presupposes a necessary evaluative subject: something that ranks possible universes and selects the best. The present account posits no such subject. T, S, and Φ are structural roles, not agents. They permit contingency; they do not rank it. The Leibnizian version gets traction against classical theism, where a necessary perfect Being must choose the best; it loses traction against a structural account with no such Being to rank outcomes. An impersonal version of the same demand fares no better. Axiarchism (Leslie, *Value and Existence* [-@leslie1979]) drops the chooser and grounds the demand in value itself: the good, on this view, tends toward its own actuality with no one selecting it. But a value that actualizes itself still actualizes some determinate configuration rather than the field of alternatives it leaves unactualized, and picking one over the rest is exactly the ranking operation the reply above blocks, run without an agent to perform it; value monism inherits the subject's job without inheriting a subject to do it. Structure permits contingency; it does not rank it, personally or impersonally. Sharper still: the Leibnizian objection, applied to classical theism, generates exactly the collapse the theist wanted to avoid. If the Maximally Great Being is necessarily perfect and necessarily creates the best, the MGB's freedom collapses into predetermined output. The objection is a better argument against classical theism than against the present account.

*Third.* The Spinozan propagation version goes severest. Necessity propagates through grounding relations. If the ground is necessary and the relation is grounding, the grounded is necessary. A necessary structural base cannot ground contingent content, because grounding transmits modal status. The argument has smuggled in contingency it has no right to.

::: {.lemma}
**Constitutive Grounding Non-Propagation** · **L9** · *Lemma toward Modal Collapse Resistance*

Two relations must be kept apart. □(T∧S∧Φ) and □◇C are not ground and grounded but one fact under two readings: by the Modal Identity, the necessity of the structural conditions just is the necessary possibility of change read modally, so □◇C carries its necessity by identity, not by transmission across a grounding relation. The structural conditions also ground the particular changes, but only in part: to be a change at all is to instantiate T, S, and Φ, so the roles enter every change as a necessary structural constituent, while what makes a given change occur rather than another, its initial conditions, its open quantum outcome ([§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7)), lies outside them. The necessity of the conditions is compatible with the contingency of what is conditioned. □(T∧S∧Φ) ⊢ □◇C, not □C. (Modal Identity: [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6))


:::

Spinozan propagation holds only if T, S, and Φ are the *full* ground of each particular change: only if fixing the structural conditions fixes which changes occur. They are not. The roles ground the *possibility* of change and enter each actual change as a necessary structural constituent, but they are never the whole of what grounds a given change: which change occurs turns on contingent specifics (initial conditions, the open quantum outcome of [§7.7](nature-alone.html#sec-7-7)) that the roles leave undetermined. Grant even the strongest grounding-necessitarian principle, that a full ground necessitates what it grounds; a merely partial ground does not, and T, S, and Φ are at most a partial, structural ground of any particular change. That T, S, and Φ are necessary entails any actual change instantiates them; it does not entail any particular change had to occur.

A kindred move presses through mereology. Schaffer's [-@schaffer2010] priority monism holds that the cosmos is the fundamental object and all its parts derive from it by ontological grounding. If grounding transmits necessity, every part is necessary. The reply is the same in mereological vocabulary. Priority monism by itself does not decide whether the cosmos fully or only partly grounds each configuration of its parts. Blocking collapse requires the additional thesis that the necessary structural base underdetermines those configurations; it cannot be read off monism alone. Priority monism does not generate modal collapse once the partial/full ground distinction is drawn.

The Lewisian plurality, which proposes a different reduction of modality, is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). Williamson's necessitism, which gives the necessity claim its formal vocabulary, is [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6). Sider's structuralism, which deflates the necessity claim rather than embracing it, is [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7). The Whiteheadian process alternative, which relocates Substance into verb form, is [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8). The simultaneous-causation response, which grounds an atemporal production of the world, is [§5.1.3](rival-ultimates.html#sec-5-1-3).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms misreads what the argument establishes and what grounding does. The Consequence Argument targets determinism, which the present account is not committed to: □◇C fixes what is structurally possible, not which possibilities are actualized, and the structural roles do not by themselves fix laws, initial conditions, or outcomes, whichever quantum interpretation obtains. The Leibnizian best-world version presupposes a necessary evaluative subject the present account does not posit, and is, in fact, a sharper argument against classical theism than against the present account. Spinozan propagation holds only if T, S, and Φ fully ground each particular change rather than partly. The roles ground the possibility of change and enter each actual change as a necessary constituent, but the contingent specifics that fix which change occurs lie outside them, so a merely partial ground does not propagate modal status in the Spinozan sense.

Spinoza wrote the *Ethics* *more geometrico* (Latin: "in the geometrical manner", his method of presenting metaphysics in the form of definitions, axioms, and propositions). The necessitarian conclusion he reached (God is nature, nature is necessary, every mode follows with the force of geometrical demonstration) has haunted rationalist metaphysics ever since. Most of his successors tried to restore contingency by loosening the grounding relation between substance and mode. The structural account restores it by a different line: by clarifying what was grounded in the first place. T, S, and Φ ground the *possibility* of change, not the necessity of any particular change. The stage may be necessary without the argument thereby making every detail of the play necessary. Spinoza saw what happens if the necessary base fully grounds its modes, so that necessity transmits unrestricted; he saw correctly. The mistake was not in following the logic. It was in assuming the base must be the full ground of what follows from it.

Necessity at the base permits contingency at the leaves.

### 4.4.10 Gasking's Parody of the Ontological Argument {#sec-4-4-10}

Gaunilo, a Benedictine monk of Marmoutiers, replied to Anselm's *Proslogion* in the late eleventh century: the ontological argument's form, if sound, would prove the existence of a perfect lost island (an island than which no more perfect could be conceived), and since no such island exists, the argument's form cannot be sound. His parody was the first great demonstration that an argumentative form can be tested by seeing what else the form delivers. Nine centuries later, Douglas Gasking extended the tradition in a manuscript circulated in the late 1970s and published after his death: the greatest conceivable achievement, he argued, would be creating the universe while not existing, since creation from nothing without resources or powers is a greater feat than creation by an omnipotent being. If maximal greatness entails necessary existence in the Anselmian tradition, parody-greatness entails necessary non-existence. The parody is deliberately absurd. Its point is methodological: an argument whose form licenses its own *reductio* never really licenses its conclusion.

Gaunilo's *Pro Insipiente* (c. 1078) set the template. Gasking's "Proof of the Non-Existence of God" (commonly cited 1978; published posthumously in *Language, Logic and Causation*, 1996) modernized it. Mackie (*The Miracle of Theism*, 1982) and Oppy (*Ontological Arguments and Belief in God*, 1995; *Arguing About Gods*, 2006) developed the parody tradition into a general diagnostic: an argumentative form that delivers one impressive conclusion can usually be adapted to deliver its opposite, revealing that the form's apparent productivity rests on hidden premises about greatness, predication, or modal reasoning. Plantinga (*God, Freedom, and Evil*, 1974a) responded that the modal ontological argument survives parody because the parody premises are not genuinely possibly instantiated in the way the original premises are. Grim ("There Is No Set of All Truths," 1984) opened a different parody-adjacent front via Cantorian diagonalization (the powerset technique that, given any proposed totality, generates an element outside it) against omniscience. Adams ("Flavors, Colors, and God," 1987) and van Inwagen ("Ontological Arguments," 1977) canvassed the conditions under which a parody does and does not mirror its target. The tradition's shared assumption is that arguments with modal conclusions are particularly susceptible to parody because modal space is abundant enough to contain mirror-image premises the original argument cannot exclude.

Brought to bear on the present argument, the parody tradition tests whether □(T∧S∧Φ) (the necessity of Time, Space, and Substance together) is earned by content or by form. If the argument's machinery, the Modal Identity from [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6), S5 / Necessary Possibility from [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1) (the modal-logic system in which whatever is necessary or possible at any world is necessary or possible at every world), and the ∅ result from [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7) (the null state, the absolute absence of being), could be redeployed to produce inverted or absurd conclusions, the machinery is suspect. A parody that successfully mirrored the argument's form would deliver a structural result the argument cannot accept, revealing the necessity claim rests on hidden premises rather than on the form the argument presents. The question is whether the formal structure is neutral between its intended conclusion and a parody-conclusion, or whether the content of T, S, and Φ does work the form alone cannot carry.

A clarification before the moves. The argument's conclusion is not 'T, S, and Φ are great and therefore necessary.' It is 'T, S, and Φ are the structural requirements of any change, any extension, any persistence, and therefore no medium can be without them.' The content is functional, not evaluative. A parody that substitutes an evaluatively defined alternative ('maximal Non-Being,' 'greatest achievement of non-existence') is not running the argument's form with new content. It is running a different form entirely, one the present argument never uses. Three forms of the parody; each breaks at a point where the present argument differs from the Anselmian one.

*First.* The inversion move runs Gasking's exact trick on the present argument. The greatest conceivable being, the objector presses, is one whose existence is not presupposed by the categories of existence: a being that grounds the structure without instantiating it. This is the exact move classical theists make for God. By parallel reasoning, there must be a maximally great Non-Being that grounds the structure while instantiating no structural role. If the ontological argument's form is legitimate, the parody's form is equally legitimate.

The parody fails at the point the original argument is made. Gasking's greatest-achievement move trades on a category confusion the structural account explicitly rejects. Greatness in the ontological tradition is defined by impressiveness — by what it would be more impressive for a being to be. The structural argument does not work with this concept. It works with Functional Potency: the capacity to act, cause, and affect. Non-existence possesses zero potency. A non-existent cause cannot produce a manifest effect. 'Necessary Non-Existence' is not a form of greatness: it *is* the ultimate state of causal inertness, which *is* what ∅ names. The structural roles possess the full functional architecture that makes causal efficacy possible at all. The parody inverts the argument's definition of greatness and then treats the inversion as a *reductio*. The inverted definition, not the argument, generates the absurdity. Swap 'impressiveness' for 'potency' and the parody cannot even begin: a non-existent ground is not more potent than a structural one. It is maximally impotent.

*Second.* The S5 symmetry move targets the logical machinery directly. The argument moves from ◇C to □◇C via S5, applied to change-permission. By parallel reasoning, ¬◇C should yield □¬◇C: the necessary impossibility of change. If the logical machinery licenses the first move, it licenses the second. But the second contradicts the first. The S5 system powers both, so the argument's conclusion rests on a prior decision about which modal premise to start with.

The parallel fails because the two premises are not symmetric. ◇C (change is possible) is defended by the Cartesian certainty that change is occurring in the very act of doubt and the subsequent derivation that change requires T, S, and Φ. ¬◇C (change is impossible) has no equivalent step. There is no Cartesian certainty that change is impossible, because the certainty of doubting would itself refute the certainty of impossibility. The parody's starting premise conflicts with the book's Cartesian datum if doubting is correctly analyzed as change. That is a substantive premise about the act, not an analytic truth and not yet a freestanding cross-world proof. S5 preserves whichever modal premise is supplied; it does not establish the asymmetry by itself. The machinery is the same. The inputs are not. This is where the present reply converges with Plantinga's (1974a): a modal argument survives parody only when the parody's mirror premise is not genuinely possibly instantiated. On the book's act analysis, ¬◇C is dialectically unstable because asserting or considering it occurs through an ordered cognitive performance. The force of that reply remains act-side and depends on the argument connecting the performance to real change.

*Third.* Oppy's general indictment presses the crispest version. Any argument attempting to derive substantive ontological conclusions from conceptual premises is suspect in principle, because conception does not deliver existence. The structural argument is such an argument: it conceives change and derives structural necessity. The parody argues, equally validly, that it conceives non-existence and derives structural absence. Both conclusions rest on the same epistemic error: confusing what can be coherently thought with what must ontologically obtain.

The argument does not derive existence from conception. It derives structural conditions from the content of any possible thought. The Cartesian datum (that thought is occurring) is not a conceptual premise but a phenomenally given fact. The subsequent derivation proceeds from what any thought-event structurally requires, not from the conceptual content of any particular thought. Oppy's indictment applies to arguments of the form 'there is a concept of X; therefore X exists.' The argument has a different form: 'there is a phenomenally given fact F; F requires structural conditions T, S, Φ; therefore T, S, Φ obtain.' The parody cannot be reformulated in the same way because there is no phenomenally given fact of non-existence: non-existence is not a fact that can be phenomenally given, because phenomenal givenness requires the very structural conditions non-existence is defined as lacking. The parody can be conceived. It cannot be given. Oppy's indictment targets the wrong kind of argument.

A kindred move drops Gasking's inversion for Grim's Cantorian diagonalization. In its original form (Grim 1984) the target is omniscience: if there is a set of all truths, the powerset argument generates a truth outside it, so the set (and the omniscience that would survey it) is incoherent.

*The Incomplete Universe* (Grim 1991) presses the result much harder, generalizing it past omniscience to any totality of facts: if a world is conceived as a maximal consistent collection of truths, the same diagonalization shows there is no such collection, and the universe considered as a totality of facts is essentially open and incomplete.

This is the more aggressive form, and it bears on the present argument more directly than the omniscience version, since the exhaustion claim can look like just such a totality. Applied here rather than to theism, the Grim-style move argues: if T, S, and Φ exhaust necessary existence, there is a fact about that exhaustion standing outside the structure, and the exhaustion claim is incoherent.

The reply follows the same path against both forms. Facts about exhaustion are statements about the structural roles, made by reasoners instantiating the roles. The meta-fact is not outside the structure; it is within the structure, at a higher level of description. What the diagonalization defeats is the pretension of a totality of *all truths* surveyed from beyond the domain it totalizes; the exhaustion claim is not that. It is the narrower claim that exactly three structural conditions are necessary for any being, and its own meta-statements are themselves further instances of T, S, and Φ at work, not truths inspecting the structure from outside. The account never asserts a closed totality of facts; it asserts the necessity of the conditions under which any fact is stated at all.

The Lewisian modal realism the parody sometimes implicates is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). The modal-collapse worry that the necessity claim generates absurd consequences is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9). Williamson's necessitism, which embraces necessity at the type level rather than rejecting it, is [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6). Sider's structuralism, which deflates rather than embraces necessity, is [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7). The Whiteheadian process alternative is [§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8). Modal fictionalism's attempt to deflate the whole apparatus is [§4.4.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-4). The chained-origin counterexamples, which press the modal logic itself rather than the argument's form, are [§4.4.11](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-11).

*What converges.* Each of the three parodies breaks at a point where the present argument differs from the Anselmian one. Gasking's inversion trades on a category confusion the structural account rejects: greatness on the present view is Functional Potency rather than impressiveness, and necessary non-existence is maximal impotence rather than maximal greatness. The S5 symmetry move fails because the two premises are not symmetric: ◇C is defended by a Cartesian certainty that change is occurring, and ¬◇C is dialectically unstable because asserting or considering it occurs through an ordered cognitive performance. Oppy's indictment targets arguments that move from concept to existence; the present argument moves from a phenomenally given fact of change to its structural conditions, and the parody cannot be reformulated in the same way because non-existence cannot be phenomenally given.

Gaunilo's island vanishes beneath a wave the moment it is conceived: not because islands cannot be perfect, but because an argument that proves an island by its mere conceivability has confused what is contained in a concept with what is contained in the world. Gasking's non-existent creator performs an identical trick, translated into the idiom of twentieth-century analytic theism. The argument survives both because it never performs the trick either parody is designed to expose. It does not move from the concept of change to the existence of structure. It moves from the phenomenal fact of change — the thinking now going on — to the structural conditions that make the thinking possible. Constructing the parody supplies an actual structured performance and therefore rebuts a denial aimed at the performance itself. It does not alone establish that every possible world realizes the same loaded types; that broader result depends on the separate modal and role-to-type arguments.

### 4.4.11 Chisholm’s Paradox: Chained Origins {#sec-4-4-11}

Roderick Chisholm asked a question in 1967 about Adam and Noah (Chisholm 1967). Adam lived 930 years, Noah 950. Surely Adam could have lived a year longer, and Noah a year less: nothing in either man's essence hangs on a single year. Grant the concession once and a world opens in which Adam lives 931 and Noah 949. Grant it again from there, and again, and the two lifespans trade places entirely — a world in which the man who lives 950 years is Adam and the man who lives 930 is Noah, which is to say a world in which each is the other. Every step was innocent. The destination is not. Chisholm's Paradox is the ancestor of every later argument that possibility is *chained*: that what is possible depends on where the question is asked from, and that iterating small admissible variations carries one somewhere no single leap could have reached.

Hugh Chandler (1976) ran the structure on artifacts rather than patriarchs, and aimed it at exactly the machinery this book uses — his paper is titled "Plantinga and the Contingently Possible," and the modal apparatus of Plantinga (1974b) turns on the same transfer principle the present argument turns on. A bicycle assembled from a given set of parts could have been assembled with one part swapped; from *that* world, another swap is admissible; and the chain terminates in an assembly too distant from the original to have been possible for the original bicycle. Nathan Salmon developed the sharpest version on Kripke's table: the table made from a given hunk of wood H could have been made from the slightly different hunk H′, and a table made from H′ could have been made from H″ — which was not possible for the original table (N. Salmon 1981, 1989; the example descends from Kripke 1980). Salmon then drew the conclusion the others resisted. Metaphysical accessibility — the relation a world bears to those worlds that count as possible *relative to it* — is not transitive; so S4, the axiom licensing the collapse of a two-step modal chain into a single step, fails for the metaphysical operator, and the S5 transfer fails with it. Graeme Forbes answered by keeping the logic and locating the trouble in vagueness, first through degree-theoretic treatments and then through counterpart-theoretic ones (Forbes 1984, 1985). Lewis answered through the inconstancy of counterpart relations: on counterpart theory, no individual literally exists in more than one world, and its modal properties are read off the individuals elsewhere that most resemble it — and which resemblance relation is in play shifts with context (Lewis 1968, 1986). Timothy Williamson supplies the epistemicist option, on which such a series has a sharp cutoff that is unknowable rather than absent (Williamson 1994). Behind all of them stands Kripke's origin essentialism, the thesis that a thing could not have come from a wholly different origin and still be that thing (Kripke 1980). The dispute is sixty years old and has produced no settled verdict.

Brought to bear on the present argument, the objection targets the logic directly rather than the ontology, which makes it more dangerous than most of this section's entries. Necessary Possibility is established at [§2.1.10](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-10): whatever is possible, its possibility is necessary (◇P → □◇P), with the bilateral companion that whatever is impossible, its impossibility is necessary (¬◇P → □¬◇P). It is packaged into S5 at [§2.1.4](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-4); the move from the actuality of change to its necessary possibility at [§2.3](the-argument.html#sec-2-3) runs on it, and so does the Modal Identity of [§2.6.6](the-argument.html#sec-2-6-6). If possibility is chained, the transfer is unsound, and no amount of care about T, S, and Φ — Temporality, Spatiality, and Physicality, the three structural Conditions — repairs it. The objector here concedes the framework, concedes possible-worlds semantics, concedes origin essentialism, and produces cases. That is the hardest kind of objection to answer, because there is nothing exotic to reject.

A clarification before the moves, and a distinction the replies turn on. The argument's ◇ means *real possibility*: membership in one fixed global domain W, the complete range of ways Reality permits ([§1.2.1](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-1), [§2.1](the-argument.html#sec-2-1)). And two readings of any modal claim about a particular thing have to be kept apart. A *de dicto* claim is about a proposition — "it is possible that some table was made from different wood." A *de re* claim is about a thing — "this table is such that it possibly was made from different wood." The first says something about what the range of possibilities contains; the second says something about what a particular object could have survived. Three forms of the objection press at three different resolutions: the chained-origin move as Chisholm and Chandler state it, Salmon's principled rejection of transitivity, and the counterpart-theoretic inconstancy version. Each reply below diagnoses the cases rather than denying them, which is the more demanding standard: the intuitions driving the series are genuine, and an account that merely contradicted them would have explained nothing.

*First.* The chained-origin move holds that the series of small variations is individually innocent and jointly unacceptable, so possibility must be relative to a starting point. Each link is possible relative to its predecessor; the endpoint is not possible relative to the origin; therefore what is possible varies with where the question is asked.

The reply begins by separating the two readings, because on one of them there is no case at all. Read *de dicto*, "a table made from slightly different wood" is among the least exotic possibilities ever entertained in philosophy: furniture workshops witness it by the thousand daily. Every such table is already among the ways Reality permits, and no act of carpentry puts it there — the carpenter never once consults the accessibility relation. The cases become cases only on the *de re* reading: could *this very table* have originated in H″ and still be *it*? That is a question about how much origin-swapping identity tolerates. It is a substantive and interesting question. It is not a question the transfer principle was ever answering, because the transfer ranges over the modal status of propositions and not over the persistence of a token individual across worlds. The distinction is the same one [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1) draws against counterpart theory, running in the other direction: what the argument needs across worlds is instantiation of a structural role, never a numerically identical token recurring, and the chained-origin cases press exclusively on tokens.

*Second.* Salmon's version blocks that reply by refusing the relabeling. His ◇, he insists, is the metaphysician's own unrelativized operator and not a disguised accessibility relation; the cases show that operator to be non-transitive, and calling the variation "accessibility" redescribes the problem rather than answering it.

The reply takes the global question directly. Ask of the far link: is a table made from H″ among the ways Reality permits, or not? The question admits one answer. If yes, it was in W all along, and what varied along the chain was never membership but tolerable distance from a shifting anchor — a fact about the essentialist premise, not about the logic. If no, then no sequence of intermediate worlds puts it there, since traversing intermediates is not a way of enlarging the range. Either way, nothing has entered or left the domain.

The chain also cannot travel without paying. To move from H to H′ to H″, the argument must concede at every link that the intermediate origin is possible; that concession is what licenses the step. But a conceded possibility, run through the transfer, is a necessary possibility: each step certifies its own destination as a permanent member of the domain. Meanwhile no step removes anything, because unreachability is not eviction — that an origin cannot be reached from a given anchor is silent on whether it is in the range at all. So the chain deposits members and withdraws none. Pursued to its end, the argument has populated the global domain it set out to fragment, and the only thing still varying at the far link is the *de re* label: which of those necessarily possible tables counts as *this* one.

One further pressure, the difference-maker point of [§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5). If "possible at one world, impossible at another" states a fact about a single unrelativized operator, then something must make the difference between the two worlds. That something would have to concern what possibility itself answers to, and a fact of that kind is arrangement-independent and structural — which is precisely the cross-world stability the objection was contesting. The variation hypothesis consumes the resource it needs.

The candor the rest of this chapter keeps is owed here too. Salmon can plant on the disputed point and hold that the unrelativized operator simply is non-transitive, taking the cases as primitive data about it rather than as evidence to be diagnosed. Against a philosopher who does that, none of the above is a formal refutation, because its load-bearing premise is the fixed-domain reading he declines. What the reply secures is narrower and still worth having: the objection cannot be run without conceding, link by link, the very possibilities whose global standing is at issue, and the position it defends turns out to be a position about a relation between worlds rather than about the range those worlds jointly compose.

*Third.* The counterpart-theoretic version drops non-transitivity in favor of inconstancy. On Lewis's treatment, a *de re* modal claim about the table is made true by what happens to the table's counterparts — the objects in other worlds that resemble it most in whatever respects the conversation is weighting. Weight origin heavily and the H″-table is no counterpart of this table; weight function or appearance instead and it is. So "possibly made from H″" comes out true in one conversation and false in another, and any transfer principle stated over such claims inherits the instability.

The reply is that inconstancy of this kind is variation in representation, not variation in the domain. What shifts with context is which similarity respects a *de re* predication tracks — a fact about the semantics of counterpart talk. Nothing shifts in which worlds are among the ways Reality permits, and the whole plurality remains available to every context that draws on it. The inconstancy defense is also an awkward ally for the objector, since it concedes that the chained-origin data are produced by a context-sensitive representational device rather than discovered in the logic of possibility. A phenomenon that varies with conversational salience is not the sort of thing a modal axiom is answerable to.

A kindred move presses the vagueness directly rather than through counterpart semantics, and it is the most honest form of the objection. Each origin-swap is tolerable, the endpoints are not, and no step is the step at which identity lapses. That is a sorites — a chain of individually harmless steps whose endpoints differ in a way no single step seems to introduce, as in the grain-by-grain removal that turns a heap into a non-heap — run on essence rather than on heaps. Forbes proposes degrees of counterpart-hood; supervaluationism proposes that the claim be assessed on every admissible way of sharpening the vague predicate; Williamson's epistemicism proposes a sharp cutoff that no one is in a position to locate. The present account takes no stand among the three, and does not need to: sorites series do not show that the predicates involved are world-relative. They show that the predicates are *tolerant* — that they survive small changes in their subject matter. Treating tolerance as evidence against a modal transfer principle mislocates the finding, though it is an interesting mislocation, and one worth the sixty years it has occupied. What the counterexamples establish is that *de re* origin essentialism gradates. Reading them as a refutation of the transfer requires one additional step: letting ◇ mean "reachable from the world of evaluation." That is a legitimate operator with a genuinely non-S5 logic, and it is not the operator in which the conclusions of metaphysics are stated. When Salmon writes that the far origin was not possible for the table *originally*, that adverb is carrying the argument, and it is a word about starting points.

The status reading that makes this diagnosis available is fixed at [§1.2.6](groundwork.html#sec-1-2-6) and [§2.1.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-7): the claim is not that a necessity operator scopes over a possibility operator by climbing an accessibility relation, but that whatever is possible has its possibility as a settled status. The Bottleneck at [§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5) marks the single point at which a rival can disagree. Lewis's concrete plurality, whose counterpart theory supplies the third move's machinery, is [§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1). Williamson's necessitism is [§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6). Sider's structuralism is [§4.4.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-7). The modal-collapse worry is [§4.4.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-9). Gasking's parody, which tests the argument's form rather than its logic, is [§4.4.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-10).

*What converges.* Each of the three forms turns on a relation between worlds rather than on the range the worlds compose. The chained-origin move is a case only on the *de re* reading, and the transfer never ranged over token identity. Salmon's principled version asks a global question that admits one answer either way, and cannot advance its chain without certifying, at every link, a permanent member of the domain it means to fragment. The counterpart-theoretic version relocates the variation into context-sensitive representation, where it is no longer the sort of fact a modal axiom answers to. Underneath all three is a sorites on essence, and tolerance is not world-relativity.

Chisholm's Adam and Noah do not trade places. What the series shows is that "same man" bears a great deal of counterfactual stretching without anyone being able to say where it snaps, which is a fact about the elasticity of identity under supposition and not a discovery about the range of ways Reality permits. The lifespans were always in that range. The question the chain makes vivid is only ever which of them we are still entitled to call Adam's.

## 4.5 What the Rivals Carried {#sec-4-5}

This is the chapter's reckoning. The engagements do not all end with one verdict. Some rivals are internally incoherent on the book's analysis. Some realize the same structural roles under another vocabulary. Some are compatible specifications of those roles. Some remain coherent only by taking on explanatory cost. Some do not contest the ground at all but the machinery used to reach it. Some identify a question the chapter does not settle. And one is no rival at all: it converges on the same modal floor and stops short of the structural conclusion. Keeping these verdicts distinct is part of the argument's discipline.

### Verdicts by rival type

#### 1. Denial attempts

**Null-state and domain-external absence.** The proposal that nothing at all obtains dissolves rather than supplies a rival state: ∅ is not a world with unusual contents but the failure of the conditions under which a state or world could be specified ([§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7)). This is an **incoherence verdict**.

**Onset from absence.** A first temporal order, first placement, or first causal production presupposes the domain it claims to originate ([§2.1.5](the-argument.html#sec-2-1-5)). This is also an **incoherence verdict**, but it is limited to onset from domain-external absence. It does not by itself prove that every possible world realizes the full Conditions.

**Humean and deflationary accounts.** Humean regularity, Best-System accounts, conventionalism, and modal deflation can preserve a real manifold, patterns, or local reachability. Where they do, they retain directed order, differentiation, or bearing at least at role-resolution. Their strongest forms are therefore ordinarily **relocation verdicts**, not contradictions. They remain live where they reject the book's type-level or necessity claims ([§4.1.4](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-4)).

**Strict temporal unreality.** Two theses must be kept apart here. A thesis denying any ordering whatever does defeat the possibility of a world-state, but it does so by collapsing into the null-state case already treated above, not by any independent result about time. McTaggart's own strict-unreality reading is weaker, and its verdict is weaker to match: the retorsion from 1908 diagnoses the act side, since the paper's writing, its publication, and its century of reception deploy succession, distinction, and persistence in the course of denying them, but the object side is left untested, because an error theorist may still propose a non-temporal ground of the apparent order. The verdict is therefore **act-side incoherence with the object-side error theory open**, not incoherence outright — the shape of [§3.3.3](convergence.html#sec-3-3-3) rather than of [§2.7](the-argument.html#sec-2-7). B-theory is neither thesis: it retains a temporal ordering and receives a different verdict below ([§4.2.5](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-5)).

#### 2. Priority attempts

**Changeless and non-temporal grounds.** A ground that claims to produce, sustain, or answer to the changing order must stand in some real dependence relation to it. The chapter establishes that this relation cannot be wholly structureless. The full theological assessment of divine eternity, simplicity, and simultaneity belongs to Chapter 5. The verdict here is **structural burden plus deferred theological engagement**, not a complete refutation of every classical-theist account ([§4.2.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-1)).

**Source-of-possibility accounts.** No candidate whose own status is stated in modal terms can ground the global modal domain it already inhabits. A committed essence-prior or transcendence theorist may nevertheless posit a primitive external ground. The verdict is **internal modal-ground exclusion and an open grounding gloss**, not universal contradiction ([§4.1.10](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-10)).

**Dispositionalism about modality.** The nearest rival and the closest ally: like the present account, it locates modality in reality rather than in a plurality of concrete worlds, and its objections to Lewis are largely the book's own. It grounds possibility in the powers of actual objects, and powers are borne. The global case has no bearer, and iterating potentiality does not supply one, since the possibility that there be bearers presupposes a bearer. The verdict is **shared diagnosis of the rivals, with grounding that reaches every case but the one at issue** ([§4.1.12](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-1-12)).

**Lewisian plurality.** Concrete Lewisian worlds must meet concrete spatiotemporal burdens internally. Their numerical plurality, if treated as primitive, remains a coherent but costly posit rather than a contradiction. The verdict is **structured realization plus explanatory cost** ([§4.4.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-1)).

**Necessitism.** Fixed domains of individuals are compatible with the fixed global domain of real possibilities. Necessitism neither refutes the structural conclusion nor automatically supplies its metaphysical content. The verdict is **formal compatibility with a competing ontological reading** ([§4.4.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-6)).

#### 3. Insufficiency attempts

**B-theory and block universe.** The block realizes temporal ordering, differentiation, and cross-time structure. It is compatible with the role-level framework while remaining in dispute over objective passage. The verdict is **compatibility at role-resolution, open disagreement about the passage feature** ([§4.2.6](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-2-6)).

**Whiteheadian process.** Process ontology captures cross-transition efficacy without an enduring subject. It therefore realizes the bearer-role while disputing persistent causal being as a type. The verdict is **relocation at role-resolution, type-level dispute deferred** ([§4.4.8](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-4-8)).

**Mathematical Universe Hypothesis and structural realism.** Pure mathematical structures and abstract relational fabrics need not instantiate temporal, spatial, and causal types merely by being abstract structures. When proposed as physical reality, observer-hosting reality, or a genuine change-realizer, they incur the richer realizer burden. The verdict is **conditional compatibility: abstract structures remain live, physical-realizer identity claims inherit structural requirements** ([§4.3.7](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-7), [§4.3.9](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-9)).

**Hard problem of consciousness.** Experience does not establish a structureless domain. Even irreducible qualitative features would be features of a structured ground. Whether phenomenal interiority is identical with structural self-modeling remains a constructive question for later chapters. The verdict is **no escape from structure, positive explanatory seam left open** ([§4.3.1](metaphysical-rivals.html#sec-4-3-1)).

#### 4. Apparatus attempts

A fourth kind of objection leaves the ground alone and goes after the machinery. It offers no rival world, no rival source, and no rival realizer; it argues that the semantics or the epistemology the argument runs on will not bear the weight placed on it. These verdicts are narrower than the others, and two of them cost the book something.

**Impossible worlds and relative modality.** Admitting impossible worlds multiplies representations rather than genuine alternatives, and representations are themselves structured.
